parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of each part: (i) cornea (ii) retina (iii) optic nerve.
parts.answer: (i) refracts / bends light (ii) contains light receptors that change light into impulses (iii) carries impulses to the brain

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why no image is seen if light falls on the blind spot.
parts.answer: There are no light receptors there (it is where the optic nerve leaves the eye).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student looks up from her book to watch a bird far away. What happens in her eyes?
A ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken, lens becomes fatter
B ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments become tight, lens becomes thinner
C ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments slacken, lens becomes thinner
D ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments become tight, lens becomes fatter
parts.answer: B ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments become tight, lens becomes thinner
parts.working: For a distant object the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight and the lens is pulled thinner, so light is refracted less. A is the change for a near object.

practice.stem: Ali walks out of a dark cinema into bright midday sunshine in Islamabad. His pupils quickly become smaller.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in the iris that make the pupil smaller.
parts.answer: The circular muscles contract; the radial muscles relax.
parts.working: B1 circular contract; B1 radial relax

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this response is useful.
parts.answer: Less light enters, protecting the retina from damage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of response this is and give one feature of it.
parts.answer: A reflex action; it is automatic / involuntary / rapid / does not need conscious thought.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term sense organ.
parts.answer: A group of receptor cells that respond to a specific stimulus (e.g. light, sound, touch, temperature, chemicals).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Copy and complete: Stimulus | sense organ
light | ?
sound | ?
chemicals in food | ?
temperature change | ?
parts.answer: eye; ear; tongue (and nose); skin
parts.working: B2 all four; B1 two or three

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the eye sends information to the brain.
parts.answer: Light receptors in the retina are stimulated and produce electrical impulses; impulses travel along the optic nerve (sensory neurones) to the brain.
parts.working: B1 receptors in retina stimulated / impulses; B1 along optic nerve

practice.stem: A pharmacist looks at a distant shelf and then reads the small print on a medicine label held 25 cm from her eyes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in the eye that allow the label to be seen clearly.
parts.answer: Ciliary muscles contract; suspensory ligaments slacken / become loose; lens becomes thicker / more convex (and refracts light more).

parts.label: b
parts.text: As people age, the lens becomes less elastic. Suggest why older people often find it difficult to read small print but can still see distant objects clearly.
parts.answer: The lens cannot become fat / round enough on its own when the ligaments slacken; so light from near objects is not focused on the retina, whereas the thin lens shape for distant vision is still achieved.
parts.working: B1 lens cannot become thicker / more convex; B1 near image not focused on retina

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What happens in the skin of a person who is too hot?
A arterioles near the skin surface constrict
B sweat production decreases
C arterioles near the skin surface dilate
D skin muscles shiver
parts.answer: C arterioles near the skin surface dilate
parts.working: Vasodilation of arterioles supplying skin capillaries sends more blood near the surface, so more heat is lost by radiation. A (vasoconstriction) happens when the body is too cold.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the normal core body temperature of a human (the set point).
parts.answer: About 37 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the term homeostasis.
parts.answer: Maintaining a constant internal environment; within set limits.
parts.working: B1 constant internal environment / conditions; B1 within narrow limits / around a set point

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the part of the body that monitors blood temperature.
parts.answer: The brain (hypothalamus).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how sweating helps to cool the body.
parts.answer: Water in sweat evaporates from the skin surface; evaporation uses heat energy from the skin, cooling it.
parts.working: B1 evaporation of sweat; B1 takes heat (energy) from the body / skin

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why sweating cools the body less effectively on a hot, humid day in Lahore during the monsoon.
parts.answer: Air already has a high water vapour content, so sweat evaporates more slowly; less heat is removed.
parts.working: B1 less evaporation; B1 less heat lost

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a person sweating heavily for a long time should drink water with a little salt.
parts.answer: Sweat contains water and salts, which must be replaced.

practice.stem:
A cricketer's core temperature was measured every 10 minutes during a 30-minute run and the rest afterwards.
time / min | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60
temperature / °C | 37.0 | 37.2 | 37.6 | 38.1 | 37.9 | 37.4 | 37.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the maximum rise in core temperature above the starting value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two changes in the skin that would have brought the temperature back down after 30 minutes.
parts.answer: Vasodilation of arterioles near skin surface (skin looks flushed); increased sweating.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the temperature rose during running.
parts.answer: Muscles respired more to release energy for contraction; respiration releases heat (as a by-product).
parts.working: B1 more respiration in muscles; B1 releases heat

practice.stem: A mountaineer on K2 is exposed to very cold wind and her core temperature begins to fall below the set point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain two ways in which the climber's body responds to reduce heat loss and increase heat production.
parts.answer: Vasoconstriction: arterioles to skin capillaries narrow, so less blood flows near the surface and less heat is lost by radiation. Shivering: rapid muscle contractions increase respiration, releasing heat. (Also: less sweating; hairs raised trap insulating air.)
parts.working: For each of two responses: B1 response, B1 explanation

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these responses are an example of negative feedback.
parts.answer: A fall in temperature below the set point is detected; responses act to bring the temperature back up towards the set point (reverse the change).
parts.working: B1 change from set point detected; B1 response reverses the change / returns to set point

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which neurone carries impulses from the central nervous system to an effector?
A sensory neurone
B relay neurone
C motor neurone
D receptor cell
parts.answer: C motor neurone
parts.working: Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands). Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put the parts of the reflex arc in the correct order: motor neurone, receptor, effector, relay neurone, sensory neurone.
parts.answer: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one pair out of place

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the receptor and the effector when a hand is pulled away from a hot pan.
parts.answer: Receptor: (heat / pain) receptors in the skin. Effector: muscle in the arm (biceps).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where relay neurones are found.
parts.answer: In the central nervous system / spinal cord.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two parts of the central nervous system.
parts.answer: Brain and spinal cord

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two differences between a voluntary action and a reflex action.
parts.answer: Voluntary: needs conscious thought / slower / involves the brain making a decision / can be learned. Reflex: automatic, fast, does not need conscious thought, same response every time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two differences

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of a reflex action and explain how it helps to protect the body.
parts.answer: Blinking when something approaches the eye — prevents damage to the eye (or withdrawing hand from a sharp pin — prevents injury).

practice.stem: Student A holds a 30 cm ruler at its top end. Student B places finger and thumb level with the 0 cm mark without touching it. A drops the ruler without warning and B catches it. The distance fallen is read where B catches it. Five trials gave: 16 cm, 14 cm, 13 cm, 11 cm, 10 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean distance the ruler fell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the trend in the results and suggest a reason for it.
parts.answer: The distance (reaction time) decreased with each trial; the student learned / anticipated the drop (practice effect).
parts.working: B1 decreasing trend; B1 learning / practice / anticipation

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why catching the ruler is not a reflex action.
parts.answer: It involves a decision by the brain / conscious thought; the response can be changed or improved by learning.
parts.working: B1 brain / conscious decision; B1 learned / not automatic

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
parts.answer: Have practice trials first / use the same hand and starting position / do more repeats and find a mean / use different students.

practice.stem: A boy walking barefoot in a field steps on a sharp acacia thorn and quickly lifts his foot.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pathway of the nerve impulse from the moment the foot touches the thorn to the leg moving.
parts.answer: Pain receptor in the skin of the foot stimulated; impulse along sensory neurone to spinal cord; passes across synapse to relay neurone in spinal cord; then to motor neurone; to leg muscles (effector), which contract and lift the foot.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four of: receptor in skin; sensory neurone; spinal cord / relay neurone; synapse(s); motor neurone; muscle contracts

parts.label: b
parts.text: The boy feels the pain slightly after his foot moves. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The reflex arc passes through the spinal cord and does not need the brain; impulses to the brain travel further / through more synapses, so awareness comes later.
parts.working: B1 reflex via spinal cord, not brain; B1 impulse to brain takes longer

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms (i) phototropism (ii) gravitropism.
parts.answer: (i) a response in which part of a plant grows towards or away from the direction of light (ii) a response in which part of a plant grows towards or away from gravity

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether each response is positive or negative: (i) a shoot growing towards light (ii) a root growing downwards (iii) a shoot growing upwards in the dark.
parts.answer: (i) positive phototropism (ii) positive gravitropism (iii) negative gravitropism

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A shoot is lit from one side only. Which statement explains why it bends towards the light?
A light destroys auxin on the lit side, so the lit side grows faster
B auxin collects on the shaded side and stimulates cell elongation there
C auxin collects on the lit side and stimulates cell division there
D auxin collects on the shaded side and stops cells growing there
parts.answer: B auxin collects on the shaded side and stimulates cell elongation there
parts.working: Auxin made in the shoot tip moves to the shaded side, where it causes cells to elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the light. A is a common misconception: light does not destroy auxin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the advantage to a seedling of its shoot growing upwards and its root growing downwards.
parts.answer: Shoot grows up towards light for photosynthesis; root grows down into soil for water / mineral ions and anchorage.
parts.working: B1 shoot – light / photosynthesis; B1 root – water / anchorage

parts.label: b
parts.text: A bean seedling is laid on its side in the dark. Describe and explain how the shoot responds, in terms of auxin.
parts.answer: Auxin collects on the lower side of the shoot; stimulates cell elongation on the lower side; so the shoot curves upwards (negative gravitropism).
parts.working: B1 auxin to lower side; B1 more elongation on lower side; B1 shoot bends upwards

practice.stem:
Three maize seedlings were placed in a box with light coming from one side only.
Seedling X: untreated — after 2 days it had bent towards the light.
Seedling Y: tip cut off — no bending and very little growth.
Seedling Z: tip covered with an aluminium foil cap — grew straight up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the result for seedling X.
parts.answer: Auxin is made in the tip; it moved to the shaded side; caused greater cell elongation on the shaded side, so the shoot bent towards the light.
parts.working: B1 auxin from tip; B1 moves to shaded side; B1 cells on shaded side elongate more

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the result for seedling Y.
parts.answer: The tip, which makes auxin (and detects light), was removed, so no auxin and no bending / growth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the result for seedling Z.
parts.answer: The foil cap stopped light reaching the tip; so auxin was not redistributed and the shoot grew straight up (evenly).
parts.working: B1 tip cannot detect light; B1 auxin evenly distributed

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how a synthetic auxin weedkiller kills broad-leaved weeds such as thistles in a wheat field.
parts.answer: It causes rapid, uncontrolled growth / elongation of the weeds; they cannot sustain this (use up food reserves), so they die.
parts.working: B1 rapid / uncontrolled growth; B1 plant dies / exhausts reserves

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the weedkiller does not kill the wheat.
parts.answer: Wheat (narrow-leaved) absorbs less / is less sensitive to the weedkiller.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one advantage of using a selective weedkiller rather than pulling out weeds by hand.
parts.answer: Quicker / cheaper for large areas / less labour.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Blood glucose concentration rises after a meal. Which response occurs?
A the pancreas releases glucagon and the liver converts glycogen to glucose
B the pancreas releases insulin and the liver converts glucose to glycogen
C the liver releases insulin and the pancreas stores glycogen
D the adrenal glands release insulin and muscles release glucose
parts.answer: B the pancreas releases insulin and the liver converts glucose to glycogen
parts.working: Insulin from the pancreas makes liver and muscle cells take up glucose and convert it to glycogen. A is the response to low blood glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the hormone that is released when blood glucose falls too low, and the organ that secretes it.
parts.answer: Glucagon; pancreas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how this hormone raises blood glucose.
parts.answer: It causes the liver to break down glycogen to glucose, which is released into the blood.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how type 1 diabetes is treated, and state one sign of the condition.
parts.answer: Treated by insulin injections (plus controlled diet / exercise and monitoring blood glucose). Sign: high blood glucose / glucose in urine / thirst / tiredness / weight loss.

practice.stem:
A healthy student drank a glucose solution after fasting. Her blood glucose concentration was measured.
time / min | 0 | 30 | 60 | 90 | 120
blood glucose / mg per 100 cm³ | 90 | 150 | 135 | 105 | 92

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in blood glucose from 0 to 30 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the concentration returned to normal by 120 minutes.
parts.answer: The rise was detected by the pancreas; it secreted insulin into the blood; insulin caused the liver / muscles to take up glucose and convert it to glycogen (and cells to respire more glucose).
parts.working: B1 pancreas detects / secretes insulin; B1 insulin travels in blood to liver; B1 glucose → glycogen

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the results would differ for a person with type 1 diabetes, and explain why.
parts.answer: Glucose would rise higher and stay high for longer; because the pancreas does not produce (enough) insulin.
parts.working: B1 higher / does not return to normal; B1 no / little insulin

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how an impulse passes across a synapse.
parts.answer: Impulse arrives at the end of the first neurone; vesicles release neurotransmitter into the gap; neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap; binds to receptor proteins on the next neurone; which starts an impulse in it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of the five points

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process by which the neurotransmitter crosses the gap.
parts.answer: Diffusion

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why can nerve impulses cross a synapse in one direction only?
A the synaptic gap is wider at one end
B neurotransmitter is released only from the first neurone and receptors are only on the second neurone
C the second neurone has no cell membrane
D impulses travel by electricity across the gap
parts.answer: B neurotransmitter is released only from the first neurone and receptors are only on the second neurone
parts.working: Vesicles of neurotransmitter are only in the neurone before the gap, and receptor proteins are only on the neurone after it. D is wrong: the signal crosses the gap as a chemical, not electrically.

practice.stem: A medicine, drug D, has a molecular shape very similar to a neurotransmitter but does not start impulses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how drug D affects transmission across a synapse.
parts.answer: It has a similar shape to the neurotransmitter, so it binds to the receptors; this blocks the neurotransmitter, so fewer impulses are started in the next neurone.
parts.working: B1 binds to / blocks receptors; B1 fewer / no impulses in next neurone

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a drug that blocks the receptors at synapses between motor neurones and muscles could cause paralysis.
parts.answer: Impulses cannot pass from motor neurones to muscles; so muscles do not contract.
parts.working: B1 no impulse transmitted to muscle; B1 muscles do not contract

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one role of synapses in the nervous system.
parts.answer: Ensure impulses travel in one direction / allow impulses to be passed between neurones / allow connections with many neurones.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which gland secretes adrenaline?
A pancreas
B adrenal gland
C testis
D ovary
parts.answer: B adrenal gland
parts.working: Adrenaline is secreted by the adrenal glands (above the kidneys). The pancreas secretes insulin and glucagon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the meaning of the term hormone.
parts.answer: A chemical substance produced by a gland; carried by the blood; which alters the activity of one or more specific target organs.
parts.working: B1 chemical made by gland; B1 transported in blood (to target organs)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table.
hormone | gland
insulin | ?
testosterone | ?
oestrogen | ?
parts.answer: pancreas; testes; ovaries

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two differences between nervous control and hormonal control.
parts.answer: Nervous: electrical impulses, along neurones, very fast, short-lasting. Hormonal: chemical, in blood, slower, longer-lasting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid differences

practice.stem: A goalkeeper in a hockey match in Karachi feels nervous as a penalty shoot-out begins, and his adrenal glands secrete adrenaline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three effects of adrenaline on the body.
parts.answer: Increases heart rate; increases breathing rate; dilates pupils; increases blood glucose concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how two of these effects help the goalkeeper's muscles during the shoot-out.
parts.answer: Faster heart rate delivers more oxygen and glucose to muscles; more glucose in blood is available; so more aerobic respiration releases more energy for muscle contraction.
parts.working: B1 more oxygen / glucose delivered; B1 more respiration; B1 more energy for contraction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the way in which the body responds to (i) touching a hot iron and (ii) a rise in blood glucose after a meal. Refer to the type of signal, how it travels, speed and duration.
parts.answer: (i) Nervous: electrical impulses; along neurones; very fast; short-lived response (muscle contracts). (ii) Hormonal: chemical (insulin); carried in the blood plasma; slower; longer-lasting; can affect several target organs (liver, muscles).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six comparison points, at least one from each response: electrical vs chemical; neurones vs blood; fast vs slow; short vs long-lasting; specific effector vs target organs; reflex via spinal cord vs pancreas detects change

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the control of blood glucose is an example of homeostasis.
parts.answer: It keeps the internal environment (blood glucose) constant within narrow limits; by negative feedback that reverses changes from the set point.
parts.working: B1 constant internal conditions; B1 negative feedback / returns to normal

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student records the time taken for a colour change in a results table. Which column heading is set out correctly?
A time (seconds)
B time / s
C time taken
D s / time
parts.answer: B time / s
parts.working: The heading gives the quantity, then a solidus and the unit: time / s. C has no unit; D puts the unit first.

practice.stem: Four students measured the length of the same dried bean seedling root. Their results were: 4.6 cm, 4.8 cm, 7.9 cm, 4.5 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result.
parts.answer: 7.9 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean, leaving out the anomalous result. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 4.6 cm

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the anomalous result should not be included in the mean.
parts.answer: It does not fit the pattern / is probably due to an error, so it would make the mean unrepresentative.

practice.stem:
Pondweed bubbles at different lamp distances:
distance / cm | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50
bubbles per minute | 64 | 35 | 20 | 13 | 8

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the dependent variable shown in the table.
parts.answer: Number of bubbles per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown by the results.
parts.answer: As the distance of the lamp increases, the number of bubbles decreases (from 64 at 10 cm to 8 at 50 cm).
parts.working: B1 inverse trend; B1 data quoted with units

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a suitable scale for the y-axis if the grid is 10 large squares high.
parts.answer: 1 large square = 10 bubbles per minute (0 to 70 / 100).
parts.working: B1 any linear scale that fits 64 and uses most of the grid

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of graph should be drawn to show the number of students in a class with each blood group (A, B, AB, O)?
A line graph with points joined
B bar chart with separate bars
C histogram with touching bars
D scatter graph with a line of best fit
parts.answer: B bar chart with separate bars
parts.working: Blood group is a discontinuous (categoric) variable, so a bar chart with gaps between bars is used. A histogram is for continuous data in classes.

practice.stem: A student timed how long it took for starch to be digested by amylase at different temperatures. Results: 10 °C took 240 s; 20 °C took 130 s; 30 °C took 70 s; 40 °C took 55 s; 50 °C took 180 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw a results table for these data with suitable headings. Describe what your table must include.
parts.answer: Two columns: temperature / °C and time for starch to disappear / s, with the values in the cells and no units in the cells.
parts.working: B1 headings with quantity and unit (°C, s) in heading; B1 all data entered in correct order, no units in body

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction at 30 °C using rate = 1000 ÷ time. Give your answer to 1 decimal place and state the unit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which variable goes on the x-axis of a graph of these results.
parts.answer: Temperature (the independent variable)

practice.stem: A piece of potato had a mass of 48 g. After 30 minutes in a concentrated salt solution its mass was 36 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in mass of the potato piece. Give a negative sign for a decrease.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why percentage change is used rather than the change in mass when comparing pieces.
parts.answer: The pieces had different starting masses, so percentage change allows a fair comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The student wrote '20 °C' in each cell of the temperature column and '5 min' in each cell of the time column. Explain how the table should be improved.
parts.answer: Put the units in the column headings (temperature / °C, time / min); write only numbers in the cells.
parts.working: B1 units in heading; B1 numbers only in cells

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student recorded times as 32, 41.5, 38 and 40.25 s. Suggest how these should be recorded.
parts.answer: All to the same number of decimal places (e.g. 32.0, 41.5, 38.0, 40.3 — or as whole numbers).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where the independent variable should be placed in a results table.
parts.answer: In the first (left-hand) column.

practice.stem:
Volume of oxygen collected from yeast and hydrogen peroxide:
time / min | 0 | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20
volume / cm³ | 0 | 12 | 22 | 30 | 36

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assuming a straight line between the two nearest readings, estimate the volume of gas collected at 12 minutes.
parts.answer: 25.2 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the shape of the graph that these results would give.
parts.answer: Volume increases with time, but the rate of increase gets smaller (curve levels off).
parts.working: B1 increases; B1 gradient decreases / levels off

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of gas production over the first 10 minutes.
parts.answer: 2.2 cm³/min

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two rules for plotting a line graph of these results.
parts.answer: Linear scales using more than half the grid; axes labelled with units; points plotted accurately (small crosses); smooth curve / ruled lines drawn through points.

practice.stem:
Height of a radish seedling:
day | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
height / cm | 2.0 | 3.5 | 5.5 | 8.0 | 11.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean growth rate in cm per day between day 1 and day 5.
parts.answer: 2.25 cm/day

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the growth rate is constant. Use the data to explain.
parts.answer: No: daily increases are 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0 cm, so the rate increases each day.
parts.working: B1 not constant / increasing; B1 supporting differences

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a line of best fit through the origin would be wrong for these data.
parts.answer: The points do not lie on a straight line (the curve gets steeper), and there is no reading at day 0 to show the height was zero then.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature should a biological drawing have?
A shading to show the darker areas
B clear, continuous outlines drawn with a sharp pencil
C label lines with arrowheads
D a small drawing in one corner of the space
parts.answer: B clear, continuous outlines drawn with a sharp pencil
parts.working: Biological drawings use clear, unbroken lines with a sharp pencil and no shading. Label lines should be ruled and have no arrowheads, and the drawing should be large.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four rules the student should follow when making a drawing of a hibiscus leaf.
parts.answer: Use a sharp pencil; clear continuous lines (no sketchy lines); no shading; drawing large (fill most of the space); correct proportions; label lines ruled, not crossing, touching the structure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what should be written below a drawing to show its size compared with the real specimen.
parts.answer: The magnification (e.g. × 3).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two rules for drawing label lines.
parts.answer: Ruled with a pencil; touch the structure; do not cross; no arrowheads; labels outside the drawing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a drawing should use most of the space provided.
parts.answer: So that details can be shown clearly.

practice.stem: A student draws a guava leaf. Line AB is drawn on the drawing from the tip of the leaf to the base of the blade and is 126 mm. The same distance on the real leaf is 84 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student should draw the veins on the leaf.
parts.answer: As single or double clear lines, without shading, in the correct positions / proportions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why it is important that the line used to measure the drawing is drawn in the same place as on the real leaf.
parts.answer: So that the same length is compared, giving an accurate magnification.

practice.stem: A student's drawing of a flower is 25 mm tall in a space 120 mm tall. The petals are drawn with many short sketchy lines, the centre of the flower is shaded dark, and label lines have arrowheads and cross each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three faults in the student's drawing.
parts.answer: Shading used; sketchy / broken lines; drawing too small; label lines with arrowheads / crossing; proportions wrong.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why biological drawings are not shaded.
parts.answer: Shading can hide details / outlines and makes the drawing less clear.

practice.stem: A student looked at stained onion epidermis with a light microscope and was asked to draw three adjacent cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the student drew only a few cells rather than the whole field of view.
parts.answer: To show detail of the cells clearly / it would take too long and cells would be too small.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two structures the student should draw and label in an onion epidermal cell seen with a light microscope.
parts.answer: Cell wall; nucleus; cytoplasm; (cell membrane / vacuole if visible).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the cell walls should be drawn as double lines between neighbouring cells.
parts.answer: Each cell has its own wall, so two walls lie side by side.

practice.stem: A student is asked to draw a soaked broad bean seed, split open to show the inside.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The seed is 16 mm long. The student wants the drawing to be 80 mm long. Calculate the magnification needed. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student should label the seed coat on the drawing.
parts.answer: Use a ruled line from the seed coat to the label, ending on the structure; label written horizontally outside the drawing; lines do not cross.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student should look at the real specimen rather than copying a diagram from a book.
parts.answer: Real specimens vary; the drawing should show the actual features and proportions of the specimen observed.

practice.stem: A student makes a drawing of a preserved housefly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should make sure the proportions in the drawing are correct.
parts.answer: Measure the length and width of the insect (e.g. with a ruler) and keep the same ratio in the drawing; compare positions of legs / wings relative to body.
parts.working: B1 measure specimen; B1 keep ratios / relative sizes same

parts.label: b
parts.text: The housefly is 7 mm long. The student's drawing is 105 mm long. Calculate the magnification.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one piece of apparatus to help observe the fine details of the housefly.
parts.answer: Hand lens / magnifying glass (or stereo / binocular microscope).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two safety precautions when heating test-tubes of food solution with Benedict's solution.
parts.answer: Wear eye protection / goggles; use a water bath rather than a direct flame; point the test-tube away from people; use a test-tube holder.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the apparatus used to keep the test-tubes at 80 °C and how to check the temperature.
parts.answer: Water bath (beaker of water heated / thermostatic bath); check with a thermometer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the apparatus you would use to measure each of the following: (i) the mass of a leaf (ii) the length of a root (iii) the temperature of a water bath (iv) the time for a colour change.
parts.answer: (i) (top-pan) balance (ii) ruler (iii) thermometer (iv) stop-clock / stopwatch

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the unit you would use for (i) and (ii).
parts.answer: (i) g (ii) mm or cm

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which apparatus is most suitable for measuring exactly 2.5 cm³ of enzyme solution?
A 100 cm³ beaker
B 50 cm³ measuring cylinder
C 5 cm³ syringe
D 250 cm³ conical flask
parts.answer: C 5 cm³ syringe
parts.working: A small syringe has fine graduations and measures small volumes accurately. A 50 cm³ measuring cylinder has graduations too large to read 2.5 cm³ accurately.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how to read the volume in a measuring cylinder accurately.
parts.answer: Place on a flat surface; read at eye level; read the bottom of the meniscus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A measuring cylinder has graduations every 2 cm³. The liquid lies halfway between the 36 and 38 cm³ marks. State the reading.
parts.answer: 37 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a stop-clock reading to 0.01 s does not make reaction timing more accurate than one reading to 1 s when a person starts and stops it.
parts.answer: Human reaction time (about 0.2–0.3 s) is much larger than 0.01 s, so the extra decimal places are not meaningful.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student could make three solutions of sucrose of concentration 0.5, 0.25 and 0.1 mol/dm³ from a 1.0 mol/dm³ stock, each of total volume 20 cm³. Give the volumes of stock and water for each.
parts.answer: 0.5: 10 cm³ stock + 10 cm³ water; 0.25: 5 cm³ stock + 15 cm³ water; 0.1: 2 cm³ stock + 18 cm³ water (measured with syringes / measuring cylinder, mixed well).
parts.working: 1 mark per correct pair of volumes

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the student should use a different syringe for the stock solution and the water.
parts.answer: To avoid contaminating / changing the concentration of the solutions.

practice.stem: Three students measured the same plant shoot: 12.4 cm, 12.6 cm, 12.5 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the range of the three readings.
parts.answer: 0.2 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: The ruler used had a zero error: the zero mark was 0.3 cm from the end used. All readings were 0.3 cm too large. State the name for this type of error and give the corrected mean.
parts.answer: Systematic error; corrected mean = 12.2 cm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why repeating the measurement would not remove this error.
parts.answer: Every repeat has the same error, in the same direction.

practice.stem: A student timed how long it took for pieces of apple, cut by hand with a knife, to turn brown in air on the bench. She judged the end point by eye.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two sources of error in this method.
parts.answer: Difficult to judge the exact moment the colour changes / end point is subjective; temperature of room not controlled; different sized pieces; timing errors starting/stopping clock.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each error, suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: Compare with a colour standard / use a colorimeter; use a water bath; cut pieces with a cork borer / to the same size; use a data logger.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student repeats an experiment three times and gets very similar results each time. What does this show?
A the results are accurate
B the results are repeatable / reliable
C there are no systematic errors
D the hypothesis is proved
parts.answer: B the results are repeatable / reliable
parts.working: Close agreement between repeats shows the results are repeatable (reliable). They could all still be wrong by the same amount if there is a systematic error, so A and C do not follow.

practice.stem: A student investigated the effect of temperature on the number of leaf discs floating in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution under a lamp. She used one tube at each of 20 °C and 40 °C, cutting discs from different leaves with scissors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student's method may give unreliable results.
parts.answer: Only one tube per temperature / no repeats, so an anomalous result cannot be identified; leaves of different sizes / ages used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three improvements to the method.
parts.answer: Repeat each temperature three times and calculate a mean; use leaf discs of the same size cut with a cork borer; use a water bath / thermostatically controlled; keep light intensity the same; use more temperatures / smaller intervals.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student investigates how the concentration of salt solution affects the change in length of potato strips. What is the independent variable?
A the change in length of the strips
B the concentration of salt solution
C the temperature of the solutions
D the starting length of the strips
parts.answer: B the concentration of salt solution
parts.working: The independent variable is the one the student changes on purpose: salt concentration. A is the dependent variable; C and D are controlled variables.

practice.stem: A student set up three tubes: A — yeast + sugar solution; B — yeast + water; C — boiled yeast + sugar solution. She counted bubbles of gas from each tube for 5 minutes at 30 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the student included tube C with boiled yeast.
parts.answer: As a control; to show that the gas / change is caused by living yeast (enzymes are denatured by boiling).
parts.working: B1 control; B1 shows result is due to living / active yeast

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one variable that must be the same in all tubes.
parts.answer: Volume / concentration of sugar solution; mass of yeast; temperature.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write a hypothesis for this investigation.
parts.answer: Yeast produces more carbon dioxide when sugar is present (or the more sugar, the more gas).

practice.stem: A student tests four fruit drinks sold in a Lahore market to compare their reducing sugar content using Benedict's solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify (i) the independent variable (ii) the dependent variable.
parts.answer: (i) the type of drink / sugar content of drink (ii) colour of Benedict's after heating (or time for colour change)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept the same.
parts.answer: Volume of drink; volume of Benedict's solution; temperature of water bath; time of heating.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a suitable control for this investigation.
parts.answer: A tube of water (instead of drink) with Benedict's heated in the same way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find the effect of pH on the time taken for amylase to digest starch. Include the independent, dependent and controlled variables, how you would take measurements and how you would make results reliable.
parts.answer: Use buffers at pH 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 (independent); mix fixed volumes of starch and amylase with buffer; keep at 35 °C in a water bath; every 30 s remove a drop into iodine on a spotting tile; record time until iodine stays orange-brown (dependent); keep concentrations, volumes and temperature constant; repeat three times and find mean; control with boiled enzyme / water.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: at least 5 pH values / buffers; how pH is controlled (buffer solutions); fixed volumes / concentrations; temperature controlled with water bath; iodine test at regular intervals; end point when iodine no longer turns blue-black; time recorded; repeats and mean; control (boiled enzyme); safety (goggles)

practice.stem:
A student in Lahore placed 2 g of grated potato into each of four boiling tubes and added 10 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide solution of different concentrations. Potato contains the enzyme catalase. After 2 minutes she measured the height of the foam. She did three trials at each concentration.
Concentration / %: 5 | 10 | 15 | 20
Trial 1 foam height / mm: 14 | 27 | 41 | 52
Trial 2 foam height / mm: 16 | 29 | 22 | 55
Trial 3 foam height / mm: 15 | 31 | 43 | 55

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result in the table.
parts.answer: 22 mm (15 % hydrogen peroxide, trial 2)
parts.working: B1 22 mm at 15 % – far below the other two trials (41 and 43 mm).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean foam height for 15 % hydrogen peroxide, leaving out the anomalous result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the concentration of hydrogen peroxide and the height of the foam.
parts.answer: As the concentration increases, the foam height increases steadily (roughly linear: mean heights 15, 29, 42 and 54 mm, about 12–14 mm more for every 5 % increase).
parts.working: B1 higher concentration → taller foam; B1 quoting data, e.g. mean 15 mm at 5 % rising to 54 mm at 20 %, or 'steady/roughly linear increase'. Do not accept 'directly proportional' (the line would not pass through the origin).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the gas that forms the bubbles in the foam.
parts.answer: oxygen
parts.working: B1 oxygen (catalase breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen).

practice.stem:
Two beakers each contained 50 g of chopped apple pulp from apples bought in a Peshawar market. 2 cm³ of pectinase was added to beaker A and 2 cm³ of water to beaker B. Both were kept at 40 °C for 15 minutes and then filtered.
Volume of juice from A = 18.5 cm³
Volume of juice from B = 7.4 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why the student set up beaker B with water instead of pectinase.
parts.answer: As a control, to show that the extra juice is caused by the pectinase.
parts.working: B1 control / comparison / shows effect is due to enzyme.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the volume of juice when pectinase was used.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how pectinase increases the volume of juice released.
parts.answer: It breaks down pectin, which holds plant cell walls together, so cells separate/break open and release more juice.
parts.working: B1 pectin broken down; B1 cell walls weakened / cells release juice.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation.
parts.answer: Any two: mass of apple pulp; volume of liquid added; temperature; time left before filtering; type/ripeness of apple; size of pulp pieces.

practice.stem:
Three tubes were kept at 35 °C for 10 minutes and then tested with iodine solution.
Tube A: 5 cm³ starch + 1 cm³ amylase → yellow-brown
Tube B: 5 cm³ starch + 1 cm³ boiled and cooled amylase → blue-black
Tube C: 5 cm³ starch + 1 cm³ distilled water → blue-black

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the result in tube A.
parts.answer: Amylase digested the starch (to maltose/reducing sugar), so no starch was left to turn iodine blue-black.
parts.working: B1 starch broken down by amylase; B1 so no starch present / iodine stays yellow-brown.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why tube B stayed blue-black.
parts.answer: Boiling denatured the amylase, so its active site changed shape and it could not digest starch; starch remained.
parts.working: B1 boiled enzyme denatured; B1 starch not digested / still present.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the purpose of tube C.
parts.answer: A control to show that starch does not break down by itself (without enzyme).
parts.working: B1 control / starch does not break down without amylase.

practice.stem: A student timed how long it took an enzyme reaction to finish at different temperatures. In her table she wrote the column heading 'Time' and wrote values such as '45 s', '62 s' and '80 s' in the cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a correct column heading for the time column.
parts.answer: Time / s (or time (s))
parts.working: B1 quantity and unit in the heading.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is wrong with writing '45 s' in each cell of the table.
parts.answer: Units should be in the heading only, not in the cells.
parts.working: B1 units in heading, numbers only in cells.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name a piece of apparatus to measure exactly 5.0 cm³ of enzyme solution.
parts.answer: a syringe (or graduated pipette / 10 cm³ measuring cylinder)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the student should use a new syringe for the enzyme and for the substrate.
parts.answer: So the enzyme does not mix with the substrate and start reacting before timing begins (no contamination).

practice.stem:
Celery extract was mixed with hydrogen peroxide in a conical flask. The oxygen produced was collected over water in an inverted measuring cylinder.
Time / s: 0 | 30 | 60 | 90 | 120 | 150 | 180
Volume of oxygen / cm³: 0 | 6.5 | 12.0 | 16.5 | 19.5 | 21.0 | 21.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production during the first 60 s. Give your answer in cm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 12.0 cm³ per minute
parts.working: M1 12.0 cm³ in 60 s (1 minute); A1 12.0 cm³/min.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate between 60 s and 120 s, in cm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 7.5 cm³ per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why no more oxygen was collected after 150 s.
parts.answer: All the hydrogen peroxide (substrate) had been broken down, so there was no substrate left for the catalase to act on.
parts.working: B1 substrate / hydrogen peroxide used up; B1 so no more enzyme–substrate complexes / no more product formed (enzyme still present).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one source of error in this method and how it could be reduced.
parts.answer: Some oxygen escapes before the bung is put in – use a flask with a side arm/tap funnel so the peroxide is added with the bung already in place (or use a gas syringe).
parts.working: B1 error (gas lost before bung fitted / bubbles hard to read / reading meniscus of cylinder); B1 matching improvement.

practice.stem:
A student mixed 5 cm³ of 1 % starch solution with 5 cm³ of amylase solution. Every 10 s she placed one drop of the mixture into iodine solution on a spotting tile. She recorded the time when the iodine first stayed its original colour.
Amylase concentration / %: 0.25 | 0.5 | 1.0 | 2.0
Time for starch to disappear / s: 480 | 250 | 130 | 70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction, 1000 ÷ time, for each amylase concentration. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: B2 all four correct; B1 for two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what colour the iodine solution stays when all the starch has been digested.
parts.answer: yellow-brown (orange-brown)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the effect of amylase concentration on the rate of reaction.
parts.answer: The rate increases as amylase concentration increases; it roughly doubles each time the concentration doubles (2.1 → 4.0 → 7.7 → 14.3).
parts.working: B1 higher concentration gives higher rate; B1 data quote / roughly proportional.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The drops were tested every 10 s. Explain why the times recorded are not exact.
parts.answer: The starch may have disappeared at any time in the 10 s since the previous test, so each time could be up to 10 s too long.
parts.working: B1 end point lies between two tests / uncertainty of up to 10 s; test more often.

practice.stem:
A protease solution was added to a cloudy milk powder suspension at five temperatures. The time taken for the mixture to become clear was recorded.
Temperature / °C: 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60
Time to clear / s: 300 | 160 | 85 | 120 | did not clear within 600

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction, 1000 ÷ time, at 40 °C. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the milk powder suspension becomes clear.
parts.answer: Protease breaks down the protein (casein) particles that make it cloudy into soluble amino acids/peptides.
parts.working: B1 protease digests protein; B1 products are soluble / particles disappear.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the mixture at 60 °C did not clear within 600 s.
parts.answer: At 60 °C the protease was denatured – the active site changed shape so protein could not bind and be digested.
parts.working: B1 denatured; B1 active site shape changed / substrate no longer fits.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe how the student could keep each tube at the stated temperature.
parts.answer: Stand the tubes in a thermostatically controlled water bath (and check with a thermometer), letting both solutions reach the temperature before mixing.
parts.working: B1 water bath / thermometer check / pre-incubate solutions.

practice.stem: In Karachi a laundry tested a biological washing powder and a non-biological washing powder on cotton cloths stained with egg and with cooking oil, at 40 °C and at 90 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the enzymes in the biological powder that digest (i) an egg stain and (ii) a cooking-oil stain.
parts.answer: (i) protease; (ii) lipase

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the biological powder removed more of the stains at 40 °C than the non-biological powder.
parts.answer: The enzymes break the large insoluble stain molecules into small soluble molecules (amino acids; fatty acids and glycerol) which wash out in the water.
parts.working: B1 enzymes digest stain molecules; B1 products soluble / washed away.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the biological powder was no better than the non-biological powder at 90 °C.
parts.answer: At 90 °C the enzymes are denatured, so they can no longer digest the stains.
parts.working: B1 high temperature denatures enzymes; B1 active site changes shape / no digestion.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of washing clothes at 40 °C rather than 90 °C.
parts.answer: Less energy/fuel used to heat the water (cheaper), or delicate fabrics are not damaged.

practice.stem:
Four wells, each 6 mm across, were cut in a dish of starch agar. 0.1 cm³ of a different solution was put in each well and the dish was left for 24 hours, then flooded with iodine solution. The diameter of the clear circle was measured (6 mm means no clear zone beyond the well).
0.5 % amylase: 12 mm
1 % amylase: 18 mm
2 % amylase: 24 mm
2 % amylase, boiled: 6 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the agar turned blue-black but there was a clear (yellow-brown) zone around some wells.
parts.answer: Iodine turns blue-black with starch in the agar; around the wells amylase diffused out and digested the starch, so there was no starch to stain.
parts.working: B1 iodine + starch gives blue-black; B1 amylase diffused and digested starch near the well.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the area of the clear circle for the 1 % amylase. Use area = πr². Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the boiled amylase gave no clear zone beyond the well.
parts.answer: Boiling denatured the amylase so it could not digest starch.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the diameter is only an estimate of enzyme activity.
parts.answer: Clear zones may not be perfect circles / edge of the zone is blurred / diffusion rate also affects size.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Starch solution and amylase were kept at 37 °C until all the starch had been digested. Samples were then tested with iodine solution and with Benedict's solution (heated). Which results are expected?
A iodine blue-black; Benedict's stays blue
B iodine yellow-brown; Benedict's brick red
C iodine blue-black; Benedict's brick red
D iodine yellow-brown; Benedict's stays blue
parts.answer: B iodine yellow-brown; Benedict's brick red
parts.working: No starch remains, so iodine stays yellow-brown; starch has become maltose, a reducing sugar, so Benedict's turns brick red. C would only be seen if some starch were still undigested.

practice.stem: Maize grains were soaked for 2 days so they began to germinate. Some were boiled. All grains were cut in half and placed cut side down on starch agar. After 24 hours the agar was flooded with iodine solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict what the agar around the germinating seeds looked like after adding iodine, and explain.
parts.answer: A clear yellow-brown area around each seed; germinating seeds make amylase, which diffused into the agar and digested the starch; the rest of the agar was blue-black.
parts.working: B1 yellow-brown/clear zone round seed; B1 amylase produced by germinating seed; B1 starch digested near seed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the boiled seeds.
parts.answer: A control: boiling kills the seeds and denatures their enzymes, showing that the clear zones are due to enzymes from living seeds.
parts.working: B1 control; B1 enzymes denatured / no amylase activity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the seeds were cut in half and placed cut side down.
parts.answer: So enzymes from inside the seed can diffuse directly into the agar (the seed coat does not block them).
parts.working: B1 contact of inner tissue with agar.

practice.stem: Small discs of filter paper soaked in catalase extract sink when dropped into hydrogen peroxide solution. As oxygen is produced, bubbles stick to the disc and it floats to the surface. Hydrogen peroxide solutions of up to 5 % are available, with distilled water, a hole punch, beakers, forceps, a stopwatch and a water bath.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the concentration of hydrogen peroxide affects the activity of catalase, using the floating disc method described above.
parts.answer: A plan that changes peroxide concentration, keeps other variables constant, measures time for discs to float, repeats, and states how results show activity.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: use at least 5 concentrations (e.g. 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 %), made by diluting with distilled water; same volume of peroxide in each beaker (e.g. 25 cm³); same size discs (cut with same hole punch) soaked in the same catalase extract for the same time; same temperature (water bath, e.g. 25 °C) / same pH (buffer); place disc at bottom with forceps and start stopwatch; record time for disc to rise to the surface; repeat at least 3 times per concentration and calculate a mean; rate = 1 ÷ time / shorter time = higher activity; control with 0 % peroxide or boiled-extract disc; safety: eye protection/gloves with peroxide.

practice.stem:
Lactase breaks down lactose in milk into glucose and galactose. A student added 1 cm³ of lactase to 10 cm³ of milk in five tubes, each with a buffer of different pH, at 30 °C. After 10 minutes she dipped a glucose test strip into each tube and read the glucose concentration from a colour chart.
pH: 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8
Glucose reading / arbitrary units: 0.5 | 2.0 | 5.5 | 6.5 | 3.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the pH at which lactase was most active in this investigation.
parts.answer: pH 7

parts.label: b
parts.text: Lactose is a reducing sugar. Explain why glucose test strips were used instead of Benedict's solution.
parts.answer: Milk already contains lactose, which gives a positive Benedict's test, so Benedict's cannot show whether lactose has been broken down; the strips detect only glucose, the product.
parts.working: B1 lactose/milk would also turn Benedict's orange/red (positive before and after); B1 strips specific to glucose / product of the reaction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The true optimum pH may not be exactly 7. Describe how the student could find the optimum pH more precisely.
parts.answer: Repeat using smaller pH intervals around the peak, e.g. pH 6.0, 6.2, 6.4 … 8.0, with buffers, and repeat each to get means.
parts.working: B1 narrower range between pH 6 and 8; B1 smaller intervals (e.g. 0.2 or 0.5) / repeats.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the glucose reading at pH 4 was very low.
parts.answer: At pH 4 the enzyme's shape/active site is changed (denatured), so lactose no longer fits and few enzyme–substrate complexes form.
parts.working: B1 active site shape changed / denatured; B1 substrate cannot bind / fewer complexes.

practice.stem: A student investigated catalase in potato. He cut potato pieces by eye, dropped them into 10 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide in a measuring cylinder and measured the foam height with a ruler 'when it looked highest'. The laboratory windows were open and the room temperature changed from 24 °C to 31 °C during the lesson. He did one trial for each condition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When a classmate repeated one condition twice using the same method, the foam heights were 48 mm and 36 mm. Calculate the percentage by which the second result is lower than the first.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify three sources of error in the student's method and suggest an improvement for each.
parts.answer: Pieces cut by eye – cut with a cork borer and ruler to the same size/mass; foam measured while still rising – measure at a fixed time (e.g. exactly 60 s); room temperature changed – use a water bath; only one trial – repeat three times and calculate a mean; foam surface uneven – measure at eye level / use a narrow measuring cylinder.
parts.working: B1 each error and B1 each matching improvement, max 3 pairs.

practice.stem:
2 g of liver was added to 20 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide of different concentrations. The volume of oxygen collected in a gas syringe in 2 minutes was recorded.
Concentration / %: 1 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10
Volume of oxygen in 2 min / cm³: 4.0 | 8.1 | 15.8 | 20.5 | 21.9 | 22.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen production at 4 % hydrogen peroxide, in cm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 7.9 cm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the results.
parts.answer: Volume increases steeply and almost proportionally from 1 % to 4 %, then levels off above about 6–8 % at about 22 cm³.
parts.working: B1 increase at low concentrations; B1 levels off/plateau with data (about 22 cm³ from 8 %).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why increasing the concentration above 8 % has almost no effect.
parts.answer: All the active sites of the catalase are occupied (enzyme saturated), so the amount of enzyme now limits the rate.
parts.working: B1 active sites all in use / saturated; B1 enzyme concentration is limiting factor.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict how the results at 10 % would change if 4 g of liver were used instead of 2 g, and explain.
parts.answer: More oxygen (higher plateau), because there are more enzyme molecules / active sites available.
parts.working: B1 more oxygen / higher rate; B1 more catalase / active sites.

practice.stem:
Equal volumes of hydrogen peroxide were added to samples of different tissues. Oxygen was collected for 5 minutes.
Tissue | mass / g | oxygen in 5 min / cm³
liver | 2.0 | 46
potato | 5.0 | 30
apple | 4.0 | 6.0
boiled liver | 2.0 | 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen production per gram of tissue per minute for liver, potato and apple.
parts.answer: liver 4.6; potato 1.2; apple 0.3 cm³ per g per min

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the volumes have to be divided by the mass of tissue before the tissues are compared.
parts.answer: Different masses were used; more tissue contains more catalase, so per gram makes the comparison fair.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why liver produced the most oxygen per gram.
parts.answer: Liver cells contain a lot of catalase because liver cells carry out many reactions (metabolism) that produce hydrogen peroxide, which is toxic and must be removed.
parts.working: B1 more catalase in liver; B1 to remove toxic hydrogen peroxide made in metabolism.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement defines an enzyme?
A a protein that acts as a biological catalyst
B a carbohydrate that speeds up reactions in cells
C a hormone that controls the rate of respiration
D a fat that is used up in chemical reactions
parts.answer: A a protein that acts as a biological catalyst
parts.working: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions and are not changed. B is wrong because enzymes are proteins, not carbohydrates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the term substrate.
parts.answer: The substance (molecule) that an enzyme acts on.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by the term active site.
parts.answer: The region of the enzyme molecule where the substrate binds.
parts.working: B1 part of enzyme where substrate fits/binds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the products formed when lipase acts on fat.
parts.answer: fatty acids and glycerol

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Amylase digests starch but does not digest protein. What is the reason?
A Protein molecules are too large to enter the cell.
B The shape of protein does not fit the active site of amylase.
C Amylase is denatured by protein.
D Protein is only digested at high temperature.
parts.answer: B The shape of protein does not fit the active site of amylase.
parts.working: The active site of an enzyme is complementary in shape to one substrate, so only starch fits amylase. A is wrong because digestion happens outside cells in the gut.

practice.stem: In the human gut, protease in the stomach digests the protein in a meal of daal and roti, while amylase from the pancreas digests the starch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why each enzyme can catalyse only one type of reaction.
parts.answer: The active site has a specific shape; only a substrate with a complementary shape fits; it forms an enzyme–substrate complex; the reaction happens and products leave; other molecules do not fit so are not acted on.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: active site specific shape; complementary to substrate; enzyme–substrate complex forms; products released / enzyme unchanged; other substrates do not fit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the information by naming the substrate or product for each enzyme.
(i) amylase: starch → ?
(ii) protease: ? → amino acids
(iii) catalase: hydrogen peroxide → ? + ?
parts.answer: (i) maltose (simple reducing sugar); (ii) protein; (iii) water + oxygen

parts.label: b
parts.text: Enzymes are described as 'biological catalysts'. Explain what is meant by a catalyst.
parts.answer: A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction and is not changed by the reaction.
parts.working: B1 speeds up reaction; B1 not changed / not used up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In one experiment a single enzyme molecule converted 2.5 × 10⁴ substrate molecules into product each second. Calculate how many substrate molecules it would convert in 5 minutes. Give your answer in standard form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why one enzyme molecule can convert so many substrate molecules.
parts.answer: The enzyme is not used up or changed in the reaction; after products leave the active site it is free to bind another substrate molecule.
parts.working: B1 not changed/used up (catalyst); B1 active site reused for next substrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An enzyme from the human small intestine was tested at different temperatures. Above 45 °C its activity fell quickly. What is the best explanation?
A The substrate molecules move too slowly.
B The enzyme is denatured and its active site changes shape.
C The enzyme molecules are used up in the reaction.
D The products break down into the substrate.
parts.answer: B The enzyme is denatured and its active site changes shape.
parts.working: High temperature breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's shape, so the substrate no longer fits. A is wrong: molecules move faster, not slower, when heated.

practice.stem:
The activity of an enzyme from human cells and the same type of enzyme from bacteria living in a hot spring were measured.
Temperature / °C: 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 | 70 | 80
Human enzyme activity / units: 20 | 45 | 80 | 40 | 5 | 0 | 0
Bacterial enzyme activity / units: 5 | 10 | 20 | 35 | 60 | 90 | 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum temperature for each enzyme.
parts.answer: human enzyme 40 °C; bacterial enzyme 70 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the human enzyme has no activity at 70 °C.
parts.answer: It is denatured; its active site has changed shape so the substrate cannot fit.
parts.working: B1 denatured; B1 active site shape changed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the bacterial enzyme is useful in an industrial process carried out at high temperature.
parts.answer: It works fastest at high temperature and is not denatured there.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain how the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction changes as temperature rises from 10 °C to 70 °C, for an enzyme with an optimum of 40 °C.
parts.answer: Rate rises from 10 °C to 40 °C because molecules have more kinetic energy and collide more often, forming more enzyme–substrate complexes; maximum at the optimum (40 °C); above 40 °C rate falls quickly as the enzyme is denatured, active site changes shape, substrate no longer fits; at about 70 °C there is no activity.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: rate increases to 40 °C; more kinetic energy; more collisions / more enzyme–substrate complexes; fastest at optimum; rate falls above optimum; denaturation; active site shape changed / substrate cannot fit; no activity at high temperature / irreversible.

practice.stem:
A student investigated the effect of temperature on an enzyme. The enzyme and substrate solutions were placed separately in water baths for 5 minutes, then mixed, and the time for a colour change was recorded.
Temperature / °C: 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60
Time / s: 400 | 190 | 95 | 60 | 85 | 300

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate, 1000 ÷ time, at each temperature to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: B2 all six correct; B1 four or five correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times faster the reaction was at 30 °C than at 10 °C. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 4.2 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the temperature range in which the optimum lies and describe how to find it more precisely.
parts.answer: Between 30 °C and 50 °C (near 40 °C); repeat at 1–2 °C intervals between 30 °C and 50 °C (e.g. 32, 34 … 48 °C).
parts.working: B1 30–50 °C; B1 smaller intervals in that range.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the solutions were left in the water bath for 5 minutes before they were mixed.
parts.answer: So that both the enzyme and the substrate reach the required temperature before the reaction starts.

practice.stem:
The activity of an enzyme was measured at different pH values.
pH: 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 10 | 11
Activity / units: 4 | 18 | 42 | 60 | 35 | 10 | 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum pH for this enzyme.
parts.answer: pH 8

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of pH on the activity of this enzyme.
parts.answer: Activity rises from pH 5 to a maximum at pH 8 and then falls sharply to zero at pH 11.
parts.working: B1 increase up to pH 8; B1 decrease above pH 8 with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest which part of the human gut this enzyme might work in. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Small intestine (duodenum), because conditions there are slightly alkaline.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which enzyme works best at about pH 2?
A salivary amylase in the mouth
B pepsin in the stomach
C lipase in the small intestine
D trypsin in the small intestine
parts.answer: B pepsin in the stomach
parts.working: The stomach contains hydrochloric acid, and pepsin has an optimum pH of about 2. Trypsin (D) is a protease too but works in the alkaline small intestine.

practice.stem:
Amylase and starch were mixed with buffer solutions of different pH at 35 °C. The time for the starch to disappear (iodine test) was recorded.
pH: 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9
Time / s: 360 | 150 | 75 | 60 | 110 | 290

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate, 60 ÷ time, at pH 6. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.80 per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why buffer solutions were used.
parts.answer: To keep the pH of each mixture constant at the chosen value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the results to state the optimum pH and explain how you decided.
parts.answer: pH 7 – it had the shortest time (60 s) / highest rate (1.00 per minute).
parts.working: B1 pH 7; B1 shortest time / fastest rate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables, other than pH, that must be kept the same.
parts.answer: Any two: temperature; volume/concentration of starch; volume/concentration of amylase; time between iodine tests.

practice.stem: During a meal of chicken karahi with naan, food passes from the mouth to the stomach and then to the duodenum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pepsin has an optimum pH of about 2. Explain why pepsin stops digesting protein when food passes into the duodenum.
parts.answer: The duodenum is alkaline (bile and pancreatic juice neutralise the acid); the change in pH alters the shape of pepsin's active site / denatures it; protein no longer fits, so no enzyme–substrate complexes form.
parts.working: B1 duodenum alkaline/neutral (bile, pancreatic juice); B1 active site shape altered / denatured; B1 substrate cannot bind.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Salivary amylase digests starch in the mouth. Suggest what happens to its activity when food reaches the stomach, and why.
parts.answer: It stops working because the stomach is very acidic (about pH 2), far from its optimum near pH 7, so it is denatured.
parts.working: B1 stops / activity falls; B1 acid pH denatures it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which conditions are needed for the germination of most seeds?
A light, water and warmth
B water, oxygen and a suitable temperature
C carbon dioxide, water and light
D oxygen, light and soil
parts.answer: B water, oxygen and a suitable temperature
parts.working: Seeds need water, oxygen (for aerobic respiration) and a suitable temperature (for enzymes). Light (A) is not needed because the seed uses stored food.

practice.stem: A tomato plant in a kitchen garden in Quetta has been pollinated and fertilised.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
After fertilisation, state what each of these structures develops into.
(i) ovule
(ii) ovary
parts.answer: (i) seed; (ii) fruit

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the petals after fertilisation.
parts.answer: They wither and fall off.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name of the cell formed when a male nucleus fuses with a female nucleus.
parts.answer: zygote

practice.stem:
Crushed maize grains were tested on the day they were soaked and after 4 days of germination.
Day 0: iodine test – blue-black; Benedict's test – blue
Day 4: iodine test – brown with a few black spots; Benedict's test – orange

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the results change from day 0 to day 4.
parts.answer: Starch decreases (iodine less blue-black) and reducing sugar increases (Benedict's changes from blue to orange).
parts.working: B1 less starch; B1 more reducing sugar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the enzyme responsible for these changes.
parts.answer: amylase

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what the germinating grain uses the sugar for.
parts.answer: Respiration to release energy for growth (or to build cellulose for new cells).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
After fertilisation, what does the wall of the ovule (the integuments) develop into?
A the testa (seed coat)
B the fruit wall
C the cotyledons
D the plumule
parts.answer: A the testa (seed coat)
parts.working: The integuments of the ovule harden to form the testa, which protects the seed. B is wrong because the fruit wall develops from the ovary wall, not the ovule.

practice.stem:
Twenty radish seeds were placed in each of four tubes and left for 5 days.
A: dry cotton wool, 25 °C – 0 germinated
B: moist cotton wool, 25 °C – 18 germinated
C: seeds under boiled and cooled water with a layer of oil on top, 25 °C – 0 germinated
D: moist cotton wool, in a refrigerator at 4 °C – 3 germinated

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage germination in each tube.
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 two or three correct (n ÷ 20 × 100).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which condition was missing in tube C and explain why it is needed for germination.
parts.answer: Oxygen (boiling removed dissolved oxygen and the oil stops more dissolving); needed for aerobic respiration to release energy for growth.
parts.working: B1 oxygen; B1 aerobic respiration / energy for growth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a few seeds in tube D germinated but many fewer than in tube B.
parts.answer: At 4 °C the enzymes in the seeds work very slowly (low kinetic energy), so germination is slow; it is not stopped completely.
parts.working: B1 low temperature slows enzymes; B1 slow (not zero) metabolism / respiration.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the control tube.
parts.answer: B

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events that take place from the moment a pollen grain lands on a stigma until fertilisation.
parts.answer: A pollen tube grows from the pollen grain down through the style; it enters the ovary and passes through the micropyle into an ovule; the male nucleus travels down the tube; it fuses with the female nucleus (egg cell) in the ovule.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: pollen tube grows; down style; through micropyle into ovule; male nucleus moves down tube; fuses with female nucleus/egg nucleus = fertilisation.

practice.stem:
Thirty mung bean seeds were placed on moist paper in each of four dishes at different temperatures. The number that had germinated after 4 days was counted.
Temperature / °C: 10 | 20 | 30 | 40
Number germinated: 6 | 21 | 28 | 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage germination at each temperature. Give each answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Five seedlings at 30 °C had radicle lengths of 18, 22, 20, 25 and 15 mm. Calculate the mean radicle length.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why fewer seeds germinated at 40 °C than at 30 °C.
parts.answer: 40 °C is above the optimum for the seeds' enzymes; some enzymes are denatured, so less stored food is broken down and respiration is slower.
parts.working: B1 above optimum / enzymes start to denature; B1 less food broken down / less energy for growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why seeds need water to germinate.
parts.answer: Water activates enzymes / allows stored food to be broken down and transported in solution; it makes cells swell so the testa splits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why seeds need oxygen to germinate.
parts.answer: For aerobic respiration, which releases energy for cell division and growth of the embryo.
parts.working: B1 aerobic respiration; B1 energy for growth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Farmers in Punjab sow wheat seeds in moist, loose soil rather than in waterlogged soil. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Waterlogged soil has little air, so the seeds would not get enough oxygen.

practice.stem: A student split open a soaked broad bean seed and made a large drawing. The length of the bean on the drawing was 84 mm. The actual length of the bean was 21 mm. She labelled the testa, cotyledons, plumule and radicle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of: (i) the testa; (ii) the cotyledons; (iii) the radicle.
parts.answer: (i) protects the seed (embryo); (ii) store food for the embryo during germination; (iii) grows into the root.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student measured the bean after soaking it overnight. Suggest why the soaked bean was larger than a dry bean.
parts.answer: It absorbed water (by osmosis), so its cells swelled.

practice.stem:
A student soaked mung bean seeds for different times before placing 20 seeds of each group on moist cotton wool at 25 °C. After 3 days she counted the germinated seeds and measured the radicle lengths of five seedlings from each group.
Soaking time / h: 0 | 4 | 8 | 12 | 24
Number germinated (out of 20): 9 | 14 | 18 | 19 | 11
Radicle lengths for 8 h / mm: 12, 15, 11, 14, 13

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage germination after 8 hours of soaking and after 24 hours of soaking.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean radicle length for the seeds soaked for 8 hours. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why soaking the seeds for up to 12 hours increased the number that germinated.
parts.answer: The seeds absorb water, which activates their enzymes so stored food (starch) is broken down and transported to the embryo; it also makes the seed swell and the testa split.
parts.working: B1 water absorbed / enzymes activated; B1 stored food broken down and transported for growth / testa splits.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why fewer seeds germinated after 24 hours of soaking.
parts.answer: Seeds kept under water for a long time get too little oxygen, so aerobic respiration cannot release enough energy (some embryos may die).
parts.working: B1 lack of oxygen when submerged / less aerobic respiration.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest one way to make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat with more dishes (or more seeds) for each soaking time and calculate means.
parts.working: B1 repeats / larger sample and mean.

practice.stem: You are given mung bean seeds, Petri dishes, cotton wool, water, incubators that can be set to different temperatures, and a refrigerator.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find the effect of temperature on the germination of mung bean seeds.
parts.answer: A plan with a range of temperatures, controlled variables, a measured outcome, repeats and a conclusion method.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: at least 4 temperatures (e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40 °C) using incubators/refrigerator/water baths; same number of seeds (e.g. 20) per dish, same type and age; same volume of water / moist cotton wool kept moist; same time (e.g. 4 days); same light conditions; count number germinated (radicle visible) and calculate percentage; repeat with three dishes per temperature and find mean; plot percentage against temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the function of the anther?
A to make pollen grains
B to receive pollen during pollination
C to attract insects
D to make ovules
parts.answer: A to make pollen grains
parts.working: Anthers produce pollen. The stigma (B) receives pollen.

practice.stem: A student looked at a hibiscus flower from her garden in Hyderabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the function of each part of a flower.
(i) sepal
(ii) petal
(iii) stigma
(iv) ovary
