parts.working: B1 further lamp → fewer bubbles (inverse relationship); B1 quotes paired data with units

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate of bubbling changes as the lamp is moved further away.
parts.answer: Light intensity falls with distance; light is the limiting factor, so less photosynthesis and less oxygen is released.
parts.working: B1 lower light intensity further away; B1 less photosynthesis so less oxygen (gas) produced / light is limiting

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that the student should keep the same.
parts.answer: Any two of: temperature of water; carbon dioxide (hydrogencarbonate) concentration; same piece/length of pondweed; same lamp/bulb power; time allowed to acclimatise.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid controlled variables

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest why the student placed a beaker of water between the lamp and the test tube.
parts.answer: To absorb heat from the lamp so the temperature of the pondweed stays constant.
parts.working: B1 acts as a heat shield / keeps temperature constant

practice.stem: A grower near Murree produces tomatoes in a glasshouse during winter. Paraffin heaters are burned inside the glasshouse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how burning paraffin in the heaters can increase the yield of tomatoes.
parts.answer: Burning releases heat, raising the temperature towards the optimum for photosynthesis enzymes; it also releases carbon dioxide, a raw material; so photosynthesis is faster and more sugar is made for growth.
parts.working: B1 raises temperature (enzymes work faster); B1 adds carbon dioxide (raw material/limiting factor); B1 faster photosynthesis → more glucose/growth/yield

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the grower switches on extra lamps on cloudy winter days.
parts.answer: Light intensity is low, so light is the limiting factor; lamps increase the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 light limiting on cloudy days

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the grower does not keep increasing the carbon dioxide concentration in the glasshouse.
parts.answer: Above a certain concentration another factor (light or temperature) becomes limiting so yield does not increase further; the extra cost would then be wasted.
parts.working: B1 another factor becomes limiting / rate levels off; B1 extra cost gives no extra profit

practice.stem:
Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red when in equilibrium with air, yellow when carbon dioxide concentration rises and purple when it falls. Four tubes were set up and left for 3 hours:
Tube A: leaf, bright light
Tube B: leaf, tube covered in black paper
Tube C: no leaf, bright light
Tube D: leaf, tube covered with thin gauze (dim light)
All tubes started red. After 3 hours the indicator in tube D was still red.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour of the indicator in tubes A, B and C after 3 hours.
parts.answer: A purple; B yellow; C red (unchanged)
parts.working: 2 marks all three correct; 1 mark for two correct

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the colour in tube A and in tube B.
parts.answer: A: the leaf photosynthesised faster than it respired, taking in carbon dioxide, so CO₂ fell and the indicator turned purple. B: in the dark there is no photosynthesis; respiration released carbon dioxide so the indicator turned yellow.
parts.working: B1 A photosynthesis > respiration; B1 CO₂ removed → purple; B1 B only respiration, CO₂ added → yellow

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why tube C was set up.
parts.answer: As a control, to show that the leaf caused the colour change (light alone does not change the indicator).
parts.working: B1 control to show the change is due to the leaf

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the indicator in tube D stayed the same colour.
parts.answer: In dim light the rate of photosynthesis equalled the rate of respiration, so there was no net change in carbon dioxide concentration.
parts.working: B1 photosynthesis rate = respiration rate (compensation point); B1 no net uptake or release of CO₂

practice.stem: In a pondweed investigation, relative light intensity is calculated using the formula: relative light intensity = 10 000 ÷ d², where d is the distance of the lamp from the plant in cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative light intensity at 25 cm and at 50 cm.
parts.answer: 25 cm: 16.0 units; 50 cm: 4.0 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many times greater the light intensity is at 25 cm than at 50 cm.
parts.answer: 4 times
parts.working: B1 16 ÷ 4 = 4 (halving the distance gives four times the light)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The volume of oxygen collected at 25 cm was only 2.5 times the volume collected at 50 cm. Suggest why it was not 4 times greater.
parts.answer: At the higher light intensity another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, was limiting, so the rate could not rise in proportion to light.
parts.working: B1 another factor limiting at high light (CO₂ / temperature named); B1 so rate is not proportional to light intensity / light no longer the only limiting factor

practice.stem:
The rate of photosynthesis of a crop plant (arbitrary units) was measured at 25 °C.
Light intensity / units: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
Rate at 0.04% CO₂: 0, 12, 20, 24, 24, 24
Rate at 0.10% CO₂: 0, 12, 24, 34, 40, 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the factor limiting the rate at a light intensity of 2 units for both concentrations of carbon dioxide. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Light intensity; the rate is the same at both carbon dioxide concentrations (and rises when light increases).
parts.working: B1 light intensity; B1 same rate at both CO₂ levels

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the factor limiting the rate at 0.04% carbon dioxide and a light intensity of 8 units. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide concentration; increasing CO₂ to 0.10% raises the rate, while more light does not.
parts.working: B1 carbon dioxide concentration; B1 higher CO₂ gives higher rate / plateau with more light

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate at a light intensity of 8 units when the carbon dioxide concentration is raised from 0.04% to 0.10%. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one factor that could be limiting the rate at 0.10% carbon dioxide and a light intensity of 10 units.
parts.answer: Temperature (or amount of chlorophyll / number of chloroplasts / enzymes).
parts.working: B1 temperature or another valid internal factor; not light or CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed. Your plan should include the apparatus, the method, the variables to control and how the results would be recorded.
parts.answer: Pondweed in a boiling tube of hydrogencarbonate solution placed in water baths at a range of temperatures (e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 °C); acclimatise 5 minutes; count bubbles or collect gas volume in a set time (e.g. 1 minute); keep light intensity (lamp at fixed distance), CO₂ concentration and the same piece/length of pondweed constant; repeat 3 times and calculate a mean; record in a table of temperature against bubbles per minute; plot rate against temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: water baths/thermostatic control; at least 5 temperatures with a stated range; acclimatisation time; measure bubbles/gas volume in fixed time; light at fixed distance/same lamp; same CO₂/hydrogencarbonate concentration; same plant/length of pondweed; repeats and mean; results table with units / graph

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Magnesium ions taken up by a plant are needed to make
A chlorophyll
B protein
C cellulose
D starch
parts.answer: A chlorophyll
parts.working: Magnesium is part of the chlorophyll molecule. Protein (B) needs nitrogen from nitrate ions, not magnesium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why plants need nitrate ions.
parts.answer: To make amino acids (and so proteins).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two visible signs of nitrate ion deficiency in a plant.
parts.answer: Stunted (poor) growth; yellowing of the (older, lower) leaves.
parts.working: 1 mark each: stunted/weak growth; yellow leaves

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a plant growing in soil that lacks magnesium ions grows slowly.
parts.answer: Magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll; less chlorophyll is made, so leaves turn yellow; less light is absorbed so the rate of photosynthesis falls; less glucose is available for respiration and for making new materials (e.g. cellulose, proteins) for growth.
parts.working: B1 Mg for chlorophyll; B1 less chlorophyll/yellow leaves; B1 less light absorbed/less photosynthesis; B1 less glucose for growth/energy/new cells

practice.stem:
Maize seedlings were grown for 4 weeks in jars of different solutions.
Solution 1: complete nutrient solution – mean height 32 cm, dark green leaves
Solution 2: no nitrate – mean height 11 cm, pale yellow older leaves
Solution 3: no magnesium – mean height 18 cm, yellow between the leaf veins
Solution 4: distilled water – mean height 6 cm, very pale leaves

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which solution acts as the control.
parts.answer: Solution 1 (complete nutrient solution)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean height of seedlings in solution 2 as a percentage of the mean height in solution 1. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the appearance of the seedlings in solution 3.
parts.answer: No magnesium so less chlorophyll is made; leaves turn yellow (between the veins) and less photosynthesis means slower growth.
parts.working: B1 no Mg → little chlorophyll / yellow leaves; B1 less photosynthesis → less growth

parts.label: d
parts.text: Air was bubbled through each jar. Suggest why.
parts.answer: To supply oxygen to the roots for aerobic respiration; this releases energy for active transport (uptake) of ions.
parts.working: B1 oxygen for root respiration; B1 energy for active uptake of mineral ions

parts.label: e
parts.text: Each jar was covered with black paper. Suggest why.
parts.answer: To stop algae growing in the solution (algae would compete for ions).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitrate ions are often at a higher concentration inside root hair cells than in the soil water. Explain how root hair cells absorb nitrate ions.
parts.answer: By active transport; ions move against the concentration gradient (from lower to higher concentration) using carrier proteins in the membrane; energy is released by respiration in the root cells.
parts.working: B1 active transport; B1 against the concentration gradient; B1 energy from respiration (carrier proteins)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a crop growing in waterlogged soil absorbs fewer nitrate ions.
parts.answer: Waterlogged soil contains little oxygen (air spaces filled with water); root cells carry out less aerobic respiration; so less energy is released for active transport of ions.
parts.working: B1 less oxygen in soil; B1 less aerobic respiration in roots; B1 less energy for active transport

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how adding nitrate fertiliser increases the yield of a wheat crop.
parts.answer: Nitrate is used to make amino acids and proteins; these are needed for growth of new cells (e.g. enzymes, more leaves), so the plant grows larger and produces more grain.
parts.working: B1 amino acids/proteins made; B1 more growth / more leaves / more photosynthesis → greater yield

practice.stem:
A farmer in Punjab tested different amounts of nitrate fertiliser on wheat.
Fertiliser / kg per ha: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200
Yield / tonnes per ha: 2.8, 4.1, 5.0, 5.4, 5.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in yield for each of these steps: 0 to 50 kg/ha, and 150 to 200 kg/ha.
parts.answer: 0 to 50: 1.3 tonnes/ha; 150 to 200: 0.1 tonnes/ha
parts.working: M1 subtraction from table; A1 both values

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in yield when the fertiliser is raised from 0 to 150 kg/ha. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The farmer decides to use 150 kg/ha rather than 200 kg/ha. Suggest two reasons for this decision.
parts.answer: The extra 50 kg gives very little extra yield, so the cost of the fertiliser is greater than the value of the extra crop; excess fertiliser may be washed (leached) into rivers and cause eutrophication.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: small extra yield; cost not repaid/profit; leaching/run-off; eutrophication/water pollution; another factor now limiting

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which tissue of a leaf do the cells contain the most chloroplasts?
A upper epidermis
B palisade mesophyll
C spongy mesophyll
D xylem
parts.answer: B palisade mesophyll
parts.working: Palisade mesophyll cells are packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface where light is brightest. Spongy mesophyll (C) has fewer chloroplasts and more air spaces.

practice.stem:
A student describes a section through a leaf, from top to bottom:
W – a thin, waxy layer with no cells
X – a single layer of transparent cells with no chloroplasts
Y – tall, column-shaped cells packed with chloroplasts
Z – rounded, loosely packed cells with large air spaces between them
The lowest layer of cells contains many small pores, each surrounded by a pair of bean-shaped cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name layers W, X, Y and Z.
parts.answer: W cuticle; X upper epidermis; Y palisade mesophyll; Z spongy mesophyll

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the pores in the lower layer and the cells on either side of each pore.
parts.answer: Stomata; guard cells

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how palisade mesophyll cells are adapted for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: They contain many chloroplasts to absorb light; they are near the upper surface where light intensity is greatest; they are tall/closely packed, so many fit in the layer and absorb most light.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: many chloroplasts; near upper surface; closely packed/column shape; thin walls/large vacuole pushes chloroplasts to edge

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the air spaces in the spongy mesophyll.
parts.answer: Allow gases (carbon dioxide and oxygen) to diffuse quickly through the leaf to and from the cells; provide a large surface area for gas exchange.
parts.working: B1 diffusion of CO₂ to cells / O₂ away; B1 large surface area for gas exchange

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the upper epidermis has no chloroplasts and is transparent.
parts.answer: So that light passes through to the palisade cells below.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pathway taken by a carbon dioxide molecule from the air outside a leaf to a chloroplast in a palisade cell.
parts.answer: Through an open stoma; diffuses through the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll; dissolves in the film of water on the cell surface and diffuses through the cell wall and membrane into the chloroplast.
parts.working: B1 enters via stoma; B1 through air spaces; B1 dissolves in moisture / through cell wall and membrane into chloroplast

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf during the day.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide is used up in photosynthesis, so its concentration inside the leaf is lower than in the air; it diffuses down the concentration gradient.
parts.working: B1 used in photosynthesis; B1 lower concentration inside / down concentration gradient

practice.stem:
A student painted clear nail varnish on both surfaces of a hibiscus leaf, peeled it off and counted stomata in five fields of view under a microscope. The diameter of the field of view was 0.4 mm.
Lower surface: 22, 25, 19, 24, 20
Upper surface: 3, 5, 4, 2, 6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of stomata per field of view for each surface.
parts.answer: Lower: 22; upper: 4

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the area of the field of view in mm². Use area = πr². Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of stomata per mm² on the lower surface. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 175 stomata per mm²

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why there are more stomata on the lower surface of this leaf.
parts.answer: The lower surface is shaded and cooler; so less water is lost by transpiration/evaporation than if stomata were on the upper surface.
parts.working: B1 lower surface cooler/out of direct sunlight; B1 reduces water loss

practice.stem:
A student measured leaves from the top (sunny) and the lower (shaded) branches of a mango tree.
Sun leaves: palisade layer 120 µm thick, mean leaf area 42 cm²
Shade leaves: palisade layer 60 µm thick, mean leaf area 68 cm²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the palisade thickness of sun leaves to shade leaves.
parts.answer: 2 : 1 (twice as thick)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an advantage to the tree of having a thicker palisade layer in sun leaves.
parts.answer: More layers of palisade cells / more chloroplasts; so more of the bright light is absorbed and used, giving more photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 more palisade cells/chloroplasts; B1 absorb more light → more photosynthesis

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why shade leaves have a larger surface area.
parts.answer: Light is dim in the shade; a larger area traps more of the limited light for photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 low light intensity in shade; B1 larger area absorbs more light

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why shade leaves are thinner.
parts.answer: Little light reaches deep layers, so extra layers of cells would not photosynthesise much (and would use materials/respire).
parts.working: B1 little light penetrates / thick leaf not needed

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis?
A 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
B 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
C C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
D CO₂ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂
parts.answer: A 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
parts.working: A has 6 C, 18 O and 12 H on each side. C is the equation for aerobic respiration, the reverse of photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (in the presence of light and chlorophyll)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the source of energy for photosynthesis and name the substance that absorbs it.
parts.answer: Light (from the Sun); chlorophyll

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where water used in photosynthesis enters the plant.
parts.answer: Through the root hair cells (roots)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four ways in which a plant uses the glucose made in photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Any four of: respiration to release energy; converted to starch for storage; cellulose for cell walls; sucrose for transport in phloem; amino acids/proteins (with nitrate ions); fats and oils for storage (e.g. in seeds); nectar to attract insects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why glucose is converted to starch for storage in leaf cells.
parts.answer: Starch is insoluble; so it does not affect the water potential of the cell / cause osmosis (and does not diffuse out of the cell).
parts.working: B1 starch insoluble; B1 no effect on osmosis / water potential, or compact and stays in cell

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define photosynthesis.
parts.answer: The process by which plants make carbohydrates (glucose) from raw materials (carbon dioxide and water) using energy from light.
parts.working: B1 makes carbohydrates/glucose from CO₂ and water; B1 using light energy

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of chlorophyll in photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy; and transfers it into chemical energy (for making carbohydrates).
parts.working: B1 absorbs light; B1 converts/transfers it to chemical energy

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two things that can happen to the oxygen made in a palisade cell.
parts.answer: Used in respiration in the plant's own cells; diffuses out of the leaf through the stomata into the air.

practice.stem: A maize crop was kept in a sealed chamber with 12 hours of light and 12 hours of darkness. In the light, the crop took in carbon dioxide at a rate of 30 units per hour. In the dark, it released carbon dioxide at a rate of 6 units per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net uptake of carbon dioxide by the crop over the whole 24 hours.
parts.answer: 288 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the crop releases carbon dioxide at night.
parts.answer: There is no light so no photosynthesis; respiration continues all the time and releases carbon dioxide.
parts.working: B1 no photosynthesis in dark; B1 respiration releases CO₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: The measured uptake of 30 units per hour in the light is less than the true rate of photosynthesis. Explain why.
parts.answer: During the day the plant also respires; some of the carbon dioxide used in photosynthesis comes from respiration inside the plant, so the measured uptake = photosynthesis − respiration.
parts.working: B1 respiration also happens in the light; B1 CO₂ from respiration used, so uptake underestimates gross photosynthesis

practice.stem:
A student tests a leaf for starch.
Step 1: the leaf is placed in boiling water for 1 minute.
Step 2: the leaf is placed in a tube of ethanol in a hot water bath until it turns white.
Step 3: the leaf is dipped into warm water.
Step 4: the leaf is spread on a white tile and covered with iodine solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reason for each of steps 1 to 4.
parts.answer: 1: kills the cells / stops reactions and breaks down membranes so iodine can enter; 2: removes the chlorophyll (decolourises the leaf) so the colour change can be seen; 3: softens the brittle leaf (and removes ethanol); 4: tests for starch.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the ethanol is heated in a water bath and not directly over a Bunsen burner.
parts.answer: Ethanol is flammable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour seen if the leaf contains starch and if it contains no starch.
parts.answer: Starch present: blue-black; no starch: orange-brown (colour of iodine).

practice.stem:
A potted plant with variegated leaves (green areas with chlorophyll and white areas without) was kept in the dark for 48 hours. A strip of aluminium foil was then fixed across part of one leaf and the plant was placed in sunlight for 6 hours. The leaf was then tested for starch.
Region P: green, not covered
Region Q: white, not covered
Region R: green, covered by foil

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the plant was kept in the dark for 48 hours before the experiment.
parts.answer: To destarch the leaves; the plant uses up its stored starch (converted to sugar and respired/translocated), so any starch found later must have been made during the experiment.
parts.working: B1 removes starch / destarching; B1 so starch present must come from photosynthesis during the experiment

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the colour after the iodine test in each of regions P, Q and R. Explain each prediction.
parts.answer: P (green, uncovered): blue-black – it had chlorophyll and light so photosynthesised and made starch. Q (white, uncovered): orange-brown – no chlorophyll so no photosynthesis. R (green, covered): orange-brown – no light reached it so no photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 P blue-black; B1 Q orange-brown; B1 R orange-brown; B1 Q explained (no chlorophyll); B1 R explained (no light)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which two regions show that light is needed for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: P and R

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the arrangement of tissues in a leaf allows as much light as possible to be absorbed.
parts.answer: Leaf is broad/flat with large surface area; thin so light reaches all cells; upper epidermis and cuticle are transparent; palisade layer with most chloroplasts is just below the upper surface; spongy cells also contain chloroplasts to absorb light passing through.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: large surface area; thin; transparent cuticle/epidermis; palisade near top; many chloroplasts in palisade; chloroplasts can move/spongy layer absorbs remaining light

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how guard cells control the opening of a stoma during the day and explain why this is important for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: In light, guard cells take in water and become turgid; this makes them curve apart and the stoma opens; carbon dioxide can then diffuse in for photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 guard cells absorb water/turgid; B1 stoma opens; B1 CO₂ enters for photosynthesis (O₂ leaves)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the vascular bundles in a leaf support photosynthesis and transport its products.
parts.answer: Xylem brings water (a raw material) and mineral ions such as magnesium to the mesophyll; phloem carries sucrose (and amino acids) made in photosynthesis away from the leaf to other parts of the plant; the network of veins means every cell is close to a vein; xylem also helps to support the leaf so it is held out flat to the light.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: xylem supplies water; xylem supplies mineral ions; phloem removes sucrose/amino acids; translocation to growing/storage parts; branching veins close to all cells; support/lignin keeps blade spread

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why most leaves are thin.
parts.answer: Short diffusion distance for gases (CO₂ in, O₂ out) to and from all cells; light can reach all the cells.
parts.working: B1 short diffusion distance for gases; B1 light penetrates to all cells

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a leaf has a waxy cuticle even though this reduces gas exchange through the surface.
parts.answer: It reduces water loss by evaporation; gases can still enter through the stomata.
parts.working: B1 reduces water loss (gases use stomata)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student adds biuret solution to a sample of liquid egg white and shakes the tube. What colour shows that protein is present?
A blue-black
B brick red
C purple
D cloudy white
parts.answer: C purple
parts.working: Biuret solution is blue and turns purple (violet) with protein. Blue-black is the iodine result for starch, so A is a distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which food test must be carried out in a hot water bath?
A Benedict's test for reducing sugar
B biuret test for protein
C ethanol emulsion test for fat
D iodine test for starch
parts.answer: A Benedict's test for reducing sugar
parts.working: Benedict's solution only reacts with reducing sugar when heated (about 80 °C water bath). The iodine test is done cold, so D is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the reagent used to test a food for starch.
parts.answer: iodine solution
parts.working: B1 iodine (solution); accept iodine in potassium iodide

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour of the reagent before the test and the colour seen if starch is present.
parts.answer: before: orange-brown (yellow-brown); with starch: blue-black

parts.label: c
parts.text: A potato slice gives a positive result. Suggest why a slice of ripe mango gives only a weak result.
parts.answer: most of the starch in ripe mango has been converted to sugars
parts.working: B1 starch broken down/converted to (reducing) sugar during ripening

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would test a sample of ground peanuts for fat using the ethanol emulsion test.
parts.answer: Mix/shake the crushed peanut with ethanol; pour the ethanol (liquid) into a tube of water (or add water); a cloudy white emulsion shows fat.
parts.working: B1 shake sample with ethanol; B1 add (decant) the ethanol into water; B1 cloudy/milky white emulsion = fat present

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the test tube and sample must be kept away from a Bunsen flame.
parts.answer: ethanol is flammable

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the food substance detected by each of these tests.
Test 1: iodine solution
Test 2: Benedict's solution
Test 3: biuret solution
Test 4: ethanol emulsion
parts.answer: 1 starch; 2 reducing sugar; 3 protein; 4 fat (lipid)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which test needs heating?
parts.answer: Test 2 (Benedict's)

practice.stem:
Four food samples, P, Q, R and S, were tested. Results:
P: iodine blue-black; Benedict's blue; biuret purple; emulsion clear
Q: iodine orange-brown; Benedict's brick red; biuret blue; emulsion cloudy white
R: iodine orange-brown; Benedict's blue; biuret blue; emulsion cloudy white
S: iodine blue-black; Benedict's green; biuret blue; emulsion clear

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the substances present in sample P and in sample Q.
parts.answer: P: starch and protein; Q: reducing sugar and fat
parts.working: B1 P both correct; B1 Q both correct

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which sample could be a mixture of fruit juice and coconut milk? Give a reason.
parts.answer: Q, because fruit juice gives reducing sugar and coconut milk gives fat
parts.working: B1 Q; B1 reducing sugar (from juice) and fat (from coconut milk)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one variable that should be kept the same when doing each test on the four samples.
parts.answer: volume of sample (or volume of reagent, temperature/time of heating for Benedict's)
parts.working: B1 any one sensible controlled variable

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the food test that uses copper(II) sulfate and sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: biuret test

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the food test that turns brick red.
parts.answer: Benedict's test

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of a food that gives a positive ethanol emulsion test.
parts.answer: e.g. butter, ghee, cooking oil, nuts

practice.stem:
Benedict's test was done on four samples heated for 4 minutes at 80 °C.
Tube 1 (sugarcane juice, diluted): yellow
Tube 2 (milk): green
Tube 3 (apple juice): brick red
Tube 4 (distilled water): blue

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which tube shows the most reducing sugar.
parts.answer: tube 3

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the control tube.
parts.answer: tube 4 (water)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why all tubes were heated for exactly the same time.
parts.answer: colour continues to change with time, so a fair comparison needs equal heating

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A crushed sample of a food gave these results.
iodine solution: stays orange-brown
Benedict's solution, heated: turns orange
biuret solution: stays blue
ethanol emulsion test: clear
Which food could it be?
A boiled rice
B grape juice
C cooking oil
D boiled egg white
parts.answer: B grape juice
parts.working: Only reducing sugar is present, which fits grape juice (glucose and fructose). Boiled rice would give blue-black with iodine, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to carry out the Benedict's test on a sample of honey dissolved in water. Include the safety precaution you would take.
parts.answer: Add an equal volume of Benedict's solution to the honey solution; heat in a water bath at about 80 °C for a few minutes; wear eye protection (goggles).
parts.working: B1 add Benedict's (equal volume); B1 heat in water bath (not direct flame), named time/temperature; B1 goggles/eye protection or use test-tube holder

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour change seen if a large amount of reducing sugar is present.
parts.answer: blue to brick red

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a negative result with Benedict's solution does not prove that a food contains no sugar at all.
parts.answer: some sugars, such as sucrose, are non-reducing and do not react with Benedict's solution
parts.working: B1 non-reducing sugar (sucrose) gives no colour change

parts.label: a
parts.text: A food technologist in Faisalabad tests a new flavoured milk drink. It gives a purple colour with biuret solution and a green colour with Benedict's solution. State what these results show.
parts.answer: protein present; small amount of reducing sugar present
parts.working: B1 protein; B1 (little/small amount of) reducing sugar

parts.label: b
parts.text: Biuret solution can be made by mixing two solutions. Name the two solutions.
parts.answer: sodium hydroxide (or potassium hydroxide) and copper(II) sulfate
parts.working: B1 sodium/potassium hydroxide; B1 copper sulfate

parts.label: c
parts.text: The technologist also tests plain water in the same way. Explain why.
parts.answer: it is a control, to show that the reagents alone do not give a colour change
parts.working: B1 control / to compare / show colour is due to the food

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: "Chapati gave a blue-black colour with iodine, so chapati contains only starch." Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: a positive iodine test only shows starch is present; other substances (protein, fat) may also be present and need their own tests
parts.working: B1 test only shows starch; B1 other nutrients need other tests / chapati also contains protein/fat

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could find out whether the chapati also contains protein.
parts.answer: crush with water, add biuret solution (sodium hydroxide then copper sulfate); purple shows protein

practice.stem:
A student heated 2 cm³ of each of four drinks, A to D, with 2 cm³ Benedict's solution in a water bath at 80 °C. She recorded the time for the first appearance of green.
A: 85 s
B: 240 s
C: 40 s
D: 130 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the results to put the drinks in order of reducing sugar content, highest first.
parts.answer: C, A, D, B

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the time taken links to the reducing sugar concentration.
parts.answer: the higher the concentration, the shorter the time for the colour to change

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate a relative rate of colour change for drink A as 1000/time (arbitrary units), giving your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 1000 ÷ 85 = 11.8 (arbitrary units)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way to make the end point of the test more reliable.
parts.answer: compare against a colour standard/chart, or use the same observer, white tile behind the tube, or repeat and average

practice.stem:
A student crushed 2 g each of lentils (daal), boiled rice, chicken and banana with 10 cm³ water and tested them with biuret solution.
lentils: deep purple
boiled rice: very pale lilac
chicken: purple
banana: blue

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why each crushed sample was mixed with the same volume of water.
parts.answer: so that the comparison is fair / the concentration depends only on the food

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which food contained the most protein? Explain how you decided.
parts.answer: lentils, because they gave the deepest purple

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe one hazard in this test and how to reduce it.
parts.answer: sodium hydroxide is corrosive/irritant: wear eye protection

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest an improvement so that the colours could be compared more objectively.
parts.answer: use a colorimeter, or compare with a colour chart of known protein standards

practice.stem:
Four unlabelled tubes, W, X, Y and Z, contain glucose solution, starch suspension, albumin (protein) solution and an oil-in-water mixture, in some order.
W: iodine orange-brown; Benedict's blue; biuret blue
X: iodine orange-brown; Benedict's brick red; biuret blue
Y: iodine blue-black; Benedict's blue; biuret blue
Z: iodine orange-brown; Benedict's blue; biuret purple

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the solution in each tube.
parts.answer: X: glucose; Y: starch; Z: albumin (protein)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what tube W must contain, and explain how you can tell from these results.
parts.answer: the oil-in-water mixture; W gave negative results in all three tests, and glucose, starch and albumin have already been identified in X, Y and Z, so W is the only one left (by elimination)
parts.working: B1 oil/fat; B1 negative for all three tests and the other three solutions identified (elimination)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a further test to confirm that W is the oil-in-water mixture, and state the expected result.
parts.answer: ethanol emulsion test: cloudy white

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student in Lahore tests milk for fat by shaking it with ethanol and pouring into water. The result is cloudy. Explain why this result might be unreliable unless a control is used.
parts.answer: milk itself is cloudy/white, so the cloudiness may not be due to an emulsion; a control (milk + water without ethanol) is needed for comparison
parts.working: B1 milk already cloudy/opaque; B1 compare with control

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why fats form a cloudy emulsion in this test.
parts.answer: fat dissolves in ethanol but is insoluble in water, so it forms tiny droplets when the ethanol is added to water
parts.working: B1 fat insoluble in water, droplets form

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Four glucose solutions of different concentrations were each heated with the same volume of Benedict's solution for 5 minutes. Which final colour shows the highest concentration of glucose?
A blue
B green
C yellow
D brick red
parts.answer: D brick red
parts.working: The more reducing sugar, the more precipitate forms and the colour moves blue → green → yellow → orange → brick red. Yellow (C) shows less sugar than brick red.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A doctor suspects that a patient has diabetes. Explain how a Benedict's test on the patient's urine could support this diagnosis.
parts.answer: glucose is a reducing sugar; urine of a person with diabetes may contain glucose, so the test turns green/yellow/orange/red instead of staying blue
parts.working: B1 glucose present in urine of diabetic (not normally present); B1 positive (colour change from blue) result

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the Benedict's test is not used to measure exact blood glucose concentration in a hospital.
parts.answer: it is only semi-quantitative: the colours are judged by eye and only show a rough range; it does not give a number
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: colour judged subjectively; only rough/semi-quantitative; colours overlap; slow/needs heating; other reducing sugars also react

parts.label: a
parts.text: A seed is cut in half and one half is crushed with water, then filtered. Explain why the seed must be crushed before testing it for starch and protein.
parts.answer: crushing breaks open cells (cell walls) so the starch/protein is released and can mix with the reagent
parts.working: B1 breaks cells/cell walls; B1 releases contents / larger surface area for reagent to reach

parts.label: b
parts.text: The filtrate gives a blue-black colour with iodine but the solid residue on the filter paper gives an even darker colour. Suggest why.
parts.answer: starch is insoluble (large molecules), so most stayed in the residue; only a little passed through into the filtrate
parts.working: B1 starch insoluble/large molecules; B1 most starch remains in the residue

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the result you would expect with Benedict's solution if the seed has just started to germinate, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: orange/red (positive) because amylase breaks down starch into maltose, a reducing sugar
parts.working: B1 colour change from blue (green to red); B1 starch digested to maltose/reducing sugar by amylase

practice.stem: A student had a 10 % glucose stock solution and distilled water. She wanted to make 10 cm³ each of 2 %, 4 %, 6 % and 8 % glucose standards to compare with an unknown sample using Benedict's solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of the stock solution and of distilled water needed to make 10 cm³ of each standard. Give the volumes for 2 %, 4 % and 6 %.
parts.answer: 2 %: 2 cm³ stock + 8 cm³ water; 4 %: 4 cm³ stock + 6 cm³ water; 6 %: 6 cm³ stock + 4 cm³ water

parts.label: b
parts.text: The unknown sample went the same colour as the 4 % standard after the same heating time. State the glucose concentration of the unknown, and suggest how to make the estimate more precise.
parts.answer: about 4 %; make more standards with smaller intervals (e.g. 3.5 %, 4.5 %) around 4 %
parts.working: B1 4 % (between 3 and 5 %); B1 smaller intervals / use a colorimeter

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept constant.
parts.answer: volume of Benedict's solution; volume of sample; temperature of water bath; time of heating

practice.stem:
Starch solution and amylase were mixed at 35 °C. Every 2 minutes a drop of the mixture was added to a drop of iodine solution on a spotting tile.
0 min: blue-black
2 min: blue-black
4 min: dark brown
6 min: orange-brown
8 min: orange-brown

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the time when all the starch had been digested.
parts.answer: 6 minutes
parts.working: B1 first sample to stay orange-brown

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the colour of the iodine changed during the experiment.
parts.answer: amylase digested starch into maltose (reducing sugar); iodine stays orange-brown when no starch is left
parts.working: B1 amylase breaks down starch; B1 to maltose/sugar so no blue-black

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test you could do on the mixture at 8 minutes to show a product of the reaction, and state the expected result.
parts.answer: Benedict's test: heat with Benedict's in a water bath; brick red/orange (colour change from blue)
parts.working: B1 Benedict's + heat; B1 positive colour

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the rate of starch digestion as 1/time in min⁻¹, to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to compare the reducing sugar content of three brands of orange juice using Benedict's solution. Include the variables you would control and how you would record results.
parts.answer: Same volume of each juice (e.g. 2 cm³) + same volume of Benedict's (2 cm³); heat in a water bath at the same temperature (80 °C) for the same time, or time until first colour change; compare colours with a range of glucose standards or record time; repeat three times and average; wear goggles; record in a table (brand, colour/time, repeats, mean).
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to six of: same volume juice; same volume Benedict's; water bath stated temp; same time / time to colour change; dilute juices equally if needed; standards of known glucose concentration; repeats and mean; safety (goggles); table with headings; conclusion: more sugar = redder / shorter time

parts.label: a
parts.text: A solution of the enzyme amylase is tested with biuret solution and with Benedict's solution. Predict both results and explain them.
parts.answer: biuret: purple, because amylase is a protein; Benedict's: stays blue, because there is no reducing sugar
parts.working: B1 purple + enzyme is protein; B1 Benedict's blue/negative

parts.label: b
parts.text: The amylase solution is mixed with starch suspension and left at 37 °C for 15 minutes. Predict the results of the iodine, Benedict's and biuret tests on the mixture. Explain each prediction.
parts.answer: iodine: orange-brown (starch digested); Benedict's: positive, green to brick red (maltose produced); biuret: purple (enzyme is still present, unchanged at the end of the reaction)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which molecules are joined together to form a protein?
A amino acids
B fatty acids
C glucose
D glycerol
parts.answer: A amino acids
parts.working: Proteins are chains of amino acids. Fatty acids and glycerol make fats, so B is a distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the smaller molecules that make up:
(i) starch
(ii) fats and oils
parts.answer: (i) glucose; (ii) fatty acids and glycerol
parts.working: B1 glucose; B1 fatty acids; B1 glycerol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the chemical elements found in all carbohydrates.
parts.answer: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the polysaccharide stored in the liver and muscles of humans.
parts.answer: glycogen

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the polysaccharide that forms plant cell walls.
parts.answer: cellulose

parts.label: c
parts.text: Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all made of the same smaller molecule. Name it, and state one reason why starch is a good storage molecule.
parts.answer: glucose; insoluble so it does not affect osmosis (or compact, large)
parts.working: B1 glucose; B1 insoluble/does not affect water potential/compact

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sucrose is the sugar in sugarcane. Name the two simple sugars that make one sucrose molecule.
parts.answer: glucose and fructose

parts.label: b
parts.text: Maltose is made when starch is digested. State the simple sugar it is made of.
parts.answer: glucose (two glucose units)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which one of these carbohydrates is insoluble in water: glucose, cellulose, maltose.
parts.answer: cellulose
parts.working: B1 cellulose (a polysaccharide); glucose and maltose are soluble sugars

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one element found in proteins that is not found in carbohydrates or fats.
parts.answer: nitrogen (also sulfur in some)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Different enzymes have different shapes even though they are all made of amino acids. Explain why.
parts.answer: different sequence (order) of amino acids; this makes the chain fold into a different shape
parts.working: B1 sequence/order of amino acids; B1 folds into specific shape

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a person whose diet lacks protein may not be able to make some enzymes.
parts.answer: enzymes are proteins made from amino acids obtained from dietary protein

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property of water makes it important for transporting substances in blood plasma and phloem?
A It is a solvent for many substances.
B It contains nitrogen.
C It is a source of energy.
D It is an enzyme.
parts.answer: A It is a solvent for many substances.
parts.working: Water dissolves many substances (glucose, ions, urea), so they can be carried in solution. Water provides no energy, so C is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why water is important as a solvent in living organisms. Give two examples.
parts.answer: many substances dissolve in water so they can be transported (e.g. glucose in plasma, sucrose in phloem) and so that chemical reactions (e.g. digestion, enzyme reactions) can take place in solution; urea removed in urine
parts.working: B1 substances dissolve so can be transported/react; 1 mark each for two examples: transport in blood/plasma, transport in phloem/xylem, digestion, excretion of urea in urine, reactions in cytoplasm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says fats contain the same elements as carbohydrates. State whether this is correct and give one difference in their composition.
parts.answer: correct (C, H, O); fats have much less oxygen in proportion to carbon and hydrogen

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which enzyme digests protein in the stomach?
A amylase
B lipase
C maltase
D pepsin
parts.answer: D pepsin
parts.working: Pepsin is the protease of the stomach and works in acid. Amylase digests starch, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by chemical digestion.
parts.answer: the breakdown of large insoluble molecules into small soluble molecules by enzymes
parts.working: B1 large insoluble → small soluble; B1 by enzymes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of physical (mechanical) digestion in the alimentary canal.
parts.answer: chewing by teeth; churning by the stomach muscles (also emulsification by bile)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how physical digestion helps chemical digestion.
parts.answer: it increases the surface area for enzymes to act on

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the following for each enzyme: the food it digests and the product(s).
(i) amylase
(ii) protease
(iii) lipase
parts.answer: (i) starch → maltose; (ii) protein → amino acids; (iii) fat → fatty acids and glycerol
parts.working: B1 each (substrate and product both needed)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the enzyme on the lining of the small intestine that completes the digestion of starch, and its product.
parts.answer: maltase; glucose

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the function of bile in digestion?
A It breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
B It emulsifies fats into small droplets.
C It digests starch to maltose.
D It makes the small intestine acidic.
parts.answer: B It emulsifies fats into small droplets.
parts.working: Bile emulsifies fat (physical digestion), increasing surface area for lipase. Bile contains no enzyme, so A (the action of lipase) is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the roles of hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
parts.answer: kills bacteria/microorganisms in food; gives a low (acidic) pH which is the optimum for pepsin
parts.working: B1 kills pathogens/bacteria; B1 optimum pH for pepsin/enzymes in stomach

parts.label: b
parts.text: Trypsin is a protease made by the pancreas. Suggest why trypsin does not work well in the stomach.
parts.answer: its optimum pH is about 8 (alkaline); the acid of the stomach denatures it / it works slowly at low pH
parts.working: B1 optimum pH alkaline/neutral; B1 acid denatures / changes active site shape

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the contents of the duodenum are made slightly alkaline.
parts.answer: bile (and pancreatic juice) neutralise the acid from the stomach

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of tooth used for:
(i) biting off pieces of naan
(ii) grinding food into smaller pieces
parts.answer: (i) incisors; (ii) molars (and premolars)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why food that is chewed well is digested faster.
parts.answer: chewing breaks food into smaller pieces with a larger surface area; enzymes (such as salivary amylase) can act on more of the food at once
parts.working: B1 larger surface area; B1 more contact with enzymes/faster enzyme action

practice.stem:
Three tubes contained 5 cm³ milk, sodium carbonate solution and a pH indicator (pink in alkali, colourless at about pH 7).
Tube A: + 1 cm³ lipase + 1 cm³ bile salts
Tube B: + 1 cm³ lipase + 1 cm³ water
Tube C: + 1 cm³ boiled lipase + 1 cm³ bile salts
Time for the pink colour to disappear (three repeats):
A: 12, 14, 13 min
B: 25, 29, 27 min
C: no change after 60 min

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean time for tube A and for tube B. Give your answers to the nearest minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the two results.
parts.answer: in A the fat was emulsified by bile into small droplets, giving a larger surface area for lipase, so it was digested faster
parts.working: B1 bile emulsifies; B1 larger surface area for lipase

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the pH falls as the fat is digested.
parts.answer: fatty acids are produced

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the purpose of tube C.
parts.answer: control: shows that the pH fall is caused by lipase

parts.label: a
parts.text: A piece of boiled egg white is placed in a tube with pepsin and dilute hydrochloric acid at 37 °C. After 2 hours the cloudy egg white has become clear. Explain this observation.
parts.answer: pepsin digested the protein into smaller soluble molecules (peptides/amino acids), which dissolve so the liquid clears
parts.working: B1 protein digested by pepsin; B1 products soluble

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict and explain the result if the tube had been kept at 70 °C.
parts.answer: egg white stays cloudy: pepsin is denatured (active site changes shape), so no digestion
parts.working: B1 no change; B1 denatured / active site shape lost

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the egg white was cut into small cubes of equal size.
parts.answer: equal surface area so the comparison is fair / larger surface area for faster digestion

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the products of chemical digestion must be small, soluble molecules.
parts.answer: so they can pass through the wall of the small intestine (be absorbed) into the blood/lymph
parts.working: B1 absorbed through intestine wall/membranes; B1 into blood/transported

parts.label: b
parts.text: People who have had their gall bladder removed are advised to eat less fat at each meal. Suggest why.
parts.answer: bile is not stored, so less bile is released at a meal; fat is less emulsified and is digested more slowly / poorly
parts.working: B1 less bile available (released) at once; B1 less emulsification, fat digested less

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mineral is needed to make haemoglobin?
A calcium
B iodine
C iron
D nitrogen
parts.answer: C iron
parts.working: Iron is part of haemoglobin; lack causes anaemia. Calcium is needed for bones and teeth, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a balanced diet.
parts.answer: a diet with all the nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water) in the correct amounts/proportions to meet the body's needs
parts.working: B1 all nutrients/food groups; B1 correct proportions/amounts

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the deficiency disease caused by a lack of vitamin C and state one symptom.
parts.answer: scurvy; bleeding gums (or slow wound healing)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one food rich in vitamin C.
parts.answer: citrus fruit such as oranges, lemons; guava; tomatoes

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A child living indoors for long periods develops soft, bent leg bones. Which deficiency is most likely?
A vitamin C
B vitamin D
C iron
D fibre
parts.answer: B vitamin D
parts.working: Lack of vitamin D (made in skin in sunlight) reduces calcium absorption and causes rickets. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, not bent bones.

practice.stem: A lunch of rice and chicken korma contains 60 g carbohydrate, 20 g protein and 15 g fat. Energy values: carbohydrate 17 kJ/g, protein 17 kJ/g, fat 39 kJ/g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy in the meal in kJ.
parts.working: M1 multiply each mass by its energy value; A1 1945

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which nutrient in the meal provides the most energy per gram.
parts.answer: fat

parts.label: c
parts.text: Fibre provides no usable energy. Explain why fibre is still needed in the diet.
parts.answer: it adds bulk, helping peristalsis (movement of food through the gut); prevents constipation

practice.stem: A woman in Karachi needs 18 mg of iron each day. A breakfast cereal contains 2.4 mg of iron per 100 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many grams of the cereal she would need to eat to get her daily iron requirement from cereal alone. Give your answer to the nearest gram.
parts.working: M1 18 ÷ 2.4 (= 7.5 portions of 100 g); A1 750 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why women of child-bearing age need more iron than men of the same age.
parts.answer: iron is lost in blood during menstruation; needed to make haemoglobin for new red blood cells (also for the fetus in pregnancy)
parts.working: B1 blood loss in menstruation (or pregnancy); B1 iron to make haemoglobin/red cells

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the condition caused by lack of iron.
parts.answer: anaemia

practice.stem:
Daily energy needs of two men of the same age and mass:
office worker: 9 500 kJ
construction worker: 12 000 kJ

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in daily energy needed by the construction worker compared with the office worker. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the construction worker needs more energy.
parts.answer: more physical activity; more muscle contraction needs more respiration to release energy
parts.working: B1 more activity; B1 more respiration/energy for muscles

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two health risks if the office worker regularly eats 12 000 kJ a day.
parts.answer: obesity (weight gain, fat stored); coronary heart disease / type 2 diabetes / high blood pressure

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the effects of a diet with too much saturated fat over many years.
parts.answer: fat (cholesterol) deposits build up in artery walls, especially coronary arteries; arteries narrow / blood clots form; leads to coronary heart disease / heart attack; also obesity
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: cholesterol/fat deposits in arteries; narrowing of lumen; reduced blood flow/clot; coronary heart disease/heart attack; obesity

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two changes to a typical festive meal of fried pakoras, mutton karahi and sweet halwa that would reduce this risk.
parts.answer: bake or grill instead of frying; use less ghee/oil; leaner meat or lentils/fish; more vegetables/fruit; less sugar
parts.working: 1 mark each for two sensible changes

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which organ is most water absorbed from digested food?
A stomach
B small intestine
C large intestine
D oesophagus
parts.answer: B small intestine
parts.working: Most water is absorbed in the small intestine; the colon absorbs a smaller amount. The stomach absorbs little water, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put these parts in the order that food passes through them: small intestine, mouth, large intestine, stomach, oesophagus.
parts.answer: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one adjacent pair swapped

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the oesophagus.
parts.answer: carries food from the mouth to the stomach by peristalsis

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the organ that makes bile.
parts.answer: liver

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how peristalsis moves food along the alimentary canal.
parts.answer: circular and longitudinal muscles in the wall contract and relax alternately; a wave of contraction behind the food pushes it along
parts.working: B1 muscle contraction (circular/longitudinal antagonistic); B1 wave squeezes/pushes food

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the anus and the name of the process that removes undigested food.
parts.answer: faeces leave the body through the anus; egestion

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the difference between egestion and excretion.
parts.answer: egestion removes undigested food that was never absorbed; excretion removes metabolic waste made by cells

parts.label: a
parts.text: The pancreas releases its juice into the duodenum. Name three enzymes in pancreatic juice.
parts.answer: amylase, trypsin (protease), lipase

parts.label: b
parts.text: A patient's pancreatic duct is blocked. Suggest and explain two effects on the patient's faeces and body mass.
parts.answer: faeces contain undigested fat (pale, fatty); weight loss because less food is digested and absorbed
parts.working: B1 more undigested food/fat in faeces; B1 weight loss / poor absorption

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by absorption.
parts.answer: movement of small digested food molecules (and ions) from the small intestine into the blood/lymph

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two features of a villus that help absorption.
parts.answer: thin wall (one cell thick); microvilli give large surface area; rich capillary network; lacteal

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Into which structure in a villus are the products of fat digestion mainly absorbed?
A capillary
B lacteal
C microvillus
D vein
parts.answer: B lacteal
parts.working: Fatty acids and glycerol pass into the lacteal (lymph vessel). Glucose and amino acids enter the capillaries, so A is a distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the capillary network in each villus helps to keep absorption of glucose fast.
parts.answer: blood flow carries absorbed glucose away; keeps a steep concentration gradient between the intestine and the blood
parts.working: B1 carries glucose away; B1 maintains concentration gradient (for diffusion)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some glucose is absorbed by active transport. State why active transport is needed.
parts.answer: to absorb glucose against a concentration gradient (when concentration in the lumen is lower than in the cells/blood)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that carries absorbed food from the small intestine to the liver.
parts.answer: hepatic portal vein

practice.stem: In the small intestine, folds of the lining increase surface area by a factor of 3, villi by a further factor of 10, and microvilli by a further factor of 20.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the factor by which the surface area is increased by the folds, villi and microvilli together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to calculate the absorbing surface area of a small intestine with a smooth inner surface area of 0.5 m².

parts.label: c
parts.text: A disease in children flattens the villi. Suggest and explain two effects.
parts.answer: smaller surface area so less absorption of nutrients; leads to weight loss / poor growth / deficiency (e.g. anaemia)
parts.working: B1 reduced absorption due to smaller surface area; B1 named consequence

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by assimilation.
parts.answer: movement of digested food molecules into cells, where they are used and become part of the cells

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way the body uses absorbed amino acids.
parts.answer: to make proteins (e.g. enzymes, antibodies, new cells for growth/repair)

parts.label: a
parts.text: After a meal of rice, the glucose concentration of blood in the hepatic portal vein is higher than in the hepatic vein. Explain why.
parts.answer: the liver removes excess glucose from the blood and converts it to glycogen for storage
parts.working: B1 liver takes up glucose; B1 converted to/stored as glycogen

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the hormone that stimulates the liver to do this.
parts.answer: insulin

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of the liver in dealing with excess amino acids absorbed after a high-protein meal.
parts.answer: deamination: amino group removed from excess amino acids; converted to urea; remaining part used for respiration / converted to glycogen or fat (stored)
parts.working: B1 deamination/removal of nitrogen-containing part; B1 urea formed (transported to kidneys); B1 rest used for energy/stored

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the hepatic portal vein carries blood to the liver before it reaches the rest of the body.
parts.answer: so the liver can process absorbed food first: store excess glucose, break down harmful substances (e.g. alcohol), deaminate excess amino acids

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by malnutrition.
parts.answer: eating too little, too much, or the wrong proportions of nutrients

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Name the deficiency illness caused by a lack of each:
(i) vitamin D
(ii) iron
(iii) fibre
parts.answer: (i) rickets; (ii) anaemia; (iii) constipation

practice.stem: A teenager needs 40 mg of vitamin C a day. Fresh kinnow juice contains 36 mg of vitamin C per 100 cm³. One glass holds 200 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the daily vitamin C requirement given by one glass of the juice. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The juice was left in an open jug in the sun for a day. Suggest why its vitamin C content fell.
parts.answer: vitamin C is destroyed by heat/light/oxidation by air

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why vitamin C must be eaten every day, while vitamin D can be stored.
parts.answer: vitamin C is water-soluble and excess is lost in urine (not stored); vitamin D is fat-soluble and stored in the liver/fat
parts.working: B1 vitamin C not stored/lost in urine; B1 vitamin D stored in liver/fat

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the differences in daily dietary needs between a pregnant woman and a woman of the same age who is not pregnant. Consider energy, protein, calcium and iron.
parts.answer: more energy (for the growing fetus and extra body mass); more protein for growth of fetal tissues and placenta; more calcium for fetal bones and teeth; more iron for haemoglobin in fetal blood and extra maternal blood volume; also vitamin D for calcium absorption
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to five of: extra energy + reason; extra protein + growth of fetus; extra calcium + bones/teeth; extra iron + haemoglobin/red cells; extra blood volume; vitamin D for calcium absorption

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why advice on diet during pregnancy should consider the woman's usual diet and activity.
parts.answer: needs depend on body size, activity and existing nutrient stores/deficiencies

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of cell produces antibodies?
A red blood cell
B phagocyte
C lymphocyte
D platelet
parts.answer: C lymphocyte
parts.working: Lymphocytes produce antibodies. Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens but do not make antibodies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an antigen.
parts.answer: A molecule (e.g. a protein) on the surface of a pathogen / cell that stimulates antibody production.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways in which antibodies help to destroy pathogens.
parts.answer: Bind to antigens and mark pathogens so phagocytes can engulf them; directly destroy pathogens / cause them to clump together.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the difference between an antibody and an antibiotic.
parts.answer: An antibody is a protein made by lymphocytes in the body that binds to a specific antigen; an antibiotic is a drug (medicine) taken to kill bacteria (or stop their growth).
parts.working: B1 antibody: protein made by lymphocytes / body; B1 antibiotic: drug that kills bacteria

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why antibiotics cannot be used to treat measles or influenza.
parts.answer: These diseases are caused by viruses; antibiotics only kill bacteria / do not affect viruses.
parts.working: B1 caused by virus; B1 antibiotics act on bacteria only

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a person develops active immunity after recovering from chickenpox.
parts.answer: Lymphocytes produced antibodies against the virus antigens during the infection; memory cells remain and give fast antibody production on re-infection.
parts.working: B1 antibodies made by own lymphocytes; B1 memory cells

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A newborn baby receives antibodies from its mother in breast milk. Which statement is correct?
A This is active immunity and lasts for life.
B This is passive immunity and no memory cells are made.
C This is active immunity because the baby makes memory cells.
D This is passive immunity and lasts for life.
parts.answer: B This is passive immunity and no memory cells are made.
parts.working: Antibodies from another individual give passive immunity: short-term protection with no memory cells, so it does not last. A and D wrongly say lifelong.

practice.stem: Polio vaccination campaigns in Pakistan give drops of vaccine to young children.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a vaccine contains.
parts.answer: Harmless / weakened / dead pathogen, or its antigens; which stimulate an immune response but do not cause the disease.
parts.working: B1 weakened / dead pathogen or antigens; B1 does not cause disease

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how vaccination protects a person against polio for a long time.
parts.answer: Antigens in the vaccine are recognised by lymphocytes; lymphocytes produce specific antibodies; memory cells are formed which stay in the blood; on later infection antibodies are made quickly before the person becomes ill.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person bitten by a snake may be given an injection containing ready-made antibodies against the venom. State the type of immunity this gives.
parts.answer: Passive immunity

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this injection gives immediate protection, but only for a short time.
parts.answer: The antibodies are already made, so act at once without waiting for lymphocytes to respond; they are not made by the person's body and are broken down; no memory cells are produced.
parts.working: B1 antibodies ready to act at once; B1 broken down / not replaced; B1 no memory cells

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one natural way in which a fetus gains passive immunity.
parts.answer: Antibodies cross the placenta from the mother.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does one type of antibody protect against only one type of pathogen?
A each antibody has a shape complementary to one specific antigen
B antibodies are made of carbohydrate
C each pathogen has the same antigens
D antibodies kill pathogens by digesting them
parts.answer: A each antibody has a shape complementary to one specific antigen
parts.working: Antibodies are proteins with a specific shape that fits one antigen. C is wrong: different pathogens carry different antigens.

practice.stem:
A child was given two doses of a hepatitis B vaccine, five weeks apart. Antibody concentration (arbitrary units) was measured each week after each dose.
week after dose | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
after first dose | 0 | 2 | 8 | 12 | 6 | 3
after second dose | 3 | 40 | 90 | 85 | 70 | 60

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times higher the peak antibody concentration was after the second dose than after the first dose.
parts.answer: 7.5 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the response to the second dose is faster and greater.
parts.answer: The first dose caused memory cells to be made; memory cells recognise the antigen at once on second exposure; they rapidly produce many lymphocytes / large amounts of antibody.
parts.working: B1 memory cells made after first dose; B1 recognise antigen; B1 rapid / greater antibody production

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of immunity produced by vaccination.
parts.answer: Active (artificial) immunity

practice.stem: In one region, 9,120,000 out of 9,600,000 children under five were given measles vaccine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of children vaccinated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how vaccinating a large percentage of a population also protects people who are not vaccinated.
parts.answer: Most people are immune, so the pathogen cannot easily spread / there are few people to infect; an infected person is unlikely to meet a non-immune person; so the disease is controlled (herd immunity).
parts.working: B1 most people immune / cannot pass on; B1 less chance unvaccinated person meets an infected person; B1 spread controlled / herd immunity

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why some children in a population might not be vaccinated.
parts.answer: Too young / medical condition / weak immune system / parents refuse / live in remote areas.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is a pathogen?
A any microorganism
B a disease-causing organism
C a chemical that kills bacteria
D a protein made by white blood cells
parts.answer: B a disease-causing organism
parts.working: A pathogen is a disease-causing organism. A is wrong because most microorganisms are harmless or useful.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term transmissible disease.
parts.answer: A disease in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table to give one example of each method of transmission.
method | example of how pathogen is passed
direct contact | ?
contaminated food | ?
animal (vector) | ?
parts.answer: Direct contact: through blood / body fluids (e.g. sharing needles, hepatitis B). Food: eating undercooked meat or eggs, or food handled with unwashed hands (e.g. Salmonella food poisoning, typhoid). Vector: mosquito bite (malaria / dengue) or houseflies carrying pathogens from faeces to food.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which hepatitis B virus can be passed from one person to another.
parts.answer: Infected blood (e.g. sharing needles / razors, unsterilised equipment); sexual contact; from mother to baby at birth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why barbers are advised to use a new blade for each customer.
parts.answer: A used blade could carry blood containing the virus into a cut on the next customer.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which disease is transmitted mainly through contaminated drinking water?
A cholera
B influenza
C tuberculosis
D measles
parts.answer: A cholera
parts.working: Cholera bacteria are passed on in water contaminated with faeces. Influenza, tuberculosis and measles are spread mainly by droplets in the air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how each of the following reduces the spread of disease: (i) treating sewage (ii) proper disposal of household rubbish (iii) washing hands before preparing food.
parts.answer: (i) removes / kills pathogens in faeces before water is returned to rivers (ii) prevents breeding sites for flies / rats that carry pathogens (iii) removes pathogens that could enter food

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why outbreaks of diarrhoeal disease often follow floods.
parts.answer: Floods mix sewage with drinking water supplies; people drink water containing pathogens.
parts.working: B1 sewage contaminates water; B1 pathogens ingested

parts.label: a
parts.text: Malaria is caused by a single-celled organism and transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Explain what is meant by a vector.
parts.answer: An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways people in rural Sindh can reduce the spread of malaria.
parts.answer: Sleep under insecticide-treated mosquito nets; remove standing water where mosquitoes breed; use insect repellent; spray insecticides; cover water containers.

practice.stem: A plate of cooked rice is left in a warm kitchen. It contains 50 bacteria, which divide every 20 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many bacteria there would be after 4 hours if none died.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use this information to explain why food such as cooked rice should not be left in a warm kitchen for hours.
parts.answer: Bacteria (pathogens) reproduce very quickly at warm temperatures; large numbers can build up and cause food poisoning when eaten.
parts.working: B1 rapid reproduction in warmth; B1 enough to cause disease

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which food can be stored to slow down bacterial growth.
parts.answer: Refrigerate / freeze / cover it / reheat thoroughly before eating.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by a bacterium that is spread in droplets when an infected person coughs. Suggest why TB spreads more quickly in crowded housing.
parts.answer: People are close together, so droplets are more likely to be breathed in by others; often poor ventilation so droplets stay in the air.
parts.working: B1 close contact; B1 poor ventilation / more droplets inhaled

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important for TB patients to complete their full course of antibiotics.
parts.answer: If the course is stopped early, some bacteria survive; the survivors may be resistant and multiply, spreading resistant TB.
parts.working: B1 not all bacteria killed; B1 resistant bacteria survive / spread

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of organism that causes cholera.
parts.answer: Bacterium

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how cholera is usually spread.
parts.answer: Drinking water (or eating food) contaminated with faeces containing the bacteria.
parts.working: B1 contaminated water / food; B1 with faeces from an infected person

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two ways a city can reduce cholera outbreaks.
parts.answer: Treat / chlorinate drinking water; proper sewage treatment / sanitation; boil water; hand washing.

practice.stem: A recipe for oral rehydration solution uses 2.6 g of salt (sodium chloride) and 13.5 g of glucose in 1000 cm³ of water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of salt and the mass of glucose needed to make 250 cm³ of the solution. Give each answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: salt 0.65 g; glucose 3.38 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the water used to make the solution should be boiled and cooled first.
parts.answer: To kill any pathogens in the water so the child is not infected again.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a child with cholera can die within a day if not treated.
parts.answer: Very rapid loss of water and salts in diarrhoea; severe dehydration (low blood volume) stops organs working.
parts.working: B1 rapid water / ion loss; B1 dehydration leads to organ failure / shock

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dengue fever is caused by a virus carried by Aedes mosquitoes. Explain why antibiotics are not given to treat dengue.
parts.answer: Antibiotics do not kill viruses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aedes mosquitoes breed in small amounts of clean standing water. Suggest two actions a school in Rawalpindi could take to reduce dengue during the monsoon.
parts.answer: Empty / cover water containers, flower pots, old tyres; clear blocked drains; use repellents / long sleeves; fit window screens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Typhoid is caused by a bacterium spread in food and water contaminated by faeces. State one symptom that typhoid and cholera may both cause, and explain why this is dangerous.
parts.answer: Diarrhoea (or fever / vomiting); causes dehydration / loss of water and salts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person who has recovered from cholera can still pass the disease on.
parts.answer: They may still carry the bacteria in their gut / faeces for some time; these can contaminate water or food.
parts.working: B1 still carries bacteria; B1 in faeces → water / food

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does cholera cause severe watery diarrhoea?
A The bacterium digests the wall of the large intestine.
B A toxin causes chloride ions to be secreted into the small intestine, and water follows by osmosis.
C The bacterium uses up water in the gut for its respiration.
D A toxin stops the kidneys reabsorbing water.
parts.answer: B A toxin causes chloride ions to be secreted into the small intestine, and water follows by osmosis.
parts.working: The cholera toxin causes chloride ions to be released into the small intestine. This lowers the water potential of the gut contents, so water moves out of the blood into the gut by osmosis. D wrongly blames the kidneys.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using the term water potential, how cholera bacteria in the small intestine cause dehydration.
parts.answer: Bacteria release a toxin; toxin causes chloride ions to be secreted into the lumen of the small intestine; this lowers the water potential of the intestinal contents; water moves from the blood / tissues into the gut by osmosis; lost as watery diarrhoea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why oral rehydration solution contains salts as well as water.
parts.answer: Salts (ions) are lost in the diarrhoea and must be replaced; they help the body absorb and keep water.
parts.working: B1 replace lost ions / salts; B1 help water absorption

practice.stem:
Reported cholera cases in one district:
year | number of cases
2019 | 1240
2020 | 860
2021 | 610
2022 | 2950
2023 | 720

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in cases from 2021 to 2022, to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Heavy floods occurred in this district in 2022. Suggest why this explains the change.
parts.answer: Floods contaminated drinking water with sewage; people drank water containing cholera bacteria / sanitation broke down.
parts.working: B1 sewage mixes with drinking water; B1 bacteria ingested / sanitation failure

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the trend from 2019 to 2021 and suggest one reason for it.
