parts.answer: Cases fell each year (1240 → 610); e.g. better water treatment / sanitation / vaccination / hygiene campaigns.
parts.working: B1 trend with figures; B1 reason

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a chemical barrier against pathogens?
A hairs in the nose
B hydrochloric acid in the stomach
C the skin
D phagocytosis
parts.answer: B hydrochloric acid in the stomach
parts.working: Stomach acid kills many pathogens in food, so it is a chemical barrier. Nose hairs and skin are mechanical barriers; phagocytosis is a cell defence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how each of the following helps to prevent pathogens entering the body: (i) skin (ii) mucus in the airways (iii) hairs in the nose.
parts.answer: (i) forms a barrier that pathogens cannot pass through (ii) traps pathogens (which are then removed by cilia / swallowed) (iii) trap dust and pathogens in inhaled air

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a deep cut increases the risk of infection.
parts.answer: The skin barrier is broken, so pathogens can enter the blood / tissues.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a phagocyte destroys a bacterium.
parts.answer: The phagocyte moves towards / is attracted to the bacterium; it engulfs the bacterium (surrounds it with its cytoplasm / membrane); it digests it with enzymes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other way in which white blood cells defend the body.
parts.answer: Lymphocytes produce antibodies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Smoking damages the cilia lining the trachea. Explain why smokers get more chest infections.
parts.answer: Cilia normally beat to move mucus containing trapped pathogens up to the throat; damaged cilia cannot do this; mucus and pathogens collect in the lungs and cause infection.
parts.working: B1 cilia move mucus; B1 mucus traps pathogens; B1 mucus / pathogens stay in lungs

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how blood clotting at a wound helps defend against disease.
parts.answer: The clot seals the wound; preventing pathogens from entering (and blood loss).
parts.working: B1 seals / blocks wound; B1 stops entry of pathogens

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how influenza spreads from person to person, and suggest three measures that could reduce its spread in a school.
parts.answer: Spread: infected person coughs / sneezes droplets containing the virus, which are breathed in by others (or touched on surfaces then transferred to mouth/nose). Measures: cover mouth when coughing / wear masks; wash hands regularly; keep sick pupils at home; ventilate classrooms; vaccination.
parts.working: B1 droplets from coughing / sneezing; B1 inhaled / via surfaces; 1 mark each for three measures

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a new influenza vaccine is needed most years.
parts.answer: The virus changes (mutates) and its antigens change; antibodies / memory cells from the old vaccine no longer fit the new antigens.
parts.working: B1 virus mutates / antigens change; B1 old antibodies / memory cells do not recognise it

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why diseases such as cholera and typhoid are much more common where there is no clean water supply or sewage system.
parts.answer: Faeces from infected people contain pathogens; without sewage treatment these get into rivers / wells used for drinking; people drink untreated water and are infected; flies may carry pathogens from faeces to food.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A village in Balochistan gets a new well and a simple filter-and-chlorine system. Explain how each part reduces disease.
parts.answer: Filter removes particles / some microorganisms; chlorine kills remaining pathogens.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which the body's own defences protect against swallowed bacteria.
parts.answer: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills many bacteria.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which set of conditions will a sunflower plant lose water vapour fastest?
A cool, humid, still air
B warm, humid, windy
C warm, dry, windy
D cool, dry, still air
parts.answer: C warm, dry, windy
parts.working: High temperature increases evaporation, low humidity gives a steep water vapour concentration gradient and wind removes water vapour from around the leaf. B is humid, which reduces the gradient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term transpiration.
parts.answer: Loss of water vapour from the leaves (by evaporation of water at the surfaces of the mesophyll cells) followed by diffusion of water vapour through the stomata.
parts.working: B1 loss of water vapour from leaves / aerial parts; B1 evaporation from mesophyll cell surfaces and diffusion out through stomata

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the pores in the leaf through which most water vapour leaves.
parts.answer: Stomata

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which transpiration is useful to a plant.
parts.answer: Pulls water and mineral ions up the xylem / cools the leaves / supplies water for photosynthesis and support.

practice.stem: A student uses a potometer in which the leafy shoot is fixed into a rubber bung, a capillary tube with a scale is attached and a water reservoir with a tap is connected to the tube.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why the joints of the potometer were sealed with petroleum jelly.
parts.answer: To make them airtight / stop air leaking in or water leaking out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the student could return the bubble to the start of the scale between readings.
parts.answer: Open the tap of the water reservoir / syringe to push water in.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student waited 5 minutes after changing conditions before starting a new reading.
parts.answer: To let the shoot adjust to the new conditions so the rate is steady.

practice.stem:
Transpiration rate of a rubber plant at different relative humidities (temperature kept at 25 °C).
relative humidity / % | rate of transpiration / arbitrary units
30 | 8.4
45 | 6.9
60 | 5.1
75 | 3.2
90 | 1.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of relative humidity on the rate of transpiration. Use figures from the table.
parts.answer: As humidity increases, rate decreases: from 8.4 at 30 % to 1.6 at 90 %.
parts.working: B1 inverse trend; B1 data quote with units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the decrease in rate between 30 % and 90 % humidity.
parts.answer: 6.8 arbitrary units

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the rate at 100 % humidity and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Very close to zero (but probably not zero); the air is saturated, so there is almost no concentration gradient for water vapour to diffuse out.
parts.working: B1 near zero / below 1.6; B1 no / tiny concentration gradient

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A potometer is used to measure the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot. What does the potometer actually measure?
A the volume of water evaporating from the leaves
B the rate of water uptake by the shoot
C the rate of photosynthesis
D the number of open stomata
parts.answer: B the rate of water uptake by the shoot
parts.working: The bubble moves as the shoot takes up water. Most of this water is lost in transpiration, but some is used in photosynthesis or kept in cells, so A is not exactly what is measured.

practice.stem:
A student set up a bubble potometer with a leafy shoot of a guava plant. A small electric fan was placed 50 cm from the shoot. The distance moved by the air bubble was recorded in 4 minutes at each fan setting.
Fan setting | distance moved by bubble / mm | time / min
off | 12 | 4
low | 27 | 4
high | 44 | 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of bubble movement in mm per minute for each fan setting.
parts.answer: off: 3 mm/min; low: 6.75 mm/min; high: 11 mm/min
parts.working: B2 all three correct (B1 for two correct)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe and explain the effect of wind speed on the rate of transpiration shown by these results.
parts.answer: As wind speed increases, the rate increases (3.0 → 11.0 mm/min). Wind blows away water vapour near the leaf, keeping a steep concentration gradient, so water vapour diffuses out of stomata faster.
parts.working: B1 trend with figures; B1 wind removes water vapour from around leaf / reduces humidity near leaf; B1 steeper gradient so faster diffusion through stomata

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept constant.
parts.answer: Light intensity; temperature (also: same shoot / humidity / distance of fan).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rate of transpiration increases when the temperature rises.
parts.answer: Water molecules gain kinetic energy, so more water evaporates from mesophyll cell surfaces and water vapour diffuses out faster.
parts.working: B1 more evaporation / molecules move faster; B1 faster diffusion of water vapour out of stomata

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate of transpiration decreases on a humid day in Karachi.
parts.answer: The air outside the leaf already contains much water vapour, so the concentration gradient between the air spaces and the outside air is smaller and diffusion is slower.
parts.working: B1 high water vapour concentration outside; B1 smaller concentration gradient so slower diffusion

practice.stem: A potted chilli plant was watered and its pot and soil surface were sealed in a plastic bag. It was placed on a balance in a sunny courtyard. At 9 am its mass was 412.0 g. At 3 pm its mass was 397.6 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water lost in 6 hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the starting mass that was lost. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of water loss in g per hour.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the pot and soil were covered with a plastic bag.
parts.answer: So that mass lost is due to transpiration from the plant only, not evaporation from the soil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of increasing light intensity on the rate of transpiration.
parts.answer: Rate increases (up to a point).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your answer to (a).
parts.answer: In light the stomata open (wider), so more water vapour can diffuse out of the leaf.
parts.working: B1 stomata open in light; B1 more water vapour diffuses out

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a plant transpires very little at night.
parts.answer: Stomata are closed in the dark (and it is cooler).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Four similar leaves were treated with petroleum jelly, which is waterproof, and hung up for two days. Leaf 1: no jelly. Leaf 2: jelly on the upper surface. Leaf 3: jelly on the lower surface. Leaf 4: jelly on both surfaces. Apart from leaf 4, which leaf lost the least mass?
A leaf 1
B leaf 2
C leaf 3
D all three lost the same mass
parts.answer: C leaf 3
parts.working: Most stomata are on the lower surface of a typical dicot leaf, so blocking the lower surface stops most water vapour loss. Leaf 2 still loses water through the many lower stomata.

practice.stem: In a potometer the air bubble moved 36 mm along a capillary tube in 4 minutes. The radius of the capillary bore is 0.5 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water taken up by the shoot in mm³. Use the formula volume = πr²l. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 28.3 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ per minute, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 7.07 mm³/min

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the cut end of the shoot was cut under water before it was put in the potometer.
parts.answer: To prevent air entering the xylem vessels, which would block the water column and stop water being drawn up.
parts.working: B1 stops air entering xylem; B1 air bubble would block water flow / break water column

practice.stem: On a very hot afternoon in Multan in June, a farmer notices that his cotton plants have drooping leaves, even though the soil is slightly damp. By the next morning the plants look normal again.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the plants wilted.
parts.answer: Water was lost by transpiration faster than it was absorbed by the roots; cells lost water and became flaccid (lost turgor); so the leaves and stems were no longer supported.
parts.working: B1 transpiration rate greater than water uptake; B1 cells lose turgor / become flaccid; B1 loss of support

parts.label: b
parts.text: When wilting occurs, the stomata close. Give one advantage and one disadvantage to the plant of closing its stomata.
parts.answer: Advantage: reduces water loss. Disadvantage: less carbon dioxide enters, so less photosynthesis (also less cooling / less mineral transport).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how temperature affects the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot. Your plan should include what you would change, measure and keep the same.
parts.answer: Use a potometer; vary temperature (e.g. 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 °C in a temperature-controlled room or incubator, checked with a thermometer); measure distance bubble moves in a fixed time; calculate rate; keep light intensity, humidity, air movement and same shoot constant; allow time to adjust; repeat and calculate mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: potometer / mass loss method; at least 5 temperatures stated with range; how temperature is controlled (heater / room / incubator, check with thermometer); dependent variable: bubble distance in fixed time (or mass lost); calculate rate; same shoot / same leaf area; constant light intensity; constant humidity / wind; acclimatise before timing; repeat at each temperature and find mean

practice.stem: A cactus growing in the Thar Desert has leaves reduced to spines, a thick waxy cuticle and stomata sunk in pits in a thick green stem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how each feature reduces water loss: (i) leaves reduced to spines (ii) a thick waxy cuticle (iii) stomata sunk in pits.
parts.answer: (i) smaller surface area for transpiration (ii) waterproof layer reduces evaporation from the surface (iii) humid air is trapped in the pit, reducing the concentration gradient

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the cactus stem is green.
parts.answer: The stem carries out photosynthesis instead of the leaves (contains chloroplasts).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the correct pathway taken by water as it moves through a plant?
A root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cells
B root hair cell → phloem → root cortex cells → mesophyll cells
C xylem → root hair cell → mesophyll cells → stomata
D root cortex cells → root hair cell → xylem → mesophyll cells
parts.answer: A root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cells
parts.working: Water enters root hair cells, crosses the cortex to the xylem, travels up in the xylem and then enters mesophyll cells. B is wrong because water moves in xylem, not phloem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where root hairs are found on a root.
parts.answer: Just behind the root tip.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Seedlings that are pulled out and replanted often wilt. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Root hairs are damaged / torn off when the seedlings are pulled up; so the surface area for water absorption is reduced.
parts.working: B1 root hairs damaged; B1 less surface area / less water absorbed

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how a gardener can reduce wilting when moving seedlings.
parts.answer: Move them with a ball of soil around the roots / water well / move in the evening.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how water moves from the soil into a root hair cell.
parts.answer: By osmosis; from a higher water potential in the soil (dilute solution) to a lower water potential in the cell sap; through the partially permeable cell membrane.
parts.working: B1 osmosis; B1 higher to lower water potential (soil → cell); B1 partially permeable membrane

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why root hair cells are able to absorb a lot of water.
parts.answer: Many long root hairs give a large surface area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitrate ions are absorbed by root hair cells even when their concentration in the soil is lower than in the cell. Name this process.
parts.answer: Active transport

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the root hair cells need oxygen for this process.
parts.answer: Active transport needs energy; energy is released by aerobic respiration, which uses oxygen.
parts.working: B1 needs energy; B1 from (aerobic) respiration

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why plants in waterlogged soil take up fewer mineral ions.
parts.answer: Waterlogged soil has little oxygen (air spaces filled with water), so root cells respire less aerobically and release less energy for active transport.
parts.working: B1 less oxygen in soil; B1 less respiration / energy for active transport

practice.stem: A farmer in Faisalabad added far too much fertiliser to a field of young wheat plants. A few days later the plants wilted, although the soil was moist.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the term water potential to explain why the plants wilted.
parts.answer: The fertiliser made the soil solution very concentrated, with a lower water potential than the root cells; water moved out of the root cells into the soil by osmosis; so less water reached the leaves and cells lost turgor.
parts.working: B1 soil water potential lower than root cells; B1 water leaves root cells by osmosis / cannot enter; B1 cells / plant lose turgor

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what the farmer should do to help the plants recover.
parts.answer: Water the field heavily to dilute the fertiliser.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how water moves from the root hair cell to the xylem.
parts.answer: By osmosis from cell to cell across the root cortex, down a water potential gradient (each cell has a lower water potential than the one before).
parts.working: B1 through cortex cells; B1 osmosis / water potential gradient

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how water moves up the xylem to the leaves.
parts.answer: Water evaporates from mesophyll cells and is lost by transpiration; this creates a pull (tension) on the water in the xylem; water molecules stick together (cohesion) so a continuous column is drawn up.
parts.working: B1 transpiration / evaporation at leaves; B1 creates pull / suction; B1 water molecules stick together / continuous column

practice.stem: A celery stalk with leaves was stood in water containing red dye. After some time, a thin slice was cut across the stalk and viewed with a hand lens. Small red spots were seen in a ring near the outside of the stalk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the tissue that the dye travelled through.
parts.answer: Xylem

parts.label: b
parts.text: The dye moved 84 mm up the stalk in 30 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of movement in mm per minute.
parts.answer: 2.8 mm/min

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could make the dye travel faster.
parts.answer: Place it in a warm / bright / windy place, or near a fan, to increase transpiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which description of xylem vessels is correct?
A living cells with sieve plates
B dead, hollow tubes strengthened with lignin
C living cells with many chloroplasts
D dead cells with cross walls full of pores
parts.answer: B dead, hollow tubes strengthened with lignin
parts.working: Xylem vessels are dead cells joined end to end with no cross walls, forming hollow tubes with lignified walls. A describes phloem sieve tubes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two functions of xylem.
parts.answer: Transports water and mineral ions; provides support.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how two features of xylem vessels are related to their functions.
parts.answer: No cross walls / hollow (no cytoplasm), so water flows freely as a continuous column; lignin in walls makes them strong, giving support and stopping collapse under tension; narrow tubes help the water column hold together.
parts.working: For each of two features: B1 feature, B1 linked function

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the positions of xylem and phloem in (i) a transverse section of a dicot stem and (ii) a transverse section of a dicot root.
parts.answer: (i) Stem: vascular bundles in a ring near the outside; xylem towards the centre (inside), phloem towards the outside. (ii) Root: xylem in the centre (often star / X shaped); phloem in groups between the arms of the xylem.
parts.working: Stem: B1 bundles in a ring, B1 xylem inner, phloem outer. Root: B1 xylem central, B1 phloem between xylem arms

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name given to the strand containing xylem and phloem in a leaf.
parts.answer: Vein / vascular bundle

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is translocation?
A movement of water from roots to leaves in xylem
B movement of sucrose and amino acids in phloem from sources to sinks
C loss of water vapour from leaves
D movement of mineral ions into root hairs by active transport
parts.answer: B movement of sucrose and amino acids in phloem from sources to sinks
parts.working: Translocation is the movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from regions of production or release (sources) to regions of storage or use (sinks). A is water transport in xylem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms source and sink.
parts.answer: Source: part of the plant that releases sucrose / amino acids (e.g. where they are made). Sink: part where they are used or stored.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In sugar cane, sucrose is stored in the stem. State the source and the sink in a sugar cane plant during growth.
parts.answer: Source: leaves (photosynthesis). Sink: stem (storage) — also accept growing tips / roots.
parts.working: B1 source leaves; B1 sink stem

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the tissue in which sucrose is moved.
parts.answer: Phloem

parts.label: a
parts.text: In spring a stored potato tuber starts to sprout new shoots. Explain why the tuber acts as a source at this time.
parts.answer: Stored starch is broken down to sucrose; the sucrose is transported in phloem to the growing shoots (sinks), which cannot yet photosynthesise enough.
parts.working: B1 starch → sucrose released; B1 transported to growing shoots / sinks

parts.label: b
parts.text: Later in summer the potato plant forms new tubers. Explain why the new tubers are sinks.
parts.answer: Sucrose from the leaves is transported to them and converted to starch for storage.
parts.working: B1 receive sucrose from leaves; B1 stored as starch

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why translocation can occur in both directions in a plant, unlike water transport.
parts.answer: Sources and sinks can be above or below each other (and change with season), so phloem carries substances up and down.

practice.stem: A ring of bark, including the phloem, was carefully removed all the way round the trunk of a young apple tree. After some weeks the bark just above the ring had swollen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the bark above the ring swelled.
parts.answer: The ring removed the phloem (which is in the bark); sucrose moving down from the leaves could not pass the ring; sucrose built up above the ring, and the extra sugar caused water to enter / extra growth, so the bark swelled.
parts.working: B1 phloem removed; B1 sucrose transport (down from leaves) blocked; B1 accumulation above ring

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the leaves above the ring did not wilt for several weeks.
parts.answer: The xylem, which is deeper in the stem (wood), was not removed, so water still reached the leaves.
parts.working: B1 xylem intact / inside the bark; B1 water still transported up

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the roots after a long time, and explain.
parts.answer: The roots would die; they receive no sucrose for respiration, so they cannot release energy (and eventually the whole tree dies).
parts.working: B1 roots die / stop growing; B1 no sugar for respiration

practice.stem: A student hung a cut leafy shoot of a neem tree from a balance with its cut end in a sealed flask of water (the water surface was covered with oil). She recorded the mass every hour, first in still air and then with a fan blowing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student's results could be used to show the effect of the fan.
parts.answer: Compare the mass lost per hour with and without the fan; the rate with the fan is higher.
parts.working: B1 compare rates / mass loss; B1 under the same other conditions

parts.label: b
parts.text: Without the fan the shoot lost 1.8 g in 3 hours. With the fan it lost 3.3 g in 3 hours. Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of water loss caused by the fan.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain fully how water moves from the xylem in a leaf to the air outside, and why moving air speeds this up.
parts.answer: Water passes from xylem into mesophyll cells by osmosis; it evaporates from the surfaces of mesophyll cells into air spaces; water vapour diffuses out through stomata down a concentration gradient; moving air removes water vapour near the stomata, keeping the gradient steep.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four: osmosis into mesophyll; evaporation from cell surfaces into air spaces; diffusion of water vapour through stomata; down a concentration gradient; wind removes water vapour / maintains gradient

practice.stem: Measurements on a rice plant in a field in Punjab on a clear summer day showed that water loss rose from 8 am to a peak at 2 pm and then fell. Water uptake by the roots followed a similar pattern but reached its peak about an hour later.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why water loss from the plant is greater at 2 pm than at 8 am.
parts.answer: Higher light intensity, so more stomata open wider; higher temperature, so faster evaporation and diffusion; lower humidity at midday, so steeper concentration gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: more light so stomata open wider; higher temperature, more evaporation; molecules have more kinetic energy / diffuse faster; lower humidity / steeper gradient

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate of water uptake by roots lags behind the rate of transpiration in the early afternoon.
parts.answer: Water is first lost from the leaves, creating the pull; it takes time for the pull to be transmitted down the xylem and for water to cross the root, so uptake reaches its peak later.
parts.working: B1 loss from leaves comes first / drives uptake; B1 time for pull to travel / delay in uptake

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two ways in which a hot, dry climate could be a problem for a crop such as rice, which needs a lot of water.
parts.answer: Plants may wilt / lose turgor; stomata close so less photosynthesis and lower yield; more irrigation water needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which measure helps to keep a fish population sustainable?
A using nets with a smaller mesh size
B fishing all year round
C setting a maximum catch (quota) for each boat
D catching the largest number of young fish
parts.answer: C setting a maximum catch (quota) for each boat
parts.working: A quota limits how many fish are removed so enough remain to breed. A smaller mesh (A) would catch more young fish before they breed, which harms the stock.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three reasons why it is important to conserve endangered species.
parts.answer: To maintain biodiversity; plants or animals may provide future medicines or foods; to keep food chains / webs stable; for ecotourism and income; for future generations / moral reasons; to preserve genetic variety for breeding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two methods used to conserve endangered species.
parts.answer: Protecting habitats in national parks or reserves; captive breeding programmes and release; laws against hunting / trade; seed banks for plants; education.

practice.stem: The Indus river dolphin is an endangered species found mainly in the Indus river in Pakistan. In one stretch of the river, surveys counted 1250 dolphins in an early survey and 1820 in a later survey (figures for this question).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the number of dolphins counted. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three threats to the Indus river dolphin.
parts.answer: Barrages divide the river into separate sections, isolating populations; less water in the river when it is taken for irrigation; accidental capture in fishing nets; pollution from farms, factories and sewage; dolphins trapped in irrigation canals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions that may have helped the population to increase.
parts.answer: Hunting banned / legal protection; a protected reserve; rescuing dolphins trapped in canals; educating fishing communities; monitoring by surveys.

practice.stem:
The catch of one species of fish by boats along a stretch of coast (thousand tonnes):
2000: 52; 2005: 61; 2010: 70; 2015: 48; 2020: 31

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in catch between 2010 and 2020. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the catch fell after 2010 even though more boats were fishing.
parts.answer: Overfishing: fish were removed faster than they could reproduce; too few adult fish were left to breed.
parts.working: B1 overfishing; B1 breeding stock reduced.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe three ways to make fishing in this area sustainable.
parts.answer: Quotas limiting catch; larger mesh size so young fish escape; closed seasons during breeding; no-fishing protected areas; limit the number of boats / licences; fish farming.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a sustainable resource.
parts.answer: A resource that is produced as fast as it is used, so it does not run out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how forests can be managed so that timber is a sustainable resource.
parts.answer: Replant trees to replace those cut down; selective felling (only some trees cut); leave areas protected; limit felling to the rate of regrowth; education / certification schemes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how recycling paper helps to conserve forests.
parts.answer: Fewer new trees need to be cut down to make paper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A zoo runs a captive breeding programme for a rare species of leopard, starting with only eight animals. Explain why a population that has become very small is at risk even if it is protected.
parts.answer: Little genetic variation remains; inbreeding increases the chance of harmful recessive conditions; the population may be unable to adapt to new diseases or environmental change; a single disaster could wipe it out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how zoos can reduce this risk.
parts.answer: Exchange animals between zoos in different countries; keep breeding records (studbooks) to avoid breeding close relatives; use frozen sperm / artificial insemination.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a seed bank is a useful way of conserving plant species.
parts.answer: Seeds can be stored dry and cold for many years in a small space; they keep a wide range of genetic variety and can be grown if the species dies out in the wild.
parts.working: B1 long-term storage in small space; B1 keeps genetic variety / allows replanting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Markhor are wild goats living in the mountains of northern Pakistan. Their numbers fell because of hunting. In some areas, a small number of permits are now sold each year to foreign hunters to shoot an old male, and most of the fee goes to the local community. Suggest how this scheme can help the markhor population to increase.
parts.answer: Local people earn money from living markhor, so they protect them and stop illegal hunting; only a few old males are shot, which have already bred; money is used for wildlife guards / habitat protection / community projects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one argument against this scheme.
parts.answer: Killing animals is ethically wrong; risk of corruption or too many permits; the strongest males may be removed from the gene pool.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how scientists could check whether the scheme is working.
parts.answer: Carry out regular surveys / counts of markhor in the same areas; compare numbers over years and with areas that do not have the scheme.
parts.working: B1 repeated population surveys; B1 comparison over time / with control area.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Fertiliser washes from farmland into a lake. Which sequence of events follows?
A algae grow rapidly → plants below die from lack of light → bacteria decompose dead plants → oxygen falls → fish die
B fish die → bacteria decompose fish → oxygen rises → algae grow rapidly → plants die
C algae grow rapidly → oxygen rises → bacteria die → fish die from too much oxygen
D plants die from lack of nitrate → algae die → fish die from lack of food → bacteria increase
parts.answer: A algae grow rapidly → plants below die from lack of light → bacteria decompose dead plants → oxygen falls → fish die
parts.working: Extra nitrate and phosphate cause an algal bloom; algae block light so plants die; decomposing bacteria increase and use up oxygen in aerobic respiration, so fish die. B gets the order wrong, starting with fish death.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Much of the litter on beaches near Karachi is plastic. State what is meant by saying that plastic is non-biodegradable.
parts.answer: It cannot be broken down by decomposers (bacteria and fungi), so it stays in the environment for a very long time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways in which plastic waste in the sea can harm marine animals.
parts.answer: Animals such as turtles swallow plastic bags, which block the gut and they starve; animals get tangled in nets and plastic, and drown or are injured; small pieces of plastic (microplastics) enter food chains.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways to reduce plastic pollution of the sea.
parts.answer: Use reusable cloth bags; recycle plastic; ban single-use plastic bags; proper waste collection; beach clean-ups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how untreated sewage entering a river can cause the death of fish several hundred metres downstream.
parts.answer: Sewage contains organic matter and nutrients (nitrate / phosphate); nutrients cause rapid growth of algae; algae block light so water plants cannot photosynthesise and die; bacteria (decomposers) multiply and break down sewage and dead plants; bacteria use oxygen in aerobic respiration; oxygen concentration falls so fish cannot respire and die.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Untreated sewage is also a danger to people who use the river water. Explain why.
parts.answer: It contains pathogens (e.g. bacteria causing cholera or typhoid) that can cause disease if the water is drunk.

practice.stem:
A housing estate releases untreated sewage into a river at an outlet (0 m). Samples were taken upstream (−100 m) and downstream.
distance / m: -100, 0, 200, 500, 1000, 2000
oxygen / mg/dm³: 9.2, 8.8, 4.1, 2.3, 5.0, 8.5
bacteria (relative numbers): 10, 120, 300, 260, 90, 20

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the oxygen concentration changes downstream of the outlet.
parts.answer: It falls from 8.8 mg/dm³ at the outlet to a lowest value of 2.3 mg/dm³ at 500 m; then rises again to 8.5 mg/dm³ at 2000 m.
parts.working: B1 falls to minimum at 500 m; B1 recovers further downstream (data quoted).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in oxygen concentration from the upstream site (−100 m) to the lowest value. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the data on bacteria to explain the change in oxygen concentration between 0 and 500 m.
parts.answer: Bacteria numbers increase greatly as they feed on the sewage; their aerobic respiration uses up oxygen from the water.
parts.working: B1 more bacteria feeding on sewage; B1 respiration uses oxygen.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the oxygen concentration recovers further downstream.
parts.answer: The sewage has been broken down so bacteria numbers fall; oxygen dissolves from the air / is made by photosynthesis.

practice.stem:
Students counted two kinds of animal in kick samples from four sites on a stream below a farm. Stonefly nymphs need water with a high oxygen concentration. Bloodworms (midge larvae) contain haemoglobin.
site: A (upstream), B, C, D (furthest downstream)
stonefly nymphs: 24, 2, 0, 11
bloodworms: 1, 30, 52, 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the differences in the numbers of the two animals between site A and site C.
parts.answer: Stonefly nymphs fall from 24 at A to 0 at C; bloodworms increase from 1 at A to 52 at C.
parts.working: B1 stonefly decrease; B1 bloodworm increase (data).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the information to explain these differences.
parts.answer: Site C has the least oxygen because of pollution (bacteria decomposing waste); stonefly nymphs need high oxygen so cannot survive there; bloodworms have haemoglobin, so they can obtain enough oxygen and survive with less competition.
parts.working: B1 low oxygen at polluted site; B1 stonefly need high oxygen; B1 bloodworm haemoglobin allows survival in low oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest which site, B or D, is cleaner. Give a reason.
parts.answer: D: it has more stonefly nymphs (11 v 2) and fewer bloodworms (12 v 30).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of using living organisms rather than a single chemical test to monitor pollution.
parts.answer: Organisms show the effect of pollution over a long period, not just at the moment of sampling.

practice.stem:
Farmers around a lake increased the amount of nitrate fertiliser used each year. The mean nitrate concentration in the lake water was recorded.
fertiliser / kg per hectare: 50, 100, 150, 200
nitrate in lake / mg/dm³: 2.0, 4.5, 8.0, 13.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the nitrate concentration was in the year with 200 kg/ha than in the year with 50 kg/ha.
parts.answer: 6.5 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why nitrate in the lake increased more than in proportion to the fertiliser applied.
parts.answer: Crops can absorb only a limited amount; once their need is met, extra fertiliser is not taken up and more of it is washed (leached) into the lake.
parts.working: B1 crops take up limited amount; B1 excess leached / runs off.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe three ways in which farmers and local councils could reduce eutrophication of the lake.
parts.answer: Apply only the amount of fertiliser crops need; avoid spreading before heavy rain; leave a strip of uncultivated land / trees along the lake edge; use organic manure that releases nutrients slowly; treat sewage before release.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which gas released by burning coal is the main cause of acid rain?
A carbon dioxide
B methane
C oxygen
D sulfur dioxide
parts.answer: D sulfur dioxide
parts.working: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in water in clouds to form acidic solutions that fall as acid rain. Carbon dioxide (A) is mainly linked to the enhanced greenhouse effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two greenhouse gases and give one human source of each.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide: burning fossil fuels / deforestation. Methane: cattle (digestion) / rice paddy fields / rubbish in landfill sites.
parts.working: B1 each gas; B1 each correct source.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two things a family could do to reduce the amount of carbon dioxide they produce.
parts.answer: Use public transport, walk or cycle; use solar panels; switch off lights and appliances; use energy-efficient bulbs; plant trees.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which farming activity releases large amounts of methane?
A growing rice in flooded paddy fields
B planting trees along field edges
C spraying insecticide on cotton
D harvesting wheat with a combine harvester
parts.answer: A growing rice in flooded paddy fields
parts.working: Bacteria in the waterlogged, anaerobic soil of flooded paddy fields produce methane (cattle are another major source). Planting trees (B) removes carbon dioxide and does not release methane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how increasing amounts of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere lead to global warming.
parts.answer: Heat (infrared) radiation from the Earth's surface is absorbed by greenhouse gases; more greenhouse gases trap more heat; the mean temperature of the Earth rises (enhanced greenhouse effect).
parts.working: B1 Earth radiates heat / infrared; B1 absorbed / trapped by greenhouse gases; B1 more gas → more heat retained → temperature rises.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three possible effects of climate change.
parts.answer: Melting glaciers and ice caps; sea level rise and flooding of coastal areas; more extreme weather (heatwaves, floods, droughts); changes in rainfall affecting crops; species extinction or migration; spread of insect-borne diseases.

practice.stem:
Carbon dioxide concentration in the atmosphere measured at a remote mountain observatory (values rounded to the nearest ppm):
year: 1960, 1980, 2000, 2020
carbon dioxide / ppm: 317, 339, 370, 414

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in carbon dioxide concentration, in ppm per year, between 1960 and 1980, and between 2000 and 2020.
parts.answer: 1960–1980: 1.1 ppm per year; 2000–2020: 2.2 ppm per year

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in carbon dioxide concentration from 1960 to 2020. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two human activities that have caused this increase.
parts.answer: Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) in vehicles, power stations and factories; deforestation / burning forests, so less carbon dioxide is absorbed by photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Every winter, cities in Punjab such as Lahore suffer from heavy smog. Sources include vehicle exhaust, burning of crop stubble and coal-burning factories and brick kilns. Explain how sulfur dioxide from these sources can damage lakes and forests far from the city.
parts.answer: Sulfur dioxide is carried by wind; it dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain; acid rain lowers the pH of lakes, killing fish and other aquatic organisms (aluminium released from soil); it damages leaves and roots of trees / leaches minerals from soil, so trees die.
parts.working: B1 carried by wind; B1 forms acid rain; B1 effect on lakes; B1 effect on trees / soil.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three ways to reduce sulfur dioxide pollution.
parts.answer: Use low-sulfur fuels; remove sulfur dioxide from chimney gases (scrubbers / flue-gas desulfurisation); use renewable energy (solar, wind, hydroelectric); improve kiln technology; ban burning of crop stubble.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three reasons why humans destroy natural habitats.
parts.answer: To clear land for farming / grazing; building houses and cities; building roads; extracting natural resources (mining, quarrying, timber); building dams; dumping waste.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why destroying a habitat can cause a species to become extinct.
parts.answer: The species loses its food, shelter and breeding sites; if it lives only in that habitat, the population falls until none are left.
parts.working: B1 loss of food / shelter / breeding sites; B1 population falls / cannot move elsewhere.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Large areas of forest on a hillside are cut down. Which effect is most likely in the following years?
A more transpiration from the hillside
B less soil erosion during heavy rain
C more flooding in valleys below
D more carbon dioxide absorbed from the air
parts.answer: C more flooding in valleys below
parts.working: Without trees, less rain is intercepted and absorbed by roots, so water runs off quickly and floods valleys (with soil erosion). B is wrong: erosion increases because roots no longer hold the soil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hillside forests in northern Pakistan have been cut for timber and firewood. Explain how deforestation can increase the risk of floods and landslides.
parts.answer: Fewer trees intercept rainfall; fewer roots to absorb water, so more runs off the surface quickly into rivers; roots no longer hold soil, so soil is washed away (erosion) and slopes become unstable; eroded soil fills river beds, so rivers overflow more easily.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how deforestation contributes to an increase in carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Fewer trees to remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis; burning or decay of cut trees releases carbon dioxide.
parts.working: B1 less photosynthesis; B1 burning / decomposition releases CO₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mangrove forests grow along the coast of the Indus delta. Large areas have been cut down for firewood and to make space for shrimp farms. Suggest two effects of this on fish populations in the area.
parts.answer: Young fish and shrimps lose the sheltered nursery areas among mangrove roots; less food (leaf litter, small animals); so fish populations and catches fall.
parts.working: B1 loss of breeding / nursery habitat; B1 loss of food / fewer fish.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why losing mangroves can lead to more damage to coastal villages during storms.
parts.answer: Mangrove roots trap sediment and slow down waves; without them the coast erodes and storm waves reach further inland.
parts.working: B1 roots hold soil / reduce erosion; B1 waves no longer slowed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Large mangrove replanting projects have taken place on the Sindh coast. Give one benefit of replanting other than for fish.
parts.answer: Mangroves absorb carbon dioxide; protect the coastline; provide habitats for birds and other wildlife; sustainable wood supply.

practice.stem: Satellite images showed that the forest cover in one district was 4800 km² in 1990 and 3360 km² in 2020.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of forest lost between 1990 and 2020.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean area of forest lost per year.
parts.answer: 48 km² per year

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how this loss of forest could reduce rainfall in the region.
parts.answer: Fewer trees means less transpiration; less water vapour enters the air, so fewer clouds form and less rain falls.
parts.working: B1 less transpiration; B1 less water vapour / cloud formation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the loss of forest reduces biodiversity.
parts.answer: Many species lose their habitats, food sources and breeding sites; species that depend on them in food webs are also affected, so the number of different species falls.
parts.working: B1 habitat / food loss; B1 effects through food webs / extinction / fewer species.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Explain how each of the following increases food production:
(i) chemical fertilisers
(ii) insecticides
(iii) selective breeding.
parts.answer: (i) supply mineral ions such as nitrate for growth (making proteins), so higher yield; (ii) kill insects that eat or damage crops; (iii) produce varieties with higher yield / disease resistance / drought tolerance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two problems caused by the overuse of fertilisers and pesticides.
parts.answer: Fertiliser runoff causes eutrophication; pesticides kill non-target organisms such as bees; pesticides build up in food chains; pests become resistant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A farmer grows only cotton on a very large area year after year. What is a disadvantage of this monoculture?
A The crop is easier to harvest by machine.
B Pests of cotton can spread quickly through the crop.
C More species of wild plants grow in the field.
D Soil minerals are increased each year.
parts.answer: B Pests of cotton can spread quickly through the crop.
parts.working: In a monoculture the same food plant is everywhere, so pests and diseases spread easily and build up. A is an advantage, not a disadvantage.

practice.stem:
Trials on wheat fields in Punjab measured grain yield with different amounts of nitrate fertiliser.
fertiliser / kg per hectare: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200
yield / tonnes per hectare: 2.1, 3.4, 4.2, 4.5, 4.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in yield, and the percentage increase, when fertiliser was increased from 0 to 100 kg per hectare.
parts.answer: 2.1 tonnes per hectare; 100 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of increasing fertiliser above 150 kg per hectare.
parts.answer: No further increase in yield (it stays at 4.5 t/ha).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why yield stops increasing at high fertiliser levels.
parts.answer: Another factor, such as water, light, another mineral or the crop's genetic potential, becomes limiting.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use the data to advise the farmer how much fertiliser to use. Explain your advice.
parts.answer: About 150 kg/ha (or between 100 and 150): more gives no extra yield, wastes money and the excess may run off into rivers causing eutrophication.
parts.working: B1 amount with data reason; B1 cost / pollution reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many chickens in Pakistan are reared in large intensive sheds with thousands of birds. Give two advantages of intensive livestock production.
parts.answer: Cheaper meat and eggs; more food produced from less land; less energy lost by birds moving / keeping warm, so faster growth; easier to control feeding and disease.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three disadvantages of intensive livestock production.
parts.answer: Diseases spread quickly between crowded animals; heavy use of antibiotics can lead to resistant bacteria; animal welfare concerns; waste can pollute water; high energy use for heating, lighting and feed transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A country has a population of 240 million, growing by 2 % each year. Calculate the population after 10 years. Give your answer in millions to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 292.6 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the problems a country faces in producing enough food for a growing population. Include reasons why famine may occur.
parts.answer: Rising demand for food; less farmland as cities expand; soil erosion / desertification reduces fertile land; droughts and floods (climate change) destroy crops; water shortage for irrigation; pests and diseases; poverty means people cannot buy food; war or poor transport stops distribution; high cost of fertilisers and machinery.

practice.stem: One hectare of land produces wheat containing 20 000 MJ of energy per year. A person needs about 3650 MJ of food energy per year. When cattle eat wheat, about 10 % of the energy in the wheat ends up in the beef eaten by people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many people could be fed for one year from one hectare (i) if they eat the wheat, (ii) if the wheat is fed to cattle and they eat the beef. Give answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: (i) 5.5 people (ii) 0.5 people

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why so much energy is lost when the wheat is fed to cattle.
parts.answer: Cattle use energy for respiration (movement, keeping warm); some of the food is not digested and is lost in faeces; energy lost in urine / parts not eaten (bones, hide); so only about 10 % passes to the next trophic level.
parts.working: B1 respiration / heat loss; B1 egestion / undigested food; B1 not all parts eaten / energy in excretion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why people still keep animals for food in areas where crops grow poorly.
parts.answer: Animals can graze on land too dry, steep or poor to grow crops, turning grass people cannot eat into food.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In pea plants, the allele for tall (T) is dominant to the allele for short (t). What is the genotype of a short plant?
A TT
B Tt
C tt
D T
parts.answer: C tt
parts.working: A recessive phenotype shows only when two recessive alleles are present (homozygous recessive). Tt is tall because T is dominant, so B is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Define the terms:
(i) allele
(ii) homozygous
(iii) phenotype
parts.answer: (i) a version (alternative form) of a gene; (ii) having two identical alleles of a gene; (iii) the observable features of an organism

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a dominant allele.
parts.answer: an allele that is expressed (shows in the phenotype) when present, even if only one copy

parts.label: a
parts.text: In guinea pigs, black fur (B) is dominant to white fur (b). Two black guinea pigs, both Bb, are crossed. Use a genetic diagram to show the genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring.
parts.answer: parents Bb × Bb; gametes B, b and B, b; offspring BB, Bb, Bb, bb; phenotypes 3 black : 1 white
parts.working: B1 parental genotypes; B1 gametes (one allele each); B1 offspring genotypes; B1 phenotypes with ratio 3 black : 1 white

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the probability that one offspring is white.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two heterozygous plants are crossed. What proportion of the offspring is expected to be homozygous?
A 25 %
B 50 %
C 75 %
D 100 %
parts.working: Aa × Aa gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so AA + aa = 2 out of 4 = 50 %. 75 % is the proportion showing the dominant phenotype, so C is the main distractor.

practice.stem: In a plant, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white flowers (p). Two heterozygous plants are crossed and 840 seeds are grown.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of plants with white flowers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The actual numbers were 618 purple and 222 white. Suggest why these differ from the expected numbers.
parts.answer: fertilisation is random, so ratios are only probabilities
parts.working: B1 random fusion of gametes / chance

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how a gardener could find out whether one purple-flowered plant is homozygous or heterozygous.
parts.answer: cross it with a white (homozygous recessive) plant (test cross); if all offspring purple, it is homozygous; if about half white (1 : 1), it is heterozygous
parts.working: B1 cross with white/recessive; B1 all purple → homozygous; B1 some/half white → heterozygous

practice.stem:
A family tree for an inherited condition (described in words):
Generation 1: person 1 (unaffected male) and person 2 (affected female).
Generation 2: their children are person 3 (unaffected male) and person 5 (unaffected female). Person 3 marries person 4 (unaffected female from another family).
Generation 3: persons 3 and 4 have three children: person 6 (unaffected female), person 7 (affected male) and person 8 (unaffected male).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how you can tell from the family tree that the allele for the condition is recessive.
parts.answer: persons 3 and 4 are unaffected but have an affected child (person 7); so both parents must carry a hidden (recessive) allele
parts.working: B1 unaffected parents (3 and 4) with affected child (7); B1 parents are carriers/heterozygous

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the genotypes of persons 3, 4 and 7, using D for the normal allele and d for the condition.
parts.answer: 3: Dd; 4: Dd; 7: dd

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the probability that the next child of persons 3 and 4 is affected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the ratio 3 : 1 is seen in the offspring of a cross between two heterozygous parents.
parts.answer: each parent produces two types of gamete (A and a) in equal numbers; fertilisation is random; giving 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; AA and Aa both show the dominant feature, so 3 : 1
parts.working: B1 gametes A and a in equal proportions (meiosis); B1 random fertilisation; B1 AA and Aa same phenotype → 3 : 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the meaning of 'genotype'.
parts.answer: the alleles (genetic make-up) an organism has, e.g. Aa

practice.stem:
A family tree for an inherited condition caused by a recessive allele d (normal allele D), described in words:
Generation 1: person 1 (unaffected male) and person 2 (unaffected female).
Generation 2: their children are person 3 (affected female) and person 4 (unaffected male). Person 4 marries person 5 (affected female).
Generation 3: persons 4 and 5 have two children: person 6 (unaffected male) and person 7 (affected female).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how person 7 shows that person 4 is heterozygous.
parts.answer: person 7 is dd, so she received one d allele from each parent, including person 4; person 4 is unaffected, so he also has a D allele: Dd
parts.working: B1 person 7 (dd) received d from father/person 4; B1 person 4 unaffected so has D → Dd

parts.label: b
parts.text: Before persons 4 and 5 had any children, what was the probability that person 4 was a carrier? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: 2/3: persons 1 and 2 must both be Dd (they have an affected child, person 3); their offspring are DD, Dd, Dd, dd; person 4 is unaffected, so he is one of DD, Dd, Dd, and 2 of these 3 are carriers
parts.working: M1 persons 1 and 2 both Dd, dd excluded as person 4 is unaffected; A1 2/3

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the genotype of person 6 and explain how you know.
parts.answer: Dd: he is unaffected (has D) but his mother, person 5, is dd and must have passed a d allele to him
parts.working: B1 Dd with reason (d from affected mother)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A breeder of goats in Balochistan finds that horns (h) are recessive to hornless (H). She crosses a hornless male with several horned females. Out of 24 kids, 11 have horns. Deduce the genotype of the male, with a reason.
parts.answer: Hh; the horned kids are hh, so they must have received an h allele from the male as well as from the mother
parts.working: B1 Hh; B1 horned kids need h from father

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected numbers of horned and hornless kids from this cross, out of 24.
parts.answer: Hh × hh gives 1 : 1, so 12 horned and 12 hornless

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the breeder would prefer a homozygous hornless male if she wants only hornless kids.
parts.answer: HH × hh gives all Hh, all hornless; every gamete from the male carries H
parts.working: B1 all offspring Hh; B1 all hornless/dominant allele always passed on

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which base always pairs with adenine in a DNA molecule?
A cytosine
B guanine
C thymine
D uracil
parts.answer: C thymine
parts.working: A pairs with T and C pairs with G in DNA. Uracil is not found in DNA, so D is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a gene.
parts.answer: a length of DNA that codes for a protein

parts.label: b
parts.text: Put these in order of size, smallest first: chromosome, nucleus, gene, base.
parts.answer: base, gene, chromosome, nucleus

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the structure of a DNA molecule.
parts.answer: two strands coiled into a double helix; each strand has a sequence of bases; bases pair across the strands (A with T, C with G)
parts.working: B1 two strands/double helix; B1 bases; B1 complementary pairing A–T, C–G

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A human sperm cell contains 23 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a human skin cell?
A 23
B 44
C 46
D 92
parts.working: Body cells are diploid (two sets), 2 × 23 = 46. 23 is the haploid number of gametes, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a sample of DNA, 22 % of the bases are adenine. Calculate the percentage of thymine, guanine and cytosine.
parts.answer: thymine 22 %; guanine and cytosine together 100 − 44 = 56 %, so guanine 28 % and cytosine 28 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the percentage of adenine always equals the percentage of thymine.
parts.answer: A always pairs with T across the two strands

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the sex chromosomes of a human male and a human female.
parts.answer: male XY; female XX

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use a genetic diagram to show that the chance of a baby being a boy is 50 %.
parts.answer: parents XX × XY; gametes: egg X only, sperm X or Y; offspring XX, XY in a 1 : 1 ratio (50 % boys)
parts.working: B1 parental chromosomes; B1 gametes; B1 offspring 1 : 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A goat body cell has 60 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in a goat egg cell and in a goat zygote.
parts.answer: egg: 30; zygote: 60

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important that gametes are haploid.
parts.answer: when two gametes fuse at fertilisation, the diploid number is restored; otherwise the chromosome number would double each generation
parts.working: B1 fertilisation restores diploid number; B1 prevents doubling each generation

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a gene and an allele, using an example.
parts.answer: a gene is a length of DNA coding for a characteristic/protein, e.g. the gene for flower colour; alleles are different versions of that gene, e.g. purple allele and white allele
parts.working: B1 gene definition; B1 allele as version of gene with example

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why identical twins have the same alleles but non-identical twins do not.
parts.answer: identical twins come from one zygote that splits (mitosis gives identical cells); non-identical twins come from two different eggs and sperm, which were made by meiosis and differ genetically
parts.working: B1 identical from one zygote/mitosis; B1 non-identical from two different gametes produced by meiosis

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of cell division produces gametes in humans?
A mitosis
B meiosis
C fertilisation
D binary fission
parts.answer: B meiosis
parts.working: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to make haploid gametes. Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid cells, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two uses of mitosis in the human body.
parts.answer: growth; repair of damaged tissue; replacement of cells (e.g. skin, blood cells)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of cells produced when one cell divides by mitosis, and how they compare with the parent cell.
parts.answer: two cells; genetically identical to the parent (same number of chromosomes)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare mitosis and meiosis. Give three differences.
parts.answer: mitosis gives 2 cells, meiosis 4; mitosis keeps the chromosome number (diploid), meiosis halves it (haploid); mitosis gives genetically identical cells, meiosis genetically different cells; mitosis for growth/repair, meiosis for gametes
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three paired differences

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where meiosis takes place in a flowering plant.
parts.answer: anthers (to make pollen) and ovules/ovary

practice.stem: Some cells used in medical research are grown in a flask. In good conditions each cell divides by mitosis every 20 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Starting from one cell, calculate the number of cells after 3 hours, assuming no cells die.
parts.answer: 3 hours = 180 min = 9 divisions; 2⁹ = 512 cells

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why all the cells produced are genetically identical.
parts.answer: DNA (chromosomes) is copied exactly before division; each new cell gets an identical set of chromosomes
parts.working: B1 chromosomes replicated/copied exactly; B1 each daughter cell receives identical set

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how meiosis and fertilisation together lead to genetic variation among offspring of the same parents.
parts.answer: meiosis produces gametes with different combinations of alleles/chromosomes; each gamete is genetically different; fertilisation is random, so any sperm can fuse with any egg
parts.working: B1 meiosis gives genetically different gametes; B1 different combinations of chromosomes/alleles; B1 random fertilisation

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a banana plant grown from a cutting is genetically identical to its parent.
parts.answer: it is produced by asexual reproduction, using mitosis only

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the molecule that carries a copy of a gene from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
parts.answer: mRNA (messenger RNA)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what determines the order of amino acids in a protein.
parts.answer: the sequence of bases in the gene (DNA)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why DNA does not leave the nucleus during protein synthesis.
parts.answer: DNA is too large to pass through the nuclear membrane / it is kept safe; a copy (mRNA) is made instead

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Where in a cell are proteins assembled from amino acids?
A nucleus
B ribosome
C cell membrane
D vacuole
parts.answer: B ribosome
parts.working: Ribosomes join amino acids in the order coded by mRNA. The nucleus holds the DNA and makes mRNA but does not assemble the protein, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the information in a gene is used to make a protein.
parts.answer: the gene's base sequence is copied into mRNA in the nucleus; mRNA moves to the cytoplasm; to a ribosome; the ribosome reads the base sequence and joins amino acids in the correct order to make the protein
parts.working: 1 mark each for four of: mRNA made from gene in nucleus; mRNA moves out to cytoplasm; ribosome; base sequence read (three bases per amino acid); amino acids joined in specific order

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gene contains 1 260 bases that code for a protein. Each amino acid is coded for by three bases. Calculate the number of amino acids in the protein.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One base in this gene is changed. Explain how this could stop the protein working.
parts.answer: the change alters the base sequence (gene mutation); so a different amino acid may be inserted; the protein folds into a different shape, e.g. an enzyme's active site changes
parts.working: B1 base sequence changed; B1 different amino acid sequence; B1 different shape/active site so protein does not function

parts.label: a
parts.text: All body cells of a person contain the same genes, but insulin is made only in certain cells of the pancreas. Explain this.
parts.answer: only some genes are expressed (switched on) in each cell type; the insulin gene is expressed only in those pancreas cells
parts.working: B1 genes switched on/off (expressed) differently; B1 insulin gene only expressed in pancreas cells

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why bacteria given a human insulin gene can make human insulin.
parts.answer: the base code is read in the same way in bacteria (universal code); the bacteria's ribosomes join amino acids in the order coded for by the gene, making the same protein
parts.working: B1 genetic code is the same/universal; B1 bacterial ribosomes make the same amino acid sequence

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by codominance.
parts.answer: both alleles in a heterozygote are expressed in the phenotype; neither is dominant
parts.working: B1 both alleles expressed; B1 in heterozygote

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the possible genotypes of a person with blood group A.
parts.answer: Iᴬ Iᴬ or Iᴬ i

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A man of blood group AB and a woman of blood group O have a child. Which blood groups are possible for the child?
A A or B only
B AB or O only
C A, B, AB or O
D O only
parts.answer: A A or B only
parts.working: Father Iᴬ Iᴮ × mother i i gives Iᴬ i (group A) or Iᴮ i (group B). AB needs both Iᴬ and Iᴮ but the mother gives only i, so B is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A woman with blood group A (genotype Iᴬ i) and a man with blood group B (genotype Iᴮ i) have children. Use a genetic diagram to show all the possible blood groups of their children.
parts.answer: parents Iᴬ i × Iᴮ i; gametes Iᴬ, i and Iᴮ, i; offspring Iᴬ Iᴮ (AB), Iᴬ i (A), Iᴮ i (B), i i (O)
parts.working: B1 gametes; B1 offspring genotypes; B1 phenotypes; B1 all four groups identified

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that their first child has blood group O.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a flower, the allele for red petals (Cᴿ) and the allele for white petals (Cᵂ) are codominant. Heterozygous plants have red-and-white streaked petals. Two streaked plants are crossed and 200 seeds are grown. Calculate the expected numbers of red, streaked and white plants.
parts.answer: Cᴿ Cᵂ × Cᴿ Cᵂ gives 1 : 2 : 1; red 50, streaked 100, white 50

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a gardener who wants only streaked plants cannot get them by crossing streaked plants, but can by crossing red with white.
parts.answer: streaked × streaked gives three phenotypes (homozygotes appear); red × white (Cᴿ Cᴿ × Cᵂ Cᵂ) gives all Cᴿ Cᵂ, all streaked
parts.working: B1 streaked × streaked gives red and white too; B1 red × white gives all heterozygous/streaked

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the food chain  algae → water flea → small fish → heron,  which organism is the secondary consumer?
A algae
B water flea
C small fish
D heron
parts.answer: C small fish
parts.working: The small fish eats the primary consumer (water flea), so it is the secondary consumer. The heron is the tertiary consumer, so D is wrong.

practice.stem:
A food web in a wheat field in Punjab:
wheat is eaten by grasshoppers, field mice and sparrows
grasshoppers are eaten by sparrows and frogs
field mice are eaten by snakes and owls
sparrows are eaten by owls
frogs are eaten by snakes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the producer in this food web.
parts.answer: wheat

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write out one food chain from the web that has four organisms.
parts.answer: e.g. wheat → grasshopper → frog → snake (or wheat → grasshopper → sparrow → owl)
parts.working: B1 correct chain with arrows pointing to the eater

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one organism that is both a primary and a secondary consumer.
parts.answer: sparrow

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the source of energy for the whole food web.
parts.answer: the Sun (light energy)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State what is meant by:
(i) a producer
(ii) a consumer
parts.answer: (i) organism that makes its own organic nutrients, usually by photosynthesis; (ii) organism that gets energy by feeding on other organisms

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the role of decomposers in an ecosystem.
parts.answer: break down dead organisms and waste; release nutrients/minerals back into the soil (recycling)
parts.working: B1 break down dead material; B1 recycle nutrients

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What do the arrows in a food chain show?
A the direction in which energy is transferred
B which organism is larger
C the direction in which oxygen moves
D which organism eats more food
parts.answer: A the direction in which energy is transferred
parts.working: Arrows point from the food to the feeder, showing energy transfer. They do not show size, so B is wrong.

practice.stem:
A food web in a wheat field in Punjab:
wheat is eaten by grasshoppers, field mice and sparrows
grasshoppers are eaten by sparrows and frogs
field mice are eaten by snakes and owls
sparrows are eaten by owls
frogs are eaten by snakes

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer sprays insecticide that kills most grasshoppers. Explain two possible effects on other organisms in the web.
parts.answer: frogs decrease (less food), so snakes may eat more mice, reducing mice; sparrows eat more wheat (or fewer sparrows), affecting owls; wheat may increase (less eaten by grasshoppers)
parts.working: 2 marks each for two effects with explanation (B1 effect, B1 reason): frogs fall due to less food; sparrows rely more on wheat/fall; snakes eat more mice; wheat increases

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why food webs give a more realistic picture of feeding than food chains.
parts.answer: most animals eat more than one type of food / are eaten by more than one predator

practice.stem: In the Arabian Sea off the coast of Karachi: phytoplankton are eaten by zooplankton; zooplankton are eaten by sardines and by jellyfish; sardines are eaten by tuna; jellyfish are eaten by turtles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Construct a food web using all five organisms.
parts.answer: phytoplankton → zooplankton; zooplankton → sardine; zooplankton → jellyfish; sardine → tuna; jellyfish → turtle
parts.working: B1 producer at start; B1 all arrows from food to eater; B1 all five links correct

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the trophic level of the tuna.
parts.answer: tertiary consumer (fourth trophic level)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Plastic bags in the sea are mistaken by turtles for jellyfish. Suggest the effect on the jellyfish population if many turtles die.
parts.answer: jellyfish increase (fewer predators)

practice.stem: In a village pond in Sindh, small fish eat mosquito larvae and dragonfly nymphs. Dragonfly nymphs also eat mosquito larvae. All the fish are removed by netting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the number of mosquitoes might increase after the fish are removed.
parts.answer: fish eat mosquito larvae; fewer predators so more larvae survive to become adults
parts.working: B1 fish are predators of larvae; B1 more survive

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the dragonfly nymphs might first increase and then decrease.
parts.answer: at first more food (more mosquito larvae) and no competition from fish, so they increase; then the larger nymph population eats most of the larvae / food becomes scarce, so their numbers fall
parts.working: B1 more food (larvae) / less competition; B1 increase; B1 food runs out / competition rises so decrease

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why using fish to control mosquitoes may be better than spraying insecticide.
parts.answer: does not kill other (useful) insects / no chemical pollution or bioaccumulation / mosquitoes do not become resistant

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels.
parts.answer: energy is lost at each level (respiration, heat, movement, egestion, excretion, parts not eaten); only about 10 % passes on; too little energy remains to support another level
parts.working: B1 energy lost at each transfer; B1 named loss; B1 not enough energy for further level

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why eating plant food such as lentils feeds more people from the same area of land than eating meat.
parts.answer: shorter food chain; less energy lost, as energy is lost when crops are fed to animals
parts.working: B1 humans as primary consumers / shorter chain; B1 less energy lost between levels

practice.stem:
Energy in a grassland food chain (kJ per m² per year):
grass: 25 000
grasshoppers: 2 500
lizards: 200
hawks: 15

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of energy transferred from the producers to the primary consumers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage transferred from the primary to the secondary consumers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two ways energy is lost between trophic levels.
parts.answer: respiration (heat); movement; egestion (faeces); excretion; parts not eaten (bones, roots)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
One large mango tree is eaten by 2000 caterpillars, which are eaten by 50 birds. Which describes the pyramids of numbers and biomass for this food chain?
A both pyramid-shaped
B pyramid of numbers has a narrow base (not pyramid-shaped), pyramid of biomass pyramid-shaped
C pyramid of numbers pyramid-shaped, pyramid of biomass has a narrow base
D neither pyramid-shaped
parts.answer: B pyramid of numbers has a narrow base (not pyramid-shaped), pyramid of biomass pyramid-shaped
parts.working: One tree supports many caterpillars, so the bottom bar of the number pyramid is narrowest, but the tree has the greatest biomass, so the biomass pyramid is pyramid-shaped. C has them the wrong way round.

practice.stem: A field of fodder crop receives 1 500 000 kJ of light energy per m² per year and fixes 15 000 kJ per m² per year in photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the light energy that is fixed by the crop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Goats eat all the energy fixed by the crop and convert 10 % of the energy they receive into new body tissue. Calculate the energy in the new goat tissue, in kJ per m² per year.
parts.answer: 15 000 × 0.1 = 1 500 kJ per m² per year

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why most of the light energy is not fixed by the crop.
parts.answer: light misses leaves / reflected; wrong wavelength; transmitted through leaves; used to evaporate water; photosynthesis limited by CO₂/temperature

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a pyramid of biomass is usually a better way to show a food chain than a pyramid of numbers.
parts.answer: pyramid of numbers ignores size, e.g. one tree with many insects gives an odd shape; biomass takes the mass of organisms into account so is nearly always pyramid-shaped
parts.working: B1 numbers ignores size of organisms; B1 biomass accounts for mass/always upright

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one disadvantage of measuring biomass to construct a pyramid of biomass.
parts.answer: organisms must be killed and dried to find their dry mass (or biomass changes with the season / hard to sample all organisms)
parts.working: B1 any one: organisms killed/destructive; dry mass takes time; varies with season/time of year; difficult to collect all organisms (e.g. roots, soil organisms)

practice.stem: In a lake, producers fix 36 000 kJ per m² per year. Transfer efficiency is 8 % from producers to primary consumers, and 10 % at each later transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy reaching the tertiary consumers, in kJ per m² per year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the transfer from producers to herbivores (8 %) is less efficient than the transfers between animals (10 %).
parts.answer: plant material contains much cellulose/lignin that herbivores cannot digest; so a larger proportion of the food is lost in faeces (egested); animal food is more digestible
parts.working: B1 cellulose/plant material hard to digest; B1 more energy lost in faeces/egestion

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a pyramid of energy is always upright.
parts.answer: energy is lost at every transfer between trophic levels (e.g. as heat from respiration); so each level always has less energy than the one below
parts.working: B1 energy lost at each level; B1 so less available at each higher level

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fish farms in Thailand feed farmed fish with pellets made from wild-caught smaller fish. Use ideas about energy flow to explain why this may not be sustainable.
parts.answer: much energy is lost when small fish are fed to farmed fish; more mass of wild fish is caught than farmed fish produced; wild stocks may be overfished
parts.working: B1 energy losses mean more wild fish needed than produced; B1 overfishing of wild stocks

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which factor would NOT normally limit the growth of a population of rabbits?
A food supply
B predation by foxes
C disease
D a high birth rate
parts.answer: D a high birth rate
parts.working: A high birth rate increases the population; food shortage, predators and disease limit it. A (food) is a limiting factor.

practice.stem:
Students counted clover plants in ten 0.5 m × 0.5 m (0.25 m²) quadrats placed randomly in a school field 50 m × 20 m.
Counts: 3, 5, 0, 7, 4, 6, 2, 5, 8, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of plants per quadrat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of plants per m².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate the total number of plants in the field.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State how the students made sure the quadrats were placed randomly.
