parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which shows the correct way to write the scientific name of the house sparrow in the binomial system?
A Passer Domesticus
B passer domesticus
C Passer domesticus
D PASSER domesticus
parts.answer: C Passer domesticus
parts.working: The genus has a capital first letter and the species name is all lower case (printed in italics or underlined when handwritten). A wrongly capitalises the species name.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the seven characteristics of living organisms.
parts.answer: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition
parts.working: 3 marks for all seven; 2 marks for five or six; 1 mark for three or four.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A car moves, uses fuel and gives out waste gases, but it is not alive. State two characteristics of living organisms that a car does not show.
parts.answer: growth and reproduction
parts.working: B1 growth; B1 reproduction. Accept sensitivity (detecting and responding to stimuli) as one of the two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define excretion.
parts.answer: The removal of waste products of metabolism, toxic materials and substances in excess of requirements from the body.
parts.working: B1 removal of waste products of metabolism / toxic materials; B1 substances in excess.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define sensitivity.
parts.answer: The ability to detect and respond to changes in the internal or external environment.
parts.working: B1 detect changes / stimuli; B1 respond.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A sunflower turns its head to face the sun. Name the characteristic of living organisms shown.
parts.answer: sensitivity

parts.label: a
parts.text: The deodar tree is named Cedrus deodara. State its genus.
parts.answer: Cedrus

parts.label: b
parts.text: The cedar of Lebanon is named Cedrus libani. What does the shared first name tell you about these two trees?
parts.answer: They belong to the same genus, so they are closely related.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two rules for writing a binomial name.
parts.answer: Genus first with a capital letter; species second in lower case; printed in italics or underlined when handwritten.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the vertebrate group with each set of features.
(i) feathers, a beak and wings
(ii) moist skin with no scales; larvae with gills
(iii) fur and external ears (pinnae)
(iv) dry scaly skin; lays eggs with rubbery shells on land
(v) fins, wet scales and gills
parts.answer: (i) birds; (ii) amphibians; (iii) mammals; (iv) reptiles; (v) fish

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three features that show a housefly is an insect.
parts.answer: Body in three parts (head, thorax, abdomen); three pairs of legs; one pair of antennae; wings (one or two pairs); compound eyes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature that all arthropods share.
parts.answer: Jointed legs / exoskeleton / segmented body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Maize is a monocotyledon and mustard is a dicotyledon. State how the leaf veins of the two plants differ.
parts.answer: Maize has parallel veins; mustard has a branching network of veins.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many cotyledons are found in the seed of each plant.
parts.answer: maize one; mustard two

parts.label: c
parts.text: A mustard flower has 4 petals. A lily flower has 6 petals. Which of these is a monocotyledon? Give a reason.
parts.answer: The lily – its flower parts are in multiples of three.
parts.working: B1 lily; B1 multiples of three.

practice.stem:
A student looked at four animals with a hand lens and recorded her observations.
Animal | body parts | pairs of legs | pairs of antennae | wings
1 | 3 | 3 | 1 | 2 pairs
2 | 2 | 4 | 0 | none
3 | 2 | 5 | 2 | none
4 | many similar segments | 30 | 1 | none

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the arthropod group of each animal 1 to 4.
parts.answer: 1 insect; 2 arachnid; 3 crustacean; 4 myriapod

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of legs of animal 4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one feature, other than jointed legs, that all four animals share.
parts.answer: exoskeleton / segmented body

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three features of plant cells that are not found in animal cells.
parts.answer: cellulose cell wall; chloroplasts; large permanent vacuole containing cell sap

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how plants and animals differ in the way they obtain food.
parts.answer: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis; animals feed on other organisms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why biologists classify living organisms into groups.
parts.answer: Makes it easier to identify and study organisms; shows evolutionary relationships; allows features of a new organism to be predicted; helps scientists communicate with one shared system.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the basis on which organisms are placed into the same group.
parts.answer: They share features (characteristics).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which features does a spider have?
A 3 body parts, 3 pairs of legs, 1 pair of antennae
B 2 body parts, 4 pairs of legs, no antennae
C 2 body parts, 5 pairs of legs, 2 pairs of antennae
D many body segments, many pairs of legs, 1 pair of antennae
parts.answer: B 2 body parts, 4 pairs of legs, no antennae
parts.working: Spiders are arachnids: two body parts, four pairs of legs and no antennae. A describes an insect; C a crustacean; D a myriapod.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An animal has moist skin without scales. It lays eggs in water and its young have gills. To which group does it belong?
A fish
B reptiles
C amphibians
D birds
parts.answer: C amphibians
parts.working: Moist scaleless skin, eggs laid in water and larvae (tadpoles) with gills are amphibian features. Fish (A) have scales and keep their gills as adults.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature is characteristic of organisms in the fungus kingdom?
A cells contain chloroplasts
B cells have no nucleus
C they feed by secreting enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorbing the products
D cell walls are made of cellulose
parts.answer: C they feed by secreting enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorbing the products
parts.working: Fungi feed saprotrophically by extracellular digestion. Cellulose walls (D) and chloroplasts (A) are plant features; fungal cells do have a nucleus.

practice.stem:
Key:
1 (a) has antennae … go to 2
1 (b) has no antennae … spider
2 (a) has 3 pairs of legs … butterfly
2 (b) has more than 3 pairs of legs … go to 3
3 (a) has 2 pairs of antennae … woodlouse
3 (b) has 1 pair of antennae … centipede
Animals found in a garden in Faisalabad:
E: 3 pairs of legs, 1 pair of antennae, 2 pairs of wings
F: 4 pairs of legs, no antennae
G: 7 pairs of legs, 2 pairs of antennae, hard grey exoskeleton
H: long body with about 20 segments, 1 pair of legs on each segment, 1 pair of antennae

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the key to identify animals E, F, G and H.
parts.answer: E butterfly; F spider; G woodlouse; H centipede

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the arthropod group to which F and G each belong.
parts.answer: F arachnid; G crustacean

practice.stem:
Key:
1 (a) fruit has wings … go to 2
1 (b) fruit has no wings … go to 3
2 (a) one wing … J
2 (b) two wings … K
3 (a) fruit is fleshy … go to 4
3 (b) fruit is dry with hooks … N
4 (a) one large seed … L
4 (b) many seeds … M

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Use the key to give the letter for each fruit.
(i) a mango: fleshy, with one large seed
(ii) a guava: fleshy, with many small seeds
(iii) a dry fruit covered in tiny hooks
(iv) a dry fruit with two wings
parts.answer: (i) L; (ii) M; (iii) N; (iv) K

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why each step of the key has exactly two statements.
parts.answer: Each step is a pair of contrasting statements, so every fruit fits only one of them and is sent along one route to a single end-point (a dichotomous key).
parts.working: B1 two contrasting/opposite statements so each organism fits only one / dichotomous.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A prawn is a crustacean and a locust is an insect. Give three ways in which a prawn differs from a locust.
parts.answer: Prawn has two pairs of antennae (locust one pair); prawn has more than four pairs of legs (locust three pairs); prawn has no wings (locust has wings); prawn body is cephalothorax and abdomen (locust head, thorax, abdomen).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three comparisons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Both animals have an exoskeleton. State one other feature they share.
parts.answer: jointed legs / segmented body

practice.stem: Bacteria are single-celled organisms. Some live in the soil of a rice field in Punjab.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the kingdom to which bacteria belong.
parts.answer: prokaryotes (prokaryote kingdom)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two structures found in a plant cell that are not found in a bacterial cell.
parts.answer: Any two: nucleus; mitochondria; chloroplasts; large permanent vacuole; cellulose cell wall.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two structures that are found in a bacterial cell.
parts.answer: Any two: cell wall; cell membrane; cytoplasm; ribosomes; circular DNA; plasmids.

practice.stem: Ferns grow on the shady, damp banks of streams in the Murree hills, while flowering plants such as wild roses grow nearby.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ferns and flowering plants are both in the plant kingdom. State two features shared by all plants.
parts.answer: Cells with cellulose cell walls; chloroplasts / photosynthesis; multicellular.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features that distinguish ferns from flowering plants.
parts.answer: Ferns have no flowers; they reproduce by spores not seeds; leaves called fronds.

practice.stem: Fruit bats roost in large trees in Lahore and fly out at dusk to feed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bat flies like a bird. State three features that show it is a mammal.
parts.answer: Fur/hair; external ears (pinnae); mammary glands / feeds young on milk; (whiskers).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature a bird has that a bat does not.
parts.answer: feathers / a beak / lays hard-shelled eggs

practice.stem:
Key to some animals of Pakistan:
1 (a) breathes with gills as an adult … mahseer
1 (b) breathes with lungs … go to 2
2 (a) has feathers … peacock
2 (b) has no feathers … go to 3
3 (a) has mammary glands … go to 4
3 (b) has no mammary glands … go to 5
4 (a) lives in rivers, has flippers … Indus river dolphin
4 (b) lives on mountains, has horns … markhor
5 (a) dry skin with scales … mugger crocodile
5 (b) moist skin without scales … bullfrog

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the key to identify the animal that ends at statement 5 (b).
parts.answer: bullfrog

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of the statement that separates the Indus river dolphin from the markhor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Indus river dolphin lives in water and has fins, like a mahseer fish. Explain why it is classified as a mammal, not a fish.
parts.answer: It feeds its young on milk from mammary glands; it breathes air with lungs, not gills; it has no scales.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three (mammary glands/milk must be one of them for full marks).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature is typical of a monocotyledon such as wheat?
A two cotyledons in each seed
B leaves with a branching network of veins
C flower parts in multiples of three
D flower parts in multiples of five
parts.answer: C flower parts in multiples of three
parts.working: Monocots have one cotyledon, parallel leaf veins and flower parts in threes. D (multiples of four or five) and B are dicotyledon features.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure is found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells but is NOT found in a virus?
A ribosomes
B a nucleus
C a cell wall
D genetic material
parts.answer: A ribosomes
parts.working: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells both have ribosomes (as well as cytoplasm and a cell membrane); a virus has only a protein coat and genetic material. B is wrong because prokaryotic cells have no nucleus; C is wrong because animal cells have no cell wall; D is wrong because viruses do contain DNA or RNA.

practice.stem:
Leaf A: simple, smooth edge, parallel veins
Leaf B: compound (divided into leaflets), leaflets with toothed edges
Leaf C: simple, toothed edge, branching veins
Leaf D: compound, leaflets with smooth edges

parts.label: a
parts.text: Construct a dichotomous key to identify leaves A, B, C and D. Use only features given in the descriptions.
parts.answer: 1 (a) leaf divided into leaflets (compound) … go to 2; (b) leaf not divided (simple) … go to 3. 2 (a) leaflets with toothed edges … B; (b) leaflets with smooth edges … D. 3 (a) parallel veins … A; (b) branching (net) veins … C.
parts.working: B1 first split uses a feature dividing the four into 2 + 2 (or 1 + 3); B1 each statement is a pair of contrasting statements; B1 correct observable features used throughout; B1 every leaf identified correctly with one end-point each.

practice.stem:
The base sequence of the same 300-base section of a gene was compared in four species of bird. Number of bases that differ from species W:
X: 6
Y: 27
Z: 45

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of bases that differ between species W and each of X, Y and Z.
parts.working: M1 number different ÷ 300 × 100; A1 all three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which species is most closely related to W. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: X – it has the smallest difference in base sequence, so it shared a common ancestor with W most recently.
parts.working: B1 X; B1 fewest differences / most recent common ancestor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why scientists now use DNA base sequences as well as visible features to classify organisms.
parts.answer: Visible features can be similar in unrelated organisms (e.g. due to similar habitats); DNA sequences show evolutionary relationships more accurately.
parts.working: B1 visible features can mislead; B1 DNA reflects evolutionary relationship / common ancestry.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a virus.
parts.answer: Genetic material (DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protein coat.
parts.working: B1 genetic material / DNA or RNA; B1 protein coat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Viruses are not placed in any of the five kingdoms. Suggest why.
parts.answer: They are not made of cells (no cytoplasm, cell membrane or ribosomes); they cannot carry out the characteristics of life (respiration, nutrition, excretion, growth) on their own; they can only reproduce inside a host cell.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: not cells; no cytoplasm/ribosomes/membrane; no respiration/nutrition/excretion; reproduce only inside living host cells.

practice.stem:
A student wrote this key for five beetles collected in a park:
1 Is it large? yes … go to 2; no … go to 3
2 Is it pretty? yes … beetle A; no … beetle B
3 Is it dark? yes … beetle C; no … go to 4
4 Is it fast? yes … beetle D; no … beetle E

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the questions in this key are not suitable, and suggest a better question for step 1.
parts.answer: 'Large' and 'pretty' are subjective / depend on the person; size varies with age; colours may change; better: 'Does it have wings?' or 'Does it have more than three pairs of legs?' (an observable, countable feature).
parts.working: B1 features are opinions / not measurable; B1 size varies with age or individual; B1 two contrasting statements needed at each step; B1 a suitable observable alternative question.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other rules for a good dichotomous key.
parts.answer: Each step has only two choices; each organism appears at only one end-point; use features that are present in all specimens / visible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Birds and reptiles both lay eggs with shells on land. Give two features that can be used to tell a bird from a reptile.
parts.answer: Birds have feathers; a beak; front limbs as wings; hard (chalky) eggshells, whereas reptiles have dry scales over the whole body and rubbery/leathery eggshells.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two contrasts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Birds have scales on their legs. Explain why this does not make them reptiles.
parts.answer: Classification uses several features; birds have feathers and a beak, which reptiles lack.

practice.stem: A scientist found a new organism growing on dead leaves in a forest in Swat. It is multicellular and made of thread-like hyphae. Its cells have nuclei and cell walls that are not made of cellulose, but no chloroplasts. It releases enzymes onto the dead leaves and absorbs the products.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the kingdom to which this organism belongs.
parts.answer: fungi (fungus kingdom)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons from the description why it is not a plant.
parts.answer: No chloroplasts / cannot photosynthesise; cell walls not made of cellulose.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason from the description why it is not an animal.
parts.answer: It has cell walls / it is made of hyphae.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe its type of nutrition.
parts.answer: It secretes enzymes onto dead leaves (extracellular digestion) and absorbs the soluble products (saprotrophic).
parts.working: B1 enzymes secreted outside onto food; B1 products absorbed.

practice.stem:
housefly: 3 pairs of legs, 1 pair of antennae, 1 pair of wings
butterfly: 3 pairs of legs, 1 pair of antennae, 2 pairs of wings
spider: 4 pairs of legs, no antennae, no wings, no tail
scorpion: 4 pairs of legs, no antennae, no wings, a long tail with a sting
crab: 5 pairs of legs, 2 pairs of antennae, no wings

parts.label: a
parts.text: Construct a dichotomous key to identify these five arthropods. Use only the features given.
parts.answer: 1 (a) has wings … go to 2; (b) no wings … go to 3. 2 (a) one pair of wings … housefly; (b) two pairs of wings … butterfly. 3 (a) has antennae … crab; (b) no antennae … go to 4. 4 (a) has a tail with a sting … scorpion; (b) no tail … spider.
parts.working: B1 first split divides the group with a clear feature (e.g. wings); B1 pairs of contrasting statements at each step; B1 four steps for five animals; B1 only given observable features used; B1 every animal reaches one end-point correctly.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does bread dough rise when yeast is added and the dough is left in a warm place?
A Yeast produces ethanol, which evaporates and lifts the dough.
B Yeast respires and produces carbon dioxide, which forms bubbles in the dough.
C Yeast produces oxygen, which forms bubbles in the dough.
D Heat turns water in the flour into steam.
parts.answer: B Yeast respires and produces carbon dioxide, which forms bubbles in the dough.
parts.working: Yeast respires the sugars in the dough, releasing carbon dioxide gas that is trapped as bubbles. Ethanol (A) is made but it evaporates during baking and does not make the dough rise.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which enzyme is added to crushed fruit to increase the volume of juice extracted?
A amylase
B lipase
C pectinase
D protease
parts.answer: C pectinase
parts.working: Pectinase breaks down pectin in plant cell walls, so the cells release more juice and the juice is clearer. Amylase (A) digests starch, not the cell wall material that holds juice in.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three reasons why bacteria are useful in biotechnology and genetic modification.
parts.answer: Any three of: they reproduce rapidly; they can make complex molecules; there are few ethical concerns about growing them; they contain plasmids; they share the same genetic code as other organisms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why bread dough containing yeast is left in a warm place before baking.
parts.answer: Warmth gives a temperature near the optimum for yeast enzymes; so yeast respires faster and produces more carbon dioxide, making the dough rise faster.
parts.working: B1 enzymes near optimum temperature; B1 faster respiration/more CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the yeast and the ethanol when the bread is baked.
parts.answer: The yeast is killed by the high temperature; the ethanol evaporates.

practice.stem: A student boiled some glucose solution, let it cool to 35 °C, then added yeast. A layer of vegetable oil was poured on top. A delivery tube led from the flask into a test tube of limewater.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the glucose solution was boiled and then cooled before the yeast was added.
parts.answer: Boiling removes dissolved oxygen (and kills other microorganisms); cooling prevents the yeast being killed/its enzymes denatured by heat.
parts.working: B1 removes oxygen/sterilises; B1 cooled so yeast not killed

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a layer of oil was poured onto the surface of the mixture.
parts.answer: To stop oxygen from the air dissolving in the mixture, so respiration is anaerobic.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the limewater shows and the change you would see.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide is produced; limewater turns milky/cloudy.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the student could measure the rate of respiration.
parts.answer: Count the number of bubbles entering the limewater per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of microorganism used to produce penicillin.
parts.answer: A fungus (Penicillium)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other product made on a large scale in fermenters.
parts.answer: Human insulin (by GM bacteria) / ethanol / enzymes such as pectinase or lactase / mycoprotein.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why penicillin is useful in medicine.
parts.answer: It is an antibiotic that kills (or stops the growth of) bacteria.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Lactose-free milk is made by treating milk with an enzyme. Which row is correct?
A enzyme lactase; products glucose and galactose
B enzyme lactase; products glucose and fructose
C enzyme amylase; products glucose and galactose
D enzyme maltase; products glucose only
parts.answer: A enzyme lactase; products glucose and galactose
parts.working: Lactase breaks lactose (milk sugar) into glucose and galactose. Glucose and fructose (B) are the products of sucrose digestion, not lactose.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An industrial fermenter has a jacket of cold water flowing around it. What is the main reason for this?
A to supply water as a raw material for the microorganisms
B to remove heat released by the respiring microorganisms and keep the optimum temperature
C to heat the contents so the microorganisms grow faster
D to keep the contents sterile
parts.answer: B to remove heat released by the respiring microorganisms and keep the optimum temperature
parts.working: Respiration by large numbers of microorganisms releases heat, which would denature their enzymes; the cold water jacket removes it. C is wrong because the jacket cools rather than heats.

practice.stem: In a sugar mill in Sindh, molasses from sugar cane is mixed with water and yeast in large tanks to make ethanol for use as a biofuel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for the anaerobic respiration of glucose by yeast.
parts.answer: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why air is kept out of the fermenter.
parts.answer: Ethanol is only produced in anaerobic respiration; if oxygen is present, yeast respires aerobically and produces carbon dioxide and water instead of ethanol.
parts.working: B1 anaerobic respiration needed for ethanol; B1 with oxygen yeast respires aerobically (no ethanol)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of using ethanol made from sugar cane as a fuel instead of petrol.
parts.answer: It is a renewable fuel (sugar cane can be regrown) / reduces use of fossil fuels / the crop absorbs carbon dioxide as it grows.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the enzymes in a biological washing powder that remove: (i) a blood or egg stain; (ii) a cooking oil stain.
parts.answer: (i) protease; (ii) lipase

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why biological washing powders work well at 30–40 °C.
parts.answer: The enzymes are near their optimum temperature; so they digest the stains quickly into small soluble molecules that wash away (saving energy compared with a hot wash).
parts.working: B1 near optimum temperature; B1 faster digestion of stains / soluble products wash out

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a biological washing powder is less effective in a 90 °C wash.
parts.answer: At high temperature the enzymes are denatured; the active site changes shape so the stain molecules no longer fit.
parts.working: B1 denatured; B1 active site shape changed/substrate cannot bind

practice.stem: A dairy in Lahore treats milk with lactase. Before treatment the milk contains 4.8 g of lactose per 100 cm³. After treatment it contains 0.3 g of lactose per 100 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the lactose that was broken down. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why some people need to drink lactose-free milk.
parts.answer: They do not make enough lactase (lactose intolerance); undigested lactose causes stomach pain, gas or diarrhoea.
parts.working: B1 little/no lactase produced; B1 symptoms from undigested lactose

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why lactose-free milk tastes sweeter than ordinary milk.
parts.answer: Glucose and galactose taste sweeter than lactose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four conditions that are monitored and controlled inside a fermenter used to produce penicillin, and give a reason for controlling each.
parts.answer: Temperature – kept at the optimum for the fungus's enzymes; pH – kept at the optimum for enzymes; oxygen – supplied for aerobic respiration of the fungus; nutrients (glucose, ammonium/nitrogen source) – supplied for growth and energy; waste products removed – so they do not become toxic.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four conditions with reason

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the fermenter and nutrient medium are sterilised with steam before use.
parts.answer: To kill any unwanted microorganisms; which would compete with the fungus for nutrients or contaminate/spoil the product.
parts.working: B1 kill other microorganisms; B1 competition / contamination of product

practice.stem:
A student mixed 50 g of apple pulp with 2 cm³ of pectinase at different temperatures, then filtered for 20 minutes and measured the volume of juice. A control used boiled pectinase at 40 °C.
Temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
Volume of juice / cm³: 8, 14, 21, 17, 6
Control (boiled enzyme): 5 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum temperature for pectinase in this experiment.
parts.answer: 40 °C (from these results)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a beaker of pulp with boiled pectinase was set up.
parts.answer: As a control; to show that the extra juice is due to the active enzyme (boiling denatures it).
parts.working: B1 control; B1 shows effect is due to active enzyme

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in juice volume at 40 °C compared with the control. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why less juice was collected at 60 °C.
parts.answer: Pectinase was denatured at the high temperature; so less pectin was broken down and fewer cells released juice.
parts.working: B1 enzyme denatured; B1 less pectin broken down

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest how the student could find the optimum temperature more precisely.
parts.answer: Repeat with smaller temperature intervals between 30 °C and 50 °C (e.g. every 2 °C).

practice.stem:
The table shows changes in a penicillin fermenter.
Time / hours: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120
Fungal biomass / g per dm³: 1, 6, 14, 20, 21, 21, 20
Penicillin / units per cm³: 0, 0, 2, 10, 22, 31, 35

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in biomass of the fungus over the 120 hours.
parts.answer: Biomass increases quickly from 1 g/dm³ to 20 g/dm³ by 60 hours; then levels off at about 21 g/dm³ and falls slightly to 20 g/dm³ by 120 hours.
parts.working: B1 rapid increase then levels off; B1 data quoted with units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of penicillin production, in units per cm³ per hour, between 60 and 100 hours.
parts.answer: 0.525 units per cm³ per hour

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why most of the penicillin is produced after 60 hours.
parts.answer: Penicillin is made mainly when growth of the fungus has slowed; this happens when nutrients such as glucose start to run out.
parts.working: B1 produced after main growth phase; B1 when nutrients become limiting

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the fermentation is stopped at about 120 hours.
parts.answer: Penicillin production is slowing / nutrients are used up / the fungus is starting to die, so further time is not worth the cost.

practice.stem: A fermenter is started with 50 bacteria. In ideal conditions this species of bacterium divides once every 20 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many bacteria would be present after 4 hours, assuming every cell divides every 20 minutes.
parts.answer: 204 800 bacteria

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the number of bacteria in a real fermenter does not keep increasing at this rate.
parts.answer: Nutrients are used up; waste products (e.g. acids, toxins) build up and change pH; oxygen may become limiting/overcrowding; so the rate of division slows and some cells die.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: nutrients run out; toxic waste builds up; pH changes; oxygen/space limiting; death rate rises

practice.stem:
A student mixed 50 g of flour, 2 g of dried yeast and different masses of sugar with 30 cm³ of warm water. Each dough was pushed to the bottom of a measuring cylinder and the increase in volume was measured after 30 minutes.
Mass of sugar / g: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
Increase in volume / cm³: 4, 12, 20, 24, 25

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of sugar mass on the increase in dough volume.
parts.answer: As the mass of sugar increases the volume increase rises, from 4 cm³ with no sugar to 24 cm³ at 6 g; above 6 g it levels off (25 cm³ at 8 g).
parts.working: B1 increases then levels off; B1 data quoted with units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in volume, in cm³ per minute, for the dough with 4 g of sugar. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.67 cm³ per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the dough with no sugar still increased in volume a little.
parts.answer: Yeast respired some sugars already in the flour (made from starch by amylase).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why increasing the sugar from 6 g to 8 g had little effect.
parts.answer: Sugar is no longer the limiting factor; another factor such as the amount of yeast or temperature limits the rate of respiration.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Describe how the student could keep the temperature the same for all the cylinders.
parts.answer: Stand all the cylinders in the same thermostatically controlled water bath (e.g. at 35 °C).

parts.label: f
parts.text: Suggest one improvement to make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat each sugar mass three times and calculate a mean.

practice.stem: A company grows genetically modified bacteria in a 10 000 dm³ fermenter. At the end of a batch the broth contains 1.2 g of insulin per dm³. Only 70% of this insulin is recovered when it is purified.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of purified insulin, in kg, obtained from one batch.
parts.answer: 8.4 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the contents of the fermenter are stirred continuously.
parts.answer: Mixes nutrients so all bacteria can obtain them; spreads oxygen evenly for aerobic respiration; spreads heat evenly so there are no hot spots that denature enzymes; keeps bacteria suspended.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why probes for pH and temperature are connected to a computer.
parts.answer: So that changes are detected quickly and corrected automatically, keeping conditions at the optimum.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is meant by genetic modification?
A changing the genetic material of an organism by removing, changing or inserting individual genes
B choosing parents with useful features and breeding them over many generations
C producing genetically identical offspring by asexual reproduction
D a random change in the base sequence of DNA
parts.answer: A changing the genetic material of an organism by removing, changing or inserting individual genes
parts.working: Genetic modification alters individual genes directly. B describes selective breeding, which works with whole organisms over many generations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three examples of genetic modification.
parts.answer: Any three of: bacteria producing human insulin; crop plants resistant to herbicides; crop plants resistant to insect pests; crops with added vitamins (e.g. rice containing β-carotene).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a plasmid.
parts.answer: A small circle (loop) of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main chromosome.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a recombinant plasmid.
parts.answer: A plasmid that contains a gene from another organism inserted into it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of enzyme used to cut open a plasmid.
parts.answer: Restriction enzyme

practice.stem:
The steps below describe how bacteria are modified to make a human protein, but they are in the wrong order.
P – The human gene is cut out using a restriction enzyme.
Q – The modified bacteria multiply in a fermenter.
R – The gene is joined into the plasmid using DNA ligase.
S – A plasmid is cut open with the same restriction enzyme.
T – The protein is extracted and purified.
U – The recombinant plasmid is put into a bacterium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put steps P to U in the correct order, starting with P.
parts.answer: P, S, R, U, Q, T
parts.working: 3 marks all correct; 2 marks one step out of place; 1 mark two steps out of place

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In genetic modification, which enzyme joins a human gene into a bacterial plasmid?
A restriction enzyme
B DNA ligase
C amylase
D protease
parts.answer: B DNA ligase
parts.working: DNA ligase joins the sticky ends of the gene and plasmid together. Restriction enzymes (A) cut DNA; they do not join it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how bacteria can be genetically modified to produce human insulin.
parts.answer: The human insulin gene is cut out of human DNA using a restriction enzyme; this leaves sticky ends; a bacterial plasmid is cut with the same restriction enzyme; the gene is inserted into the plasmid and joined with DNA ligase; forming a recombinant plasmid; the plasmid is taken up by bacteria; the bacteria multiply in a fermenter and express the gene, making insulin which is extracted and purified.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: restriction enzyme cuts out gene; sticky ends; plasmid cut with same enzyme; ligase joins; recombinant plasmid; inserted into bacteria; bacteria multiply/fermenter; gene expressed/insulin produced and purified

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the same restriction enzyme must be used to cut both the human DNA and the plasmid.
parts.answer: It produces matching (complementary) sticky ends; so the bases on the gene and plasmid pair up and can be joined.
parts.working: B1 same/complementary sticky ends; B1 bases pair so they join

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a sticky end.
parts.answer: A short single-stranded length of DNA (unpaired bases) left at the end of a cut piece of DNA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how growing herbicide-resistant soya benefits a farmer.
parts.answer: The farmer can spray herbicide over the whole field to kill weeds without killing the crop; so less competition for light, water and ions and a higher yield.
parts.working: B1 herbicide kills weeds not crop; B1 less competition → higher yield

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one risk of growing herbicide-resistant crops.
parts.answer: The resistance gene could spread by pollen to wild relatives producing herbicide-resistant weeds (or more herbicide used, harming other plants and reducing biodiversity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'GM bacteria make human insulin because they have human DNA inside them.' Explain what else must happen for the bacterium to make insulin.
parts.answer: The inserted gene must be expressed: the bacterium copies (transcribes) the gene and uses the code to join amino acids in the right order at its ribosomes, forming the insulin protein.
parts.working: B1 gene expressed/code read; B1 amino acids joined in correct sequence at ribosomes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why bacteria, rather than human cells, are used to produce insulin on a large scale.
parts.answer: Bacteria reproduce very rapidly, so large numbers are produced quickly; they are easy and cheap to grow in fermenters (few ethical concerns).
parts.working: B1 rapid reproduction; B1 cheap/easy to grow / no ethical concerns

practice.stem:
Cotton plants have been genetically modified to make a protein that is toxic to caterpillars which feed on them. Data from one cotton-growing district:
Before GM cotton: 12 insecticide sprays per season; yield 1.9 tonnes per ha
After GM cotton: 5 insecticide sprays per season; yield 2.4 tonnes per ha

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the number of sprays and the percentage increase in yield. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Sprays: 58.3% decrease; yield: 26.3% increase

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of growing insect-resistant genetically modified crops.
parts.answer: Advantages: less insecticide needed, saving money and reducing harm to farmers' health; fewer non-pest insects killed; higher yields/less crop damage, more food or income. Disadvantages: seeds may be expensive and must be bought each year; pests may evolve resistance to the toxin; genes may spread to wild relatives; reduced biodiversity if a single crop variety is grown widely; possible effects on non-target insects or on health not fully known.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side. 1 mark each for any six points across both sides: less insecticide; lower cost of spraying; safer for farmers/environment; higher yield; seed cost; pest resistance evolves; gene transfer to wild plants; reduced biodiversity; unknown long-term effects

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why rice has been genetically modified to contain β-carotene.
parts.answer: In some countries rice is the main food and people lack vitamin A; the body converts β-carotene into vitamin A, so the rice helps prevent vitamin A deficiency (which damages eyesight).
parts.working: B1 rice staple / diet lacks vitamin A; B1 β-carotene converted to vitamin A

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two concerns some people have about growing this rice.
parts.answer: Any two of: genes could transfer to wild rice varieties; farmers may depend on seed companies; effects on health not fully tested; reduced variety of crops grown; people may still lack other nutrients.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one alternative way of reducing vitamin A deficiency.
parts.answer: Encourage eating a varied diet with vegetables such as carrots and green leafy vegetables / vitamin supplements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before GM bacteria were used, insulin for people with diabetes was extracted from the pancreases of cattle and pigs. Explain the advantages of insulin produced by GM bacteria.
parts.answer: It is identical to human insulin, so fewer allergic reactions/side effects; it can be produced in large quantities; it is cheaper/supply does not depend on slaughtered animals; it avoids ethical and religious objections (e.g. pig products for Muslims, cattle products for Hindus).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a human gene can produce human insulin inside a bacterium.
parts.answer: The genetic code is the same (universal) in all organisms; the bacterium reads the same base triplets and joins the same amino acids in the same order.
parts.working: B1 genetic code universal; B1 same amino acid sequence made

practice.stem:
A trial compared genetically modified insect-resistant maize with non-GM maize.
Plants damaged by stem borer: GM field 3%; non-GM field 28%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in plants damaged by the stem borer in the GM field compared with the non-GM field. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why 3% of the GM plants were still damaged.
parts.answer: Some borers may be resistant to the toxin / some plants made less toxin / borers moved in from nearby non-GM plants.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Farmers are told to plant a strip of non-GM maize beside their GM maize. Explain how this slows down the evolution of resistance in the stem borer.
parts.answer: Non-resistant borers survive on the non-GM maize; they mate with any rare resistant borers from the GM field; so the resistance allele is diluted / resistant borers do not only breed with each other, and the allele does not increase quickly in frequency.
parts.working: B1 non-resistant borers survive in strip; B1 mate with resistant ones; B1 frequency of resistance allele rises more slowly

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which events happen when a person breathes in at rest?
A diaphragm contracts and flattens; external intercostal muscles contract
B diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards; external intercostal muscles contract
C diaphragm contracts and flattens; internal intercostal muscles contract
D diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards; internal intercostal muscles relax
parts.answer: A diaphragm contracts and flattens; external intercostal muscles contract
parts.working: In inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the external intercostals contract to pull the ribs up and out. B is wrong because a relaxed, domed diaphragm happens in expiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the movements of the diaphragm and the ribs when a person breathes in.
parts.answer: The diaphragm contracts and flattens (moves down); the ribs move upwards and outwards.
parts.working: B1 diaphragm contracts/flattens; B1 ribs up and out

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these movements cause air to enter the lungs.
parts.answer: The volume of the thorax increases; so the pressure inside falls below atmospheric pressure; air moves in through the trachea down the pressure gradient.
parts.working: B1 volume increases; B1 pressure decreases (below atmospheric); B1 air flows in from higher to lower pressure

parts.label: a
parts.text: List, in order, the structures that air passes through from the larynx to the alveoli.
parts.answer: Trachea → bronchus → bronchioles → alveoli
parts.working: 2 marks all in correct order; 1 mark if one error

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the rings of cartilage in the trachea.
parts.answer: Keep the trachea open (stop it collapsing) when air pressure inside falls.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the cartilage rings are C-shaped and not complete circles.
parts.answer: So the oesophagus behind the trachea can expand when food is swallowed (and the trachea stays flexible).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how air is breathed out when a person is resting.
parts.answer: External intercostal muscles and diaphragm relax; ribs move down and in and the diaphragm domes upwards (elastic recoil of lungs), so volume decreases and pressure rises, pushing air out.
parts.working: B1 muscles relax/ribs down and in/diaphragm domes up; B1 volume decreases, pressure increases, air out

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how breathing out is different when a trumpet player blows hard into the instrument.
parts.answer: The internal intercostal muscles contract; pulling the ribs down and in more forcefully; abdominal muscles contract pushing the diaphragm further up; so volume falls more and pressure rises more, forcing air out faster.
parts.working: B1 internal intercostals contract; B1 ribs pulled down and in; B1 abdominal muscles contract/push diaphragm up; max 3

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the relationship between the actions of the internal and external intercostal muscles.
parts.answer: They are antagonistic (when one contracts the other relaxes).

practice.stem: A model of the chest is made from a glass bell jar. A Y-shaped glass tube passes through a bung in the top and two balloons are attached to the branches inside the jar. The open bottom of the jar is covered by a stretched rubber sheet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which part of the human body is represented by: the balloons; the rubber sheet; the bell jar.
parts.answer: Balloons – lungs; rubber sheet – diaphragm; bell jar – rib cage / thorax (chest wall)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe and explain what happens to the balloons when the rubber sheet is pulled down.
parts.answer: The balloons inflate; because the volume inside the jar increases; so the pressure falls and air enters the balloons through the tube from the atmosphere.
parts.working: B1 balloons inflate; B1 volume in jar increases/pressure falls; B1 air enters from outside

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which the model does not show breathing accurately.
parts.answer: The bell jar is rigid so it cannot show rib movement (or the rubber sheet is pulled down, not domed and contracting; no intercostal muscles; balloons are not like alveoli).

practice.stem:
Five students counted their breaths for one minute at rest and again immediately after 2 minutes of skipping.
At rest: 14, 16, 12, 15, 13
After skipping: 27, 31, 24, 30, 26

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean breathing rate at rest and after exercise.
parts.answer: At rest: 14.0 breaths per minute; after exercise: 27.6 breaths per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean breathing rate after exercise. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student counted breaths for one full minute rather than for 10 seconds.
parts.answer: A longer count reduces the error of starting or stopping in the middle of a breath / more accurate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept the same for each student.
parts.answer: Any two of: type of exercise; duration of exercise (2 minutes); intensity/speed; time between stopping and counting; resting before the first count; same person counting.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains why air moves into the lungs when we breathe in?
A The volume of the thorax increases so the pressure inside falls below atmospheric pressure.
B The lungs expand by themselves and pull the ribs outwards.
C The pressure inside the thorax rises above atmospheric pressure.
D The diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards, sucking air in.
parts.answer: A The volume of the thorax increases so the pressure inside falls below atmospheric pressure.
parts.working: Muscle contraction increases thorax volume, lowering pressure, so air flows in from the higher atmospheric pressure. D describes breathing out, not in.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rate and depth of breathing increase during a football match.
parts.answer: Muscles contract more so they respire faster; producing more carbon dioxide which enters the blood; the increased carbon dioxide concentration in the blood is detected by the brain; the brain sends more nerve impulses to the intercostal muscles and diaphragm; so more oxygen is supplied for aerobic respiration and carbon dioxide is removed faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: more respiration in muscles; more CO₂ in blood; detected by brain; impulses to diaphragm/intercostals; more O₂ for aerobic respiration; CO₂ removed faster; (any anaerobic respiration/oxygen debt reference)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why breathing rate stays high for some minutes after the match ends.
parts.answer: Lactic acid made by anaerobic respiration must be broken down/removed; this needs extra oxygen (oxygen debt), so fast breathing continues.
parts.working: B1 lactic acid/oxygen debt; B1 extra oxygen needed to break down lactic acid in liver

practice.stem:
A trace of a person's lung volume was recorded.
At rest: highest point of each breath 3.1 dm³, lowest point 2.6 dm³, 15 breaths per minute.
During exercise: highest point 4.0 dm³, lowest point 2.4 dm³, 24 breaths per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of air breathed in with each breath (the tidal volume) at rest and during exercise.
parts.answer: At rest: 0.5 dm³; during exercise: 1.6 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total volume of air breathed in per minute at rest and during exercise.
parts.answer: At rest: 7.5 dm³ per minute; during exercise: 38.4 dm³ per minute
parts.working: M1 tidal volume × breaths per minute; A1 both

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the advantage of the change in breathing during exercise.
parts.answer: More air reaches the alveoli per minute, so more oxygen diffuses into the blood for aerobic respiration in muscles; and more carbon dioxide is removed.
parts.working: B1 more oxygen into blood for respiration; B1 more CO₂ removed

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the intensity of exercise affects the breathing rate of students. Include the method, the variables to control, how you would make the results reliable and any safety precautions.
parts.answer: Use stepping on/off a step at different rates (e.g. 10, 20, 30 steps per minute) set with a metronome for a fixed time (e.g. 3 minutes); measure resting breathing rate first and let it return to resting between trials; count breaths for 1 minute immediately after each exercise; keep same step height, same duration, same students (similar age/fitness), same time after exercise before counting; repeat for several students/three times and calculate means; safety: students with asthma or heart conditions do not take part / stop if dizzy.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: method of varying intensity; at least 3 intensities; fixed duration; resting rate measured / return to resting; breaths counted for 1 minute straight after; two controlled variables (B1 each, max 2); repeats/means; one safety point

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is NOT a feature of an efficient gas exchange surface?
A a large surface area
B a thin surface
C a good blood supply
D a thick layer of mucus over the surface
parts.answer: D a thick layer of mucus over the surface
parts.working: A thick layer of mucus would increase the diffusion distance. The alveolar surface is moist, but only with a thin film of fluid; A, B and C are all features that speed up diffusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four features of the gas exchange surface in human lungs.
parts.answer: Large surface area (many alveoli); thin walls (one cell thick); good blood supply (many capillaries); good ventilation with air; moist surface.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of the capillaries surrounding each alveolus.
parts.answer: To take up oxygen from and give carbon dioxide to the alveolus / carry blood close to the alveolus for gas exchange.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the inside surface of each alveolus is moist.
parts.answer: Gases dissolve in the moisture before diffusing across the wall.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that brings deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
parts.answer: Pulmonary artery

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how oxygen moves from the air in an alveolus into a red blood cell.
parts.answer: Oxygen dissolves in the moisture lining the alveolus; diffuses through the thin alveolar wall and capillary wall; into the plasma and red blood cell where it combines with haemoglobin.
parts.working: B1 dissolves in moisture; B1 diffusion across alveolus and capillary walls; B1 into red blood cell/joins haemoglobin

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a steep concentration gradient of oxygen is maintained between the alveoli and the blood.
parts.answer: Breathing (ventilation) keeps bringing fresh air with a high oxygen concentration into the alveoli; blood flow carries oxygenated blood away; and brings deoxygenated blood with low oxygen concentration to the alveoli.
parts.working: B1 ventilation brings fresh air; B1 blood removes oxygen; B1 deoxygenated blood continually arrives

practice.stem: In a photomicrograph of lung tissue magnified 120 times, one alveolus measures 30 mm across.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the alveolus in µm.
parts.answer: 250 µm
parts.working: M1 actual = image ÷ magnification = 30 ÷ 120 = 0.25 mm; A1 × 1000 = 250 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: The wall of the alveolus is made of a single layer of flattened cells. Explain the advantage of this.
parts.answer: Short diffusion distance; so oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse quickly between the air and the blood.
parts.working: B1 short distance; B1 faster diffusion

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why having millions of small alveoli is better than having a few large air sacs.
parts.answer: Many small alveoli give a much larger total surface area (for the same volume of lung); so more gas exchange can take place.
parts.working: B1 larger total surface area; B1 more diffusion/gas exchange

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row describes the movement of gases by diffusion in the alveoli?
A oxygen: alveolus air → blood; carbon dioxide: blood → alveolus air
B oxygen: blood → alveolus air; carbon dioxide: alveolus air → blood
C oxygen and carbon dioxide: both alveolus air → blood
D oxygen and carbon dioxide: both blood → alveolus air
parts.answer: A oxygen: alveolus air → blood; carbon dioxide: blood → alveolus air
parts.working: Oxygen is at a higher concentration in alveolar air and diffuses into the blood; carbon dioxide is at a higher concentration in the blood and diffuses out. B reverses both directions.

practice.stem: A student models organisms of different sizes as cubes with sides of 1 cm, 2 cm and 4 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of each cube.
parts.answer: 1 cm cube 6 : 1; 2 cm cube 3 : 1; 4 cm cube 1.5 : 1
parts.working: M1 surface area = 6 × side²; M1 volume = side³; A1 all three ratios

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why a large animal such as a buffalo needs lungs, while a single-celled organism does not.
parts.answer: As size increases, the surface area to volume ratio decreases; the body surface of a large animal is too small for its volume to absorb enough oxygen by diffusion and the distances to inner cells are too great; lungs provide a very large internal surface area.
parts.working: B1 larger size → smaller SA:V; B1 surface not enough to supply volume / diffusion distance too long; B1 lungs give large surface area

practice.stem: A climber travels from Karachi, at sea level, to a base camp at 5000 m in the Karakoram mountains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why there is less oxygen available to the body in a visitor to a high mountain base camp than at sea level.
parts.answer: Air at high altitude has a lower pressure, so each breath contains less oxygen; the concentration gradient between the alveoli and the blood is smaller; so less oxygen diffuses into the blood.
parts.working: B1 less oxygen per breath / lower air pressure; B1 smaller concentration gradient; B1 slower diffusion into blood

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the visitor's breathing changes when they first arrive, and why.
parts.answer: Breathing becomes faster and deeper; to bring more air (oxygen) into the alveoli per minute.
parts.working: B1 faster/deeper; B1 more oxygen into alveoli/maintain gradient

practice.stem: Blood arriving at the lungs at rest contains 10.0 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³ of blood. Blood leaving the lungs contains 19.5 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³ of blood.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen taken up by each 100 cm³ of blood as it passes through the lungs.
parts.answer: 9.5 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: At rest, 5 dm³ (5000 cm³) of blood passes through the lungs each minute. Calculate the volume of oxygen taken up by the blood per minute.
parts.answer: 475 cm³ per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: During exercise the blood flow increases to 20 dm³ per minute and blood arrives at the lungs with only 5.0 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³. Assuming it still leaves with 19.5 cm³ per 100 cm³, calculate the oxygen taken up per minute.
parts.answer: 2900 cm³ per minute

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why blood arriving at the lungs during exercise contains less oxygen.
parts.answer: Muscles use more oxygen in respiration, so more oxygen is removed from the blood in the tissues.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row gives the approximate percentages of oxygen and carbon dioxide in expired air?
A oxygen 21%; carbon dioxide 0.04%
B oxygen 16%; carbon dioxide 4%
C oxygen 4%; carbon dioxide 16%
D oxygen 21%; carbon dioxide 4%
parts.answer: B oxygen 16%; carbon dioxide 4%
parts.working: Expired air still contains about 16% oxygen and about 4% carbon dioxide. A is inspired (atmospheric) air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three differences between inspired air and expired air.
parts.answer: Expired air contains less oxygen; more carbon dioxide; more water vapour; and is warmer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three (comparative words needed)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why expired air contains more carbon dioxide than inspired air.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide is produced by respiration in cells; it diffuses from the blood into the alveoli and is breathed out.
parts.working: B1 made in respiration; B1 diffuses from blood into alveoli

practice.stem: A student set up two tubes, A and B, each containing 10 cm³ of limewater. They were connected so that when the student breathed in through a mouthpiece, air from the room bubbled through tube A, and when the student breathed out, expired air bubbled through tube B. Tube B turned milky after 15 seconds. Tube A was still clear after 3 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results in tube B.
parts.answer: Expired air contains a high concentration of carbon dioxide (about 4%); carbon dioxide turns limewater milky (cloudy).
parts.working: B1 more CO₂ in expired air; B1 CO₂ turns limewater milky

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why tube A stayed clear for much longer.
parts.answer: Inspired air contains very little carbon dioxide (about 0.04%).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one thing the student should do to make the comparison fair.
parts.answer: Use the same volume (and concentration) of limewater in each tube / breathe at the same rate and depth.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Hydrogencarbonate indicator could be used instead of limewater. State the colour it would turn in tube B.
parts.answer: Yellow

practice.stem:
A student breathed out through 5 cm³ of limewater and timed how long it took to turn milky. This was done three times at rest and three times immediately after running for 3 minutes.
At rest / s: 45, 41, 43
After running / s: 19, 23, 18

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean time for the limewater to turn milky at rest and after exercise.
parts.answer: At rest: 43.0 s; after exercise: 20.0 s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the two mean times.
parts.answer: During exercise muscles respire faster; more carbon dioxide is produced and carried to the lungs; so expired air contains more carbon dioxide (and more is breathed out per second) and the limewater goes milky sooner.
parts.working: B1 faster respiration; B1 more CO₂ in blood/expired air; B1 limewater turns milky faster

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is difficult to judge exactly when the limewater turns milky, and one way to improve this.
parts.answer: The change is gradual so the end point is subjective; compare against a standard tube of milky limewater / use a black card behind the tube / use a cross under the tube.
parts.working: B1 gradual/subjective end point; B1 valid improvement

practice.stem: At rest, a person breathes 8 dm³ of air per minute. Inspired air contains 21% oxygen and expired air contains 16% oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen absorbed by the body each minute and in one hour.
parts.answer: 0.4 dm³ per minute; 24 dm³ per hour
parts.working: M1 21% − 16% = 5%; M1 0.05 × 8 dm³ = 0.4 dm³; A1 24 dm³ per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why expired air still contains so much oxygen.
parts.answer: Some inspired air stays in the trachea and bronchi and never reaches the alveoli; air is in the alveoli only for a short time, so not all the oxygen diffuses into the blood.
parts.working: B1 air in airways not involved in gas exchange (dead space); B1 short time in alveoli / mixing with air already in lungs

practice.stem:
Inspired air contains 0.04% carbon dioxide.
At rest: expired air 4% carbon dioxide, 16% oxygen; volume breathed 7.5 dm³ per minute
During exercise: expired air 5% carbon dioxide, 15% oxygen; volume breathed 60 dm³ per minute

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide added to the air breathed out per minute at rest and during exercise. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: At rest: 0.297 dm³ per minute; during exercise: 2.98 dm³ per minute
parts.working: M1 percentage difference (4 − 0.04 = 3.96%; 5 − 0.04 = 4.96%); M1 × volume per minute; A1 both

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the expired air contains a lower percentage of oxygen during exercise.
parts.answer: Muscle cells respire faster and use more oxygen; blood returning to the lungs has less oxygen, so more oxygen diffuses into the blood from the alveoli.
parts.working: B1 more oxygen used in respiration; B1 steeper gradient/more oxygen removed from alveolar air

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which component of tobacco smoke reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry?
A tar
B nicotine
C carbon monoxide
D smoke particles
parts.answer: C carbon monoxide
parts.working: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells, so less oxygen is carried. Nicotine (B) is the addictive drug but does not block haemoglobin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the component of tobacco smoke that: (i) is addictive; (ii) causes cancer.
parts.answer: (i) nicotine; (ii) tar

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two diseases of the gas exchange system caused by smoking.
parts.answer: Any two of: lung cancer; chronic bronchitis; emphysema; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the roles of goblet cells and ciliated cells in the trachea.
parts.answer: Goblet cells secrete mucus; mucus traps dust and pathogens (bacteria); cilia beat/sweep the mucus up to the throat where it is swallowed.
parts.working: B1 goblet cells make mucus; B1 mucus traps particles/pathogens; B1 cilia move mucus up/away from lungs

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many smokers have a persistent cough and frequent chest infections.
parts.answer: Chemicals in smoke damage/paralyse the cilia; mucus is not removed and builds up in the airways; coughing is the only way to remove it; bacteria trapped in the mucus multiply, causing infections (chronic bronchitis).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: cilia damaged/stop beating; mucus accumulates (more mucus made); cough to clear mucus; bacteria breed in mucus/infection

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to the alveoli in emphysema.
parts.answer: The walls of the alveoli break down; neighbouring alveoli merge into fewer, larger air spaces (and the lungs lose elasticity).
parts.working: B1 alveolar walls break down; B1 fewer larger spaces / loss of elasticity

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person with emphysema becomes breathless even when walking slowly.
parts.answer: The surface area for gas exchange is reduced; so less oxygen diffuses into the blood; muscles do not get enough oxygen for aerobic respiration, so the person breathes faster to compensate.
parts.working: B1 smaller surface area; B1 less oxygen absorbed; B1 not enough O₂ for respiration / breathe faster

practice.stem:
A 20-year study of adults recorded deaths from lung cancer per 100 000 people per year.
Non-smokers: 10
1–14 cigarettes per day: 78
15–24 cigarettes per day: 127
25 or more cigarettes per day: 251

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the death rate is for people who smoke 25 or more cigarettes a day than for non-smokers.
parts.answer: 25.1 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown by the data.
parts.answer: The more cigarettes smoked per day, the higher the death rate from lung cancer; e.g. 10 per 100 000 for non-smokers rising to 251 per 100 000 for 25 or more a day.
parts.working: B1 positive correlation; B1 data quoted with units

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how tar in cigarette smoke can lead to lung cancer.
parts.answer: Tar contains carcinogens; they cause mutations in cells lining the airways, leading to uncontrolled cell division and a tumour.
parts.working: B1 carcinogen/causes mutation; B1 uncontrolled cell division/tumour

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why some non-smokers still die of lung cancer.
parts.answer: Other causes such as breathing other people's smoke (passive smoking), air pollution, radon or inherited factors.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the best definition of a drug?
A any substance that kills bacteria
B any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
C any substance prescribed by a doctor
D any substance that is addictive
parts.answer: B any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
parts.working: A drug is any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body; this covers medicines and misused drugs. A is too narrow because it describes only antibiotics.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For which disease would a course of antibiotics NOT be effective?
A cholera
B influenza
C tuberculosis
D typhoid
parts.answer: B influenza
parts.working: Influenza is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not affect viruses. Cholera, tuberculosis and typhoid are bacterial diseases, so the other options are treated with antibiotics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the inoculating loop is heated in a Bunsen flame until it glows red before and after use.
parts.answer: To kill any microorganisms on it, so the plate is not contaminated (and no bacteria escape afterwards).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lid of the Petri dish is held with two short pieces of tape and not sealed all the way round.
parts.answer: Oxygen can still enter, so harmful anaerobic bacteria are not encouraged to grow; the lid cannot be opened accidentally.
parts.working: B1 allows oxygen in / prevents anaerobic conditions; B1 lid stays shut.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why plates in a school laboratory are incubated at 25 °C and not at 37 °C.
parts.answer: At 37 °C (body temperature) bacteria that cause disease in humans could grow.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the plates must not be opened after incubation.
parts.answer: Large numbers of bacteria have grown, which could include harmful ones; opening would release them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what an antibiotic is.
parts.answer: A drug (medicine) that kills bacteria or stops their growth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A patient with a cold asks a doctor in Islamabad for antibiotics. The doctor refuses. Explain why.
parts.answer: Colds are caused by viruses; antibiotics do not affect viruses (they work on structures / processes found in bacteria), so they would not help and would increase the risk of resistance.
parts.working: B1 cold caused by virus; B1 antibiotics have no effect on viruses (or unnecessary use leads to resistance).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of organism from which penicillin was first obtained.
parts.answer: a fungus (mould), Penicillium

parts.label: a
parts.text: Antibiotics can kill bacteria inside the human body without harming human cells. Suggest why.
parts.answer: They act on structures or processes found in bacterial cells but not in human cells, such as the bacterial cell wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two examples of medicinal drugs other than antibiotics and what each is used for.
parts.answer: e.g. painkillers (paracetamol) to relieve pain / fever; insulin to treat diabetes. Any two medicinal drugs with a correct use.
parts.working: B1 each drug with correct use.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why antibiotics should not be shared with a friend who has similar symptoms.
parts.answer: The friend's illness may be caused by a virus or a different bacterium; the dose may be wrong; incomplete courses for both encourage resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Poultry farms sometimes add small amounts of antibiotics to chicken feed to keep the birds healthy and growing quickly. Explain why this practice can be a risk to human health.
parts.answer: Constant low doses kill susceptible bacteria and select for resistant ones; resistant bacteria multiply in the chickens; they can pass to humans through meat or the environment, so human infections become harder to treat.
parts.working: B1 selection for resistance; B1 resistant bacteria increase in the animals; B1 transfer to humans / antibiotics less effective for people.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one alternative way the farmer could keep the chickens healthy.
parts.answer: Vaccinate the birds; keep sheds clean; give birds more space; use antibiotics only to treat sick birds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an antibiotic-resistant bacterium.
parts.answer: A bacterium that is not killed (and keeps growing) when exposed to the antibiotic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why antibiotic resistance is a serious problem for the world.
parts.answer: Infections that were easy to treat may become untreatable; more people die / stay ill longer; surgery and cancer treatment become riskier; few new antibiotics are being discovered; more expensive treatments needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why some antibiotics are kept by doctors only for patients for whom other antibiotics have failed.
parts.answer: If used rarely, bacteria are less likely to become resistant to them, so they keep working.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal has a painful tooth infection caused by bacteria. His dentist gives him paracetamol and an antibiotic. State the purpose of each drug.
parts.answer: Paracetamol: a painkiller that relieves the pain (a symptom). Antibiotic: kills the bacteria causing the infection (or stops their growth).
parts.working: B1 paracetamol relieves pain / symptoms; B1 antibiotic kills bacteria / treats the cause.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the paracetamol alone would not cure the infection.
parts.answer: It only reduces pain; it does not kill the bacteria.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The dentist tells Bilal to take the antibiotic at regular times each day. Suggest why.
parts.answer: To keep the concentration of antibiotic in the blood high enough to kill the bacteria all the time.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Paper discs soaked in four different antibiotics were placed on agar covered with the same bacteria. After incubation the diameters of the clear zones were:
W: 8 mm
X: 22 mm
Y: 15 mm
Z: no clear zone
Which antibiotic would be most useful against these bacteria?
A W
B X
C Y
D Z
parts.answer: B X
parts.working: The largest clear zone shows that the most bacteria were killed or stopped from growing, so X is most effective. Z had no clear zone; the bacteria are resistant to it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which sequence describes how a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic?
A antibiotic used → bacteria learn to resist it → all bacteria pass on the learned resistance
B random mutation gives resistance → antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria → resistant bacteria reproduce
C antibiotic causes mutation for resistance → resistant bacteria die → non-resistant bacteria reproduce
D antibiotic used → bacteria form antibodies → antibodies passed to offspring
parts.answer: B random mutation gives resistance → antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria → resistant bacteria reproduce
parts.working: Resistance arises by random mutation; the antibiotic acts as a selection pressure, so resistant bacteria survive and reproduce (natural selection). A is wrong because bacteria do not 'learn' resistance; it is genetic.

practice.stem:
A student spread a harmless bacterium on a nutrient agar plate and placed five paper discs (6 mm diameter) on it. Four discs were soaked in different antibiotics and one in sterile water. After two days at 25 °C the diameters of the clear zones were measured.
penicillin 26 mm; streptomycin 18 mm; tetracycline 30 mm; erythromycin 12 mm; sterile water: no clear zone beyond the disc.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the area of the clear zone around each antibiotic disc in mm², using area = πr². Give each answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: penicillin 531 mm²; streptomycin 254 mm²; tetracycline 707 mm²; erythromycin 113 mm²
parts.working: M1 radius = diameter ÷ 2; A2 all four correct (A1 for two or three): π × 13², π × 9², π × 15², π × 6².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rank the antibiotics from most to least effective against this bacterium.
parts.answer: tetracycline > penicillin > streptomycin > erythromycin

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the disc soaked in sterile water.
parts.answer: It is a control; it shows that the clear zones are caused by the antibiotics and not by the paper disc or the water.
parts.working: B1 control; B1 shows effect is due to antibiotic.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two precautions the student should take to avoid contaminating the plate or himself.
parts.answer: Flame the forceps / loop; open the lid only slightly and briefly; tape the lid (do not seal fully) and do not open after incubation; wash hands; incubate at no more than 25 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the use of an antibiotic can lead to a population of bacteria that is resistant to it.
parts.answer: A random mutation makes some bacteria resistant; the antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria; the resistant bacteria survive and reproduce; the resistance gene is passed on so the proportion of resistant bacteria rises (natural selection).
parts.working: B1 mutation / variation; B1 non-resistant killed; B1 resistant survive and reproduce; B1 allele / gene passed on, population becomes resistant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why bacteria can become resistant much faster than animals become adapted to a new condition.
parts.answer: Bacteria reproduce very quickly (some divide every 20 minutes), so many generations occur in a short time; large populations mean more mutations.
parts.working: B1 rapid reproduction / short generation time; B1 large numbers so more mutations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: MRSA is a type of bacterium found in some hospitals. State what is unusual about MRSA.
parts.answer: It is resistant to many (most commonly used) antibiotics.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three ways in which doctors, hospitals and patients can reduce the development and spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
parts.answer: Only prescribe antibiotics when needed (not for viral infections); patients complete the course; use a range of different antibiotics; good hygiene such as hand washing and cleaning wards; isolate infected patients.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why antibiotic resistance is a bigger danger in hospitals than in most homes.
parts.answer: Many patients are ill or have weak immune systems; antibiotics are used a lot so resistant bacteria are selected; bacteria spread easily between patients.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bacterium divides into two every 20 minutes. Starting with one bacterium, calculate how many there would be after 3 hours if none die.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a patient's gut there are 5 × 10⁹ bacteria of one species. One in every 10 million of them carries a mutation for resistance to an antibiotic. Calculate the number of resistant bacteria.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why even a very rare mutation for resistance can quickly become a problem when the antibiotic is used.
parts.answer: There are already hundreds of resistant bacteria; when the antibiotic kills the others, these survive and, dividing every 20 minutes, soon form a large resistant population.
parts.working: B1 some resistant cells are present in a large population; B1 they survive and multiply rapidly.

practice.stem:
A student made garlic extract at 0 %, 25 %, 50 % and 100 % concentration and soaked 6 mm paper discs in each. The discs were placed on agar plates spread with bacteria. The diameter (in mm, including the disc) of the area with no bacterial growth was measured on three plates.
0 %: 6, 6, 6
25 %: 9, 10, 8
50 %: 12, 13, 14
100 %: 16, 18, 17

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean diameter for each concentration to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: A2 all four correct (A1 for two or three).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown by the results.
parts.answer: As the concentration of garlic extract increases, the clear zone gets larger.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the 0 % result is 6 mm and not 0 mm.
parts.answer: 6 mm is the diameter of the paper disc itself; there was no clear zone around it.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give two variables, other than those mentioned, that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Volume of extract on each disc; time discs soaked; type and amount of bacteria spread; temperature and time of incubation; depth / type of agar.

practice.stem:
A patient took an antibiotic for a bacterial infection. The doctor said to take it for 7 days, but the patient felt better and stopped after day 3. The number of bacteria in samples taken from the patient (per cm³) was:
day: 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7
bacteria per cm³: 8000, 3000, 900, 200, 600, 2500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in bacteria between day 0 and day 3. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the change in the number of bacteria after day 3.
parts.answer: The patient stopped taking the antibiotic while some bacteria were still alive; these survivors were likely the most resistant ones; they reproduced, so numbers rose again.
parts.working: B1 bacteria not all killed when course stopped; B1 survivors are more resistant; B1 they multiplied.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what the doctor might do now, and why.
parts.answer: Prescribe a different antibiotic, because the surviving bacteria may now be resistant to the first one.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A doctor tells a patient to finish the whole course of antibiotics even after she feels better. What is the main reason?
A Antibiotics also kill any viruses that are present.
B The bacteria that survive longest are the most resistant, and stopping early may let them multiply.
C The body needs time to make antibodies against the antibiotic.
D Unused antibiotics become poisonous after a few days.
