parts.answer: B The bacteria that survive longest are the most resistant, and stopping early may let them multiply.
parts.working: Stopping early leaves the most resistant bacteria alive; they can multiply and pass on resistance. C is wrong because antibodies are made against pathogens, not against antibiotics.

practice.stem:
The same antibiotic disc test was repeated on four plates.
clear-zone diameter / mm: plate 1: 21; plate 2: 23; plate 3: 14; plate 4: 22

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean clear-zone diameter without it. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: plate 3 (14 mm) is anomalous; mean = 22.0 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean if the anomalous result were included, and explain why it should be left out.
parts.answer: 20.0 mm; it is far from the other values and probably due to an error, so including it would make the mean too low.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two possible causes of the anomalous result.
parts.answer: Disc not soaked for the same time / less antibiotic on it; disc not pressed flat on the agar; more bacteria spread on that plate; plate incubated at a different temperature; diameter measured wrongly.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the zones were measured across two diameters at right angles and the values averaged.
parts.answer: The clear zones may not be perfect circles, so averaging two diameters gives a more accurate value.

practice.stem:
Samples of a gut bacterium were collected from patients in a large city. The percentage of samples that were resistant to one antibiotic was recorded.
year: 2014, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024
resistant samples / %: 18, 23, 31, 38, 46, 52

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend shown by the data.
parts.answer: The percentage of resistant samples increased every time, from 18 % in 2014 to 52 % in 2024.
parts.working: B1 increases throughout; B1 data quoted with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in percentage of resistant samples per year between 2014 and 2024.
parts.answer: 3.4 percentage points per year

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons for this trend.
parts.answer: Antibiotics bought without prescription / overused; patients not finishing courses; antibiotics used in animal feed; resistant bacteria spread through poor sanitation / contaminated water.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict, with a reason, the percentage of resistant samples in 2026 if the trend continues.
parts.answer: About 59 % (52 + 2 × 3.4 ≈ 59); accept 57–60 % with reference to the same rate of increase.
parts.working: B1 value in range with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A strain of typhoid bacteria that is resistant to most antibiotics has spread in some cities. Explain why this strain is dangerous.
parts.answer: Very few antibiotics can treat infected people, so the disease lasts longer and more people may die; the strain can spread to others.
parts.working: B1 few / no effective antibiotics; B1 more severe illness / deaths / spread.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Health workers vaccinated large numbers of children against typhoid. Explain how this helps to slow the spread of antibiotic resistance.
parts.answer: Vaccinated children become immune so fewer get typhoid; fewer cases need antibiotics, so less selection pressure for resistance; fewer infected people means less spread of resistant bacteria.
parts.working: B1 fewer infections; B1 fewer antibiotics used / less selection; B1 less transmission.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Typhoid spreads through contaminated food and water. Suggest one other measure, apart from vaccination, to reduce cases.
parts.answer: Clean, treated drinking water; boiling water; proper sewage disposal; hand washing; food hygiene.

practice.stem:
Paper discs (6 mm diameter) were soaked in different concentrations of an antibiotic and placed on agar covered with bacteria.
concentration / µg/cm³: 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16
diameter of clear area including disc / mm: 6, 6, 9, 13, 17, 21

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the lowest concentration of the antibiotic that had any effect on the bacteria. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: 2 µg/cm³; the zone is larger than the 6 mm disc only from 2 µg/cm³ upwards.
parts.working: B1 2 µg/cm³; B1 reason (6 mm = disc only).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the pattern in the results from 2 to 16 µg/cm³.
parts.answer: Each time the concentration doubles, the zone diameter increases by about 4 mm.
parts.working: B1 increases; B1 quantified (4 mm per doubling).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the zone diameter for 32 µg/cm³ if the pattern continues.
parts.answer: about 25 mm

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a doctor would want to know the lowest concentration that is effective.
parts.answer: So the dose given is high enough to kill the bacteria but not more than needed, reducing side effects and cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A clear zone has a diameter of 24 mm around a disc of diameter 6 mm. Calculate the area of agar where bacteria were killed, not counting the area under the disc. Give your answer in mm² to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 π × 12² for zone; M1 subtract π × 3²; A1 π × 135 = 424.1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the bacteria nearest the disc are killed while those further away are not.
parts.answer: The antibiotic diffuses out into the agar; its concentration falls with distance from the disc, so beyond a certain distance it is too dilute to kill bacteria.
parts.working: B1 diffusion from disc; B1 concentration decreases with distance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which describes heroin?
A an antibiotic
B a depressant that slows the activity of the nervous system
C a stimulant that speeds up the nervous system
D a hormone that builds muscle
parts.answer: B a depressant that slows the activity of the nervous system
parts.working: Heroin is a powerful, addictive depressant drug that slows down the activity of the nervous system. C describes a stimulant, the opposite effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the addictive drug in tobacco smoke.
parts.answer: nicotine

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two effects of nicotine on the circulatory system.
parts.answer: Increases heart rate; increases blood pressure; narrows blood vessels; makes blood more likely to clot.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why many smokers find it very hard to give up smoking even when they know it is harmful.
parts.answer: Nicotine is addictive; stopping causes withdrawal symptoms such as cravings and irritability.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why are some athletes banned from competition after taking anabolic steroids?
A Steroids reduce the athlete's pain from injuries.
B Steroids increase muscle growth, giving an unfair advantage.
C Steroids are antibiotics that prevent infection.
D Steroids reduce the athlete's heart rate during a race.
parts.answer: B Steroids increase muscle growth, giving an unfair advantage.
parts.working: Anabolic steroids are hormone-like drugs that increase muscle mass and strength, which is unfair to other competitors (and has health risks). A describes painkillers, not steroids.

practice.stem:
In a road-safety study in Europe, volunteers did a computer test of reaction time after drinking different amounts of alcohol.
units of alcohol: 0, 2, 4
mean reaction time / s: 0.21, 0.27, 0.36

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in reaction time after 4 units of alcohol compared with none. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A car travels at 20 m/s. Calculate how much further it travels during the driver's reaction time after 4 units than after 0 units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why alcohol increases reaction time.
parts.answer: Alcohol is a depressant; it slows the transmission of impulses in the nervous system (at synapses), so responses take longer.
parts.working: B1 depressant; B1 slows nerve impulses / synapses.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two long-term effects of drinking large amounts of alcohol.
parts.answer: Liver damage (cirrhosis); brain damage; addiction; increased risk of heart disease / high blood pressure; social problems (loss of job, violence, family problems).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by addiction to a drug such as heroin.
parts.answer: The body becomes dependent on the drug so the person feels a strong need to keep taking it; stopping causes withdrawal symptoms.
parts.working: B1 dependence / craving; B1 withdrawal symptoms when stopped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Heroin affects the nervous system at synapses. Suggest why a heroin user needs larger and larger doses to get the same effect.
parts.answer: The body becomes tolerant: the synapses / receptors adapt to the drug, so the same dose has less effect and more is needed.
parts.working: B1 tolerance; B1 nervous system / receptors adapt.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why injecting heroin increases the risk of HIV infection.
parts.answer: Users may share needles; blood containing the virus from an infected person is passed directly into the next person's blood.
parts.working: B1 shared needles; B1 infected blood enters bloodstream.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one social problem linked to heroin addiction.
parts.answer: Crime to pay for the drug; loss of job; family breakdown; homelessness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organ that breaks down alcohol in the body.
parts.answer: liver

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why people who drink large amounts of alcohol for many years often suffer liver damage.
parts.answer: Breaking down large amounts of alcohol damages liver cells; they are replaced by scar tissue (cirrhosis), so the liver cannot work properly.
parts.working: B1 liver cells damaged / killed by alcohol; B1 scar tissue / cirrhosis / reduced function.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two functions of the liver that would be affected by liver damage.
parts.answer: Breakdown of toxins / drugs; deamination of amino acids to form urea; storing glycogen; making bile; making plasma proteins.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Alcohol reduces self-control. Suggest one way this can harm a person or others.
parts.answer: Risky behaviour such as violence, unprotected sex or dangerous driving.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Anabolic steroids are similar in structure to a natural male sex hormone. Name this hormone and the organ that makes it.
parts.answer: testosterone; testes

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two harmful side effects of misusing anabolic steroids.
parts.answer: Liver damage; heart disease / high blood pressure; infertility; aggressive behaviour / mood changes; acne.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Athletes may be asked to give a urine sample at any time, not only on the day of a competition. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Steroids are often used during training to build muscle and then stopped before competitions so they are not detected; random testing catches this.
parts.working: B1 used in training / stopped before event; B1 random testing detects this.

practice.stem:
In one country the legal limit for driving is 80 mg of alcohol per 100 cm³ of blood. The table (figures for this question) shows the relative risk of a crash compared with a driver with no alcohol.
blood alcohol / mg per 100 cm³: 0, 50, 80, 100, 150
relative risk of crash: 1, 2, 4, 7, 25

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the risk of a crash is at 150 mg per 100 cm³ than at the legal limit of 80 mg per 100 cm³.
parts.answer: 6.25 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the risk changes as blood alcohol concentration increases.
parts.answer: The risk rises as blood alcohol rises; it rises slowly at first and then very steeply above about 100 mg per 100 cm³.
parts.working: B1 risk increases; B1 increase is faster at higher concentrations (with data).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some countries have lowered their limit to 50 mg per 100 cm³. Use the data to argue for this change.
parts.answer: At 50 mg the risk is 2 times, half the risk at 80 mg (4 times); lowering the limit could prevent many crashes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the risk of a crash increases.
parts.answer: Alcohol slows reaction time; it reduces judgement / self-control, so drivers take more risks.
parts.working: B1 slower reactions; B1 poor judgement / more risk-taking.
